### What did the AI answers get wrong?

Very little was clearly wrong. Two answers, both from Google AI Mode, contradicted the guideline or the usual course of the condition:

- Asked whether ultrasound therapy helps, one answer said ultrasound combined with stretching significantly improves foot function. The guideline recommends against adding therapeutic ultrasound to stretching.
- Asked what happens if plantar fasciitis is left untreated, one answer said it rarely goes away on its own. Most cases improve over months, which another answer from the same tool said too.

### How to use AI answers for heel pain

AI answers are a reasonable first look, especially for stretching. Before you follow one, check it for the part most of them skip:

- Does it name a strengthening exercise, such as a [heel raise](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/) that gets harder over the weeks?
- Does it give a dose: how long to hold, how many sets, how often?
- Does it say when to see a clinician? Pain after an injury, numbness, swelling or night pain needs one.
- Does it cite a guideline or a study, or only clinic and shop pages?

## Is an exercise app as good as physical therapy for plantar fasciitis?

Language: English · https://walkito.site/app-vs-physical-therapy-plantar-fasciitis/ · published 2026-10-11 · updated 2026-10-11

Nobody knows yet: we found no trial comparing an exercise app with physical therapy for plantar fasciitis. What the trials do show is that home exercise did about as well as physical therapy in one trial and worse than supervised clinic care in another, and that hands-on treatment added to home exercise helps short-term pain. A sensible middle path is a clinician visit to confirm the diagnosis, then the home exercises, with or without an app.

- We found no randomized trial comparing an exercise app with physical therapy for plantar fasciitis. The only study comparing a digital program with physiotherapy was observational, and its authors call the results provisional.
- Home exercise vs physical therapy is mixed: one 57-person trial found no difference over a year, while a 47-person trial found a supervised outpatient program did better.
- Hands-on treatments added to home exercise, such as dry needling, manual therapy, laser and taping, improved short-term pain or function in a 2026 review of 24 trials.
- A physical therapist can diagnose, rule out other causes and do hands-on care. An app can only guide the exercises, though the stretching and strengthening the 2023 guideline recommends are exercises you can do at home.
- See a clinician if the pain is severe, keeps getting worse, has not improved after about two weeks of home care, or comes with numbness or tingling.

### Exercise app vs physical therapy at a glance

### What does the research say?

We found no trial of an app against physical therapy for plantar fasciitis, so the closest evidence is home exercise against physical therapy:

- **Home stretching did about as well.** In a randomized trial of 57 people, home stretching and formal physical therapy showed no notable differences in pain, function or quality of life at any point over a year.
- **Supervised care did better.** In a randomized trial of 47 people, a supervised outpatient program beat a home program on pain and function at 8 weeks and 6 months.
- **Adding physical therapy to podiatry care.** In a trial of 95 people, adding physical therapy made no difference on the main measure at 6 months, though some secondary measures favoured it.

The only study of a digital program against hospital physiotherapy for plantar fasciitis followed 587 people in China. Home digital exercise was not worse for first-step pain at 3 months and cost less. But it was not randomized, only about 6% of screened patients were eligible, and its authors call the findings provisional until a randomized trial confirms them.

Across muscle and joint problems in general, a review of 37 trials found remote rehabilitation helped compared with other controls, but the advantage disappeared when it was compared with face-to-face rehabilitation. It was cheaper per person.

Source: Kaiser PB, Keyser C, Crawford AM, et al. A prospective randomized controlled trial comparing physical therapy with independent home stretching for plantar fasciitis. Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. 2022;30(14):682–689.
Source: Çil ET, Şaylı U, Subaşı F. Outpatient vs home management protocol results for plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle International. 2019;40(11):1295–1303.
Source: McClinton SM, Heiderscheit BC, McPoil TG, et al. Effectiveness of physical therapy treatment in addition to usual podiatry management of plantar heel pain: a randomized clinical trial. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2019;20(1):630.
Source: Xu W, Yao L, Wang H, et al. Home-based digital exercise versus hospital physiotherapy for plantar fasciitis: a propensity-score-matched retrospective cohort study with dual-perspective cost-utility evaluation. Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2026;58:jrm45974.
Source: Molina-Garcia P, Mora-Traverso M, Prieto-Moreno R, et al. Effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of telerehabilitation for musculoskeletal disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Annals of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine. 2024;67(1):101791.

### What does a physical therapist do that an app can’t?

Three things an app cannot do:

- **Diagnose.** Heel pain is not always plantar fasciitis. A stress fracture, a trapped nerve or an Achilles problem can feel similar and need different care.
- **Hands-on treatment.** The 2023 guideline grades manual therapy and taping A, and dry needling and laser B. All need a clinician. In a 2026 review of 24 trials, adding dry needling, laser or manual therapy to home exercise improved short-term pain, and dry needling and taping improved short-term function.
- **Watch you move.** A therapist can see how you walk, how far your ankle bends and whether you do an exercise right, and change the plan on the spot.

Not every add-on helps: a separate 84-person trial found that adding high-intensity laser or shockwave to home exercise gave no extra benefit over three months.

Source: Li Z, He S, Wu J, et al. Efficacy of physical therapy interventions delivered with home exercise programs for pain and function in plantar fasciitis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Physical Therapy. 2026;106(6):pzag056.
Source: Kosehasanogullari M, Büyükvural Şen S, Okur Yılmaz N, et al. Home exercise with or without high-intensity laser or radial shockwave therapy for plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial. Foot & Ankle International. 2026;47(3):386–397.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### What can an exercise app do well?

The exercises themselves are the part of care you can do at home, and the 2023 guideline recommends them: stretching the plantar fascia and calf (grade A) and strengthening (grade B). A good app gives you those every week, with doses that grow over time.

Apps may also help you keep going. In a 4-week trial of 80 people with muscle and joint problems, an app with remote support led to better home exercise adherence than paper handouts, though the authors call the clinical importance unclear. In a 2026 trial of 87 people with heel pain, an app-style home program and a paper handout gave similar first-step pain, with some other measures favouring the app.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Lambert TE, Harvey LA, Avdalis C, et al. An app with remote support achieves better adherence to home exercise programs than paper handouts in people with musculoskeletal conditions: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2017;63(3):161–167.
Source: Shim DW, Park KH, Lee JW, et al. Information and communications technology-based versus handout-based home exercise programs for heel pain syndrome: a prospective randomized study. Scientific Reports. 2026;16(1):13584.

### Is physical therapy worth it for plantar fasciitis?

It can be, especially at the start or when home exercise is not working. There is no standard number of visits for plantar fasciitis; in one of the trials above, the supervised group came twice a week for 8 weeks. Copays add up, so it is worth asking your insurance what it covers.

If you cannot get or afford regular visits, a clinician visit to confirm the diagnosis and check your exercises, then a home program, is a reasonable middle path. Bring your questions and ask the therapist to watch you do each exercise once.

Source: Çil ET, Şaylı U, Subaşı F. Outpatient vs home management protocol results for plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle International. 2019;40(11):1295–1303.

### What should a good plantar fasciitis app include?

If you go the home route with an app, check that it has:

- A plantar fascia stretch and calf stretches with the knee straight and bent.
- Strengthening that gets harder over the weeks, such as the [towel heel raise](https://walkito.site/exercises/towel-heel-raise/).
- Clear doses, and a way to make a bad day lighter.
- Advice on when to stop and see a clinician.
- No promise to end the pain. In our [check of 20 heel pain apps](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-apps-study/), 9 of 19 promised to end the pain or claimed proven results.

Our [buyer’s guide](https://walkito.site/best-app-for-plantar-fasciitis/) compares the main apps, and [Walkito vs Hinge Health](https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-hinge-health/) covers the option that includes a physical therapist.

### When should you see a physical therapist or doctor?

The [NHS advises](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/plantar-fasciitis/) seeing a doctor if the pain is severe or stopping your normal activities, is getting worse or keeps coming back, has not improved after 2 weeks of home care, or comes with tingling or loss of feeling, and if you have diabetes. The red flags below add a few more reasons to get checked.

### See a clinician first if

- your heel pain followed an injury or a fall
- the pain is severe or stops you doing normal activities
- it has not improved after about two weeks of home care, or keeps getting worse
- the pain comes with numbness, tingling, swelling, redness or warmth
- pain wakes you at night or is there at rest
- you have diabetes, reduced feeling in your feet or poor circulation

### If you go the home route

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) gives you the plantar fascia stretch, calf stretches with the knee straight and bent, and strength work that gets harder over time, such as the towel heel raise later in the plan, on 3, 5 or 7 days a week. It does not diagnose and has no hands-on care.

#### Do I need physical therapy for plantar fasciitis?

Not always. In one 57-person trial, home stretching did about as well as formal physical therapy over a year, but another trial found supervised clinic care better. A visit is worth it to confirm the diagnosis, and if home exercise is not helping.

#### Can I do physical therapy for plantar fasciitis at home?

You can do the exercise part at home: plantar fascia and calf stretches and strengthening, which the 2023 guideline recommends. Diagnosis and hands-on care such as manual therapy, taping or dry needling need a clinician.

#### Is virtual physical therapy as good as in person?

For muscle and joint problems in general, a review of 37 trials found no clear advantage for remote rehabilitation over face-to-face care, and it was cheaper. We found no randomized trial of virtual physical therapy for plantar fasciitis specifically.

#### How many physical therapy sessions do you need for plantar fasciitis?

There is no standard number. Trials vary; in one, the supervised group had sessions twice a week for 8 weeks. Your therapist will suggest a plan based on how you respond.

## How much does plantar fasciitis care cost?

Language: English · https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-treatment-cost/ · published 2026-10-11 · updated 2026-10-13

Home exercise costs the least: the stretches and strengthening the 2023 guideline recommends need no equipment, and the exercise apps we checked range from free to about $300 a year. Store-bought insoles cost about $40 to $60 a pair. Of the first-line options, physical therapy costs the most: in a study of US private insurance claims from 2007 to 2011, an average course of 5 to 6 visits for plantar fasciitis cost about $1,000 to $1,400. Custom orthotics, often $300 to $800, did no better than store-bought insoles in trials.

- The 2026 national Medicare-approved amount for a physical therapy evaluation is $97.87; after the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of it.
- A physical therapy visit for a privately insured patient cost $192 on average, according to the Health Care Cost Institute.
- Nearly 4 in 5 ACA plans sold to individuals and small businesses in 2024 capped physical therapy visits; 20 a year was the most common limit.
- The foot pain apps we checked cost from free to $299.99 a year in the App Store. Hinge Health and Sword are $0 through many employers and health plans.
- Custom orthotics did no better than store-bought insoles in a review of 19 trials, and a Dutch trial found them not cost-effective compared with usual care from a family doctor.

### Plantar fasciitis costs at a glance

Prices vary a lot by state, clinic and insurance plan. Use these as a starting point and ask for a quote before you book.

### How much does physical therapy cost for plantar fasciitis?

That study used claims from 2007 to 2011, so today’s costs may be higher. Newer per-visit numbers:

- **Medicare.** The 2026 national Medicare-approved amounts are $97.87 for a physical therapy evaluation, $29.06 for each 15 minutes of therapeutic exercise and $27.72 for each 15 minutes of manual therapy ([CMS fee schedule](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/physician-fee-schedule/search)). After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the approved amount ([Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/physical-therapy-services)).
- **Private insurance.** A visit for a privately insured patient cost $192 on average, according to Health Care Cost Institute data reported by [KFF Health News](https://kffhealthnews.org/health-care-costs/physical-occupational-therapy-visit-session-cap-limit-prior-authorization-aca/) in 2025. What you pay depends on your copay, coinsurance and deductible.
- **Without insurance.** Price guides from companies that sell therapy put a self-pay visit at roughly $100 to $350 or more, with the first evaluation at $150 to $400 or more ([Hinge Health](https://www.hingehealth.com/resources/articles/physical-therapy-cost-calculator)). These are rough guides, not independent surveys.

A quick way to estimate your own cost: multiply your copay by the number of visits. With a $30 copay and 8 visits, that is $240, plus anything you owe toward your deductible first.

Source: Fraser JJ, Glaviano NR, Hertel J. Utilization of physical therapy intervention among patients with plantar fasciitis in the United States. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2017;47(2):49–55.

### Does insurance cover physical therapy for plantar fasciitis?

Many plans do when it is medically necessary, but often with limits:

- **Visit caps.** Nearly 4 in 5 ACA plans sold to individuals and small businesses in 2024 limited physical therapy visits, from 20 to 60 a year, and 20 was the most common cap ([KFF Health News](https://kffhealthnews.org/health-care-costs/physical-occupational-therapy-visit-session-cap-limit-prior-authorization-aca/)).
- **Prior approval.** Therapists told [KFF Health News](https://kffhealthnews.org/health-care-costs/physical-occupational-therapy-visit-session-cap-limit-prior-authorization-aca/) that some insurers demand a new approval request every two or three visits.
- **Medicare.** There is no hard cap, but once therapy costs pass $2,480 in a year (2026), the therapist must confirm that more care is needed ([APTA](https://www.apta.org/your-practice/payment/medicare-payment/coding-billing/therapy-cap)).

Before your first visit, ask your plan three things: how many visits are covered, whether you need a referral, and what you pay per visit before and after the deductible.

### Is an app cheaper than physical therapy, and does it work as well?

An app costs less than even a few physical therapy visits. Whether it does as well is not known: we found no trial comparing an exercise app with physical therapy for plantar fasciitis. In a study in China, a digital home program cost less than half as much as hospital physiotherapy in direct medical costs over a year and was not worse for first-step pain at three months. But it was not randomized, and its authors call the results provisional.

What an app cannot do is diagnose your heel pain or give hands-on care. Our page on [exercise apps vs physical therapy](https://walkito.site/app-vs-physical-therapy-plantar-fasciitis/) goes through the trials.

Source: Xu W, Yao L, Wang H, et al. Home-based digital exercise versus hospital physiotherapy for plantar fasciitis: a propensity-score-matched retrospective cohort study with dual-perspective cost-utility evaluation. Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2026;58:jrm45974.

### Are custom orthotics worth the money?

Custom orthotics often cost $300 to $800, and some insurance plans do not pay for them or pay only for certain conditions ([GoodRx](https://www.goodrx.com/conditions/musculoskeletal/custom-orthotics-cost)). Medicare covers shoe inserts only for people with diabetes and severe diabetes-related foot disease ([Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/therapeutic-shoes-inserts)).

The trials do not show that the extra money buys better results. In a trial of 185 adults, custom insoles did no better than sham insoles at three months, and a cost analysis of the same trial found custom insoles were not cost-effective compared with usual care from a family doctor.

Store-bought arch supports cost much less, for example [Dr. Scholl’s Plantar Fasciitis insoles](https://www.drscholls.com/products/advanced-pain-relief-plantar-fasciitis-orthotic-insoles) at $39.99, [Powerstep Pinnacle](https://powerstep.com/products/pinnacle-insoles) at $54.95 and [Superfeet High Arch](https://www.superfeet.com/products/all-purpose-support-high-arch) at $59.99. The 2023 guideline advises against relying on insoles alone for short-term pain relief, so pair them with the exercises. More in [insoles vs exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/).

Source: Whittaker GA, Munteanu SE, Menz HB, Tan JM, Rabusin CL, Landorf KB. Foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(5):322–328.
Source: Rasenberg N, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, Fuit L, et al. Custom insoles versus sham and GP-led usual care in patients with plantar heel pain: results of the STAP-study - a randomised controlled trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(5):272–278.
Source: Rasenberg N, van Middelkoop M, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, El Alili M, Bindels P, Bosmans J. Cost-effectiveness of custom-made insoles versus usual care in patients with plantar heel pain in primary care: cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open. 2021;11(11):e051866.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### What do other plantar fasciitis treatments cost?

- **Podiatrist visit.** About $165 on average for a new patient without insurance ([Mira](https://www.talktomira.com/post/how-much-does-it-cost-to-see-a-podiatrist-without-insurance)). The 2026 national Medicare-approved amount for a standard new-patient office visit is $117.57.
- **Cortisone shot.** The 2026 national Medicare-approved amount for the injection itself in an office is $60.46; the drug and any separate visit can add to that.
- **Night splint.** $49.95 to $56.95 at list price from [Powerstep](https://powerstep.com/products/dorsal-night-splint). See [night splints for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/night-splints-plantar-fasciitis/).
- **Shockwave therapy.** UCHealth charged $550 for a package in 2023; bundled prices on [MDsave](https://www.mdsave.com/procedures/shockwave-therapy-for-plantar-fasciitis/d28bfbc9) run $2,602 to $3,890. Some insurers do not pay for it: Cigna lists it as unproven for plantar fasciitis ([policy](https://static.cigna.com/assets/chcp/pdf/coveragePolicies/medical/mm_0097_coveragepositioncriteria_plantar_fasciitis_treatments.pdf)).
- **Surgery.** $3,431 to $9,434 for a plantar fasciotomy ([MDsave](https://www.mdsave.com/procedures/plantar-fasciotomy/d784f9c5)).

### What is the cheapest way to start?

A low-cost order that follows the guideline:

- Start the plantar fascia stretch, calf stretches and a strengthening exercise such as the [towel heel raise](https://walkito.site/exercises/towel-heel-raise/). They cost nothing.
- Add store-bought arch supports if you want extra comfort, together with the exercises.
- See a doctor or physical therapist if the pain has not improved after about two weeks of home care ([NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heel-pain/)), or sooner for the warning signs below.
- Leave the costly options, such as shots, shockwave and surgery, for later, and decide on them with a clinician.

Our [plantar fasciitis exercises guide](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) shows each exercise step by step.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### See a clinician first if

- your heel pain followed an injury or a fall
- the pain is severe or stops you doing normal activities
- it has not improved after about two weeks of home care, or keeps getting worse
- the pain comes with numbness, tingling or swelling
- you have diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) gives you the plantar fascia stretch, calf stretches with the knee straight and bent, and strength work that gets harder over time, such as the towel heel raise later in the plan, on 3, 5 or 7 days a week. It is a weekly or yearly subscription; the price is shown in the store.

#### How much is physical therapy for plantar fasciitis without insurance?

Price guides from therapy companies put a self-pay visit at roughly $100 to $350 or more, and the first evaluation at $150 to $400 or more. Multiply by the number of visits your therapist suggests to estimate the total.

#### Will insurance pay for plantar fasciitis treatment?

Many plans pay for physical therapy when it is medically necessary, but many cap visits; 20 a year was the most common cap in ACA plans sold in 2024. Some plans do not pay for custom orthotics, and some insurers, such as Cigna, do not pay for shockwave therapy.

#### Does Medicare cover orthotics for plantar fasciitis?

Medicare covers therapeutic shoes and inserts only for people with diabetes and severe diabetes-related foot disease. For outpatient physical therapy, you pay 20% of the approved amount after the Part B deductible.

#### What can I do if I can’t afford physical therapy?

Start with the free home exercises the 2023 guideline recommends: plantar fascia and calf stretches and strengthening. If you can afford one visit, use it to confirm the diagnosis and check your exercises. The NHS advises seeing a doctor if heel pain has not improved after 2 weeks of home care.

## Free YouTube videos or an exercise app for plantar fasciitis?

Language: English · https://walkito.site/youtube-vs-app-plantar-fasciitis/ · published 2026-10-11 · updated 2026-10-11

Free videos can be enough if you pick a good one: we found no trial comparing YouTube routines with an exercise app for plantar fasciitis. The catch is picking. In our check of the 50 most-viewed plantar fasciitis videos, only 9 included a plantar fascia stretch, a calf stretch and strengthening, the three exercise types the 2023 guideline recommends. An app mainly adds structure; in trials, digital tools usually helped people do their exercises a bit more often, at least in the first weeks.

- We found no trial comparing free YouTube videos with an exercise app for plantar fasciitis.
- Of the 50 most-viewed plantar fasciitis videos we checked, 9 covered all three exercise types the guideline recommends, 15 had neither a plantar fascia stretch nor strengthening, and 9 said when to see a doctor.
- Published reviews of plantar fasciitis videos disagree: one rated 67% of 140 plantar fasciitis and heel spur videos poor or very poor for reliability, another found most of the 79 most-viewed videos useful.
- In a trial of people with heel pain, AI-made exercise videos and free paper leaflets gave the same adherence (73% vs 71%), but the video group did harder exercises more accurately.
- Heavy heel raises may speed early improvement, but how to dose them is not settled: in one trial, people who set their own load did as well as those on a fixed plan.

### Free videos vs an exercise app at a glance

Video numbers are from [our study of the 50 most-viewed plantar fasciitis videos](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-youtube-study/), October 2026. App numbers are from [our check of heel pain apps](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-apps-study/) (19 apps, Walkito not counted), based on store listings and websites, not on using each app.

### Are YouTube videos for plantar fasciitis any good?

Some are, many are not. In our check of the 50 most-viewed videos, with 75 million views between them:

- 15 of 50 had neither a plantar fascia stretch nor any strengthening.
- 9 of 50 said when to see a doctor, and none of the top 10 did.
- 17 of 50 titles promised a fast or permanent result.
- 34 of 50 sold something, such as a product or a paid program.
- On the plus side, 46 of 50 gave a clear dose, such as how many reps or how long to hold.

Published reviews disagree. One rated 67% of 140 plantar fasciitis and heel spur videos poor or very poor for reliability. Another, of the 79 most-viewed videos, found 30% high quality and most of them useful and in line with guidelines; the largest share of high-quality videos came from health professionals such as physiotherapists. A third, of 50 videos, found most were low quality and that videos by doctors scored higher.

Source: Yüce A, Ocak O, Gur V, et al. YouTube Videos About Plantar Fasciitis and Calcaneal Spurs Are Insufficient and Poor Quality. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2023;113(3).
Source: Feyzioğlu Ö, Öztürk Ö, Muğrabi S. Video-Based Information About Plantar Fasciitis Reflects Current Treatment Guidelines. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2023;113(6).
Source: Satılmış AB, Cengiz T. Analysis of Plantar Fasciitis Videos on YouTube: Quality and Reliability Assessment. Cureus. 2025;17(2):e78993.

### How do you know if a plantar fasciitis video is good?

Check for these before you follow a routine:

- A plantar fascia stretch, such as pulling your toes back.
- Calf stretches, ideally with the knee straight and bent.
- At least one strengthening exercise, such as a [heel raise with a towel under the toes](https://walkito.site/exercises/towel-heel-raise/).
- A clear dose: how many reps or seconds, and how often.
- Advice on when to see a doctor.
- A named clinician, such as a physical therapist or doctor.
- No promise of a fast or permanent result, and no hard sell.

Stretching is graded A and strengthening B in the 2023 guideline, so a routine with only stretches leaves out part of what is recommended. [Our study page](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-youtube-study/) lists which of the top 50 videos include all three.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### What does an app add over free videos?

Mainly structure: a set plan, reminders and a record of what you did. The evidence that this matters is real but modest:

- **Heel pain, app vs handout.** In a trial of 87 people with plantar fasciitis or Achilles pain, an app-based program and a paper handout gave similar first-step pain; foot function scores favoured the app at 4 and 24 weeks.
- **Heel pain, video vs leaflet.** In a trial of 103 people with plantar fasciitis or Achilles pain, AI-made videos and free AAOS leaflets gave the same adherence (73% vs 71%), but the video group did the harder exercises, such as towel curls, more accurately.
- **Muscle and joint pain.** An app with remote support improved adherence over paper handouts in a 4-week trial of 80 people, and a web-based program gave a small improvement at 3 weeks in a trial of 305 people.

Exercise videos alone may not be what helps. A Cochrane review found that 5 of 6 trials of different ways of delivering exercise, such as supervised sessions, refresher sessions or audio and video tapes to take home, improved adherence. But a later review in adults 45 and older with back pain or hip or knee arthritis found audio or video cues did not improve adherence, while booster sessions with a physiotherapist did for people with arthritis.

Source: Lang S, McLelland C, MacDonald D, et al. Do digital interventions increase adherence to home exercise rehabilitation? A systematic review of randomised controlled trials. Archives of Physiotherapy. 2022;12(1):24.
Source: Shim DW, Park KH, Lee JW, et al. Information and communications technology-based versus handout-based home exercise programs for heel pain syndrome: a prospective randomized study. Scientific Reports. 2026;16(1):13584.
Source: Ülgen NK, Nazlıgül AS, Yiğit N, et al. AI-Generated Exercise Videos vs Traditional Leaflets: A Novel Approach to Home Exercise Education in Achilles Tendinitis and Plantar Fasciitis: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2026;11(2):24730114261436388.
Source: Lambert TE, Harvey LA, Avdalis C, et al. An app with remote support achieves better adherence to home exercise programs than paper handouts in people with musculoskeletal conditions: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2017;63(3):161–167.
Source: Bennell KL, Marshall CJ, Dobson F, et al. Does a Web-Based Exercise Programming System Improve Home Exercise Adherence for People With Musculoskeletal Conditions?: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Journal of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation. 2019;98(10):850–858.
Source: Jordan JL, Holden MA, Mason EE, et al. Interventions to improve adherence to exercise for chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010;2010(1):CD005956.
Source: Nicolson PJA, Bennell KL, Dobson FL, et al. Interventions to increase adherence to therapeutic exercise in older adults with low back pain and/or hip/knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;51(10):791–799.

### Does a plan that gets harder matter?

Heavy heel raises may speed early improvement. In a trial of 48 people, heel raises that got heavier scored 29 points better than plantar fascia stretching on a foot function score at 3 months, with no difference at 1, 6 or 12 months.

In a trial of 70 people, those who chose their own load (as heavy as they could manage) did as well as people following a fixed progression. And in a trial of 180 adults, adding heel raises to advice and a heel cup made no significant difference to pain at any point over a year. The 2023 guideline says more research is needed on the dose and timing of exercise.

If you use a free routine, you can make it harder yourself as it gets easier. An app plans that for you, which helps if you would rather not.

Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.
Source: Riel H, Jensen MB, Olesen JL, et al. Self-dosed and pre-determined progressive heavy-slow resistance training have similar effects in people with plantar fasciopathy: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2019;65(3):144–151.
Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, et al. Does a corticosteroid injection plus exercise or exercise alone add to the effect of patient advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy? A randomised clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57(18):1180–1186.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Good free plantar fasciitis exercise resources

These are free and include strengthening, not just stretches:

- [AAOS Foot and Ankle Conditioning Program](https://orthoinfo.aaos.org/en/recovery/foot-and-ankle-conditioning-program), from the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons.
- [Mayo Clinic foot stretches](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/plantar-fasciitis/multimedia/foot-stretches-to-prevent-plantar-fasciitis/img-20008230), illustrated, with a towel exercise.

- [United Lincolnshire NHS leaflet](https://www.ulh.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Plantar-fasciitis-Exercises.pdf) (PDF).
- Our own [plantar fasciitis exercises guide](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/), with a video for each exercise.

### When is an app worth it?

If a free routine with all three exercise types is going well, there is no need to pay for anything. An app may be worth it if:

- you keep stopping and want a set plan and reminders
- you want the exercises to get harder without planning it yourself
- you want to track whether things are changing

Either way, see a doctor or physical therapist if the pain has not improved after about two weeks of home care ([NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heel-pain/)). ## Best apps for foot pain, by problem

Language: English · https://walkito.site/best-apps-for-foot-pain/ · published 2026-10-11 · updated 2026-10-11

No foot pain app has been tested in a published trial, so there is no proven best one. We checked 16 apps for flat feet, Achilles pain, ankle sprains, bunions and ball of foot pain: 2 named a licensed clinician as the creator, 5 promised to end pain or gave a quick timeline, and only 1 cited a specific study. The research supports the exercises, not any one app, so pick an app that gives the right exercises for your problem.

- Of 16 foot pain apps we checked in the App Store and Google Play, none had a published trial, 2 named a licensed clinician as the creator and 1 cited a specific study.
- 5 of 16 promised to end pain or gave a quick timeline, such as “eliminate pain” or “results in just 6 weeks”.
- For ankle sprains, an app version of a proven exercise program did as well as a printed booklet, not better.
- Flat feet exercises can reduce pain but did not realign the foot in a review of 10 trials.
- For bunions and ball of foot pain, the evidence for exercise is weak or missing; shoes, pads and a clinician matter more.

### Foot pain apps by problem at a glance

Some apps cover more than one problem. Checked October 11, 2026, in the US App Store and Google Play.

### Best apps for flat feet

Look for foot and arch strengthening, such as the short foot exercise. Be wary of any app that promises a new arch: in a 2024 review of the short foot exercise, there was no clear overall change in arch height (navicular drop); only programs longer than 6 weeks showed one.

- [Arch: Flat Feet Trainer](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6755728858) (iPhone). Subscription. Says “live pain-free” and “See significant results in just 6 weeks”, and “BACKED BY SCIENCE” without naming a study.
- [ArchFix](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6743368281) (iPhone, Android). Free, with nothing to buy. Offers “preventive and corrective exercises”. No clinician named.

Our [flat feet exercises guide](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-exercises/) shows the exercises from the trials.

Source: Hoang NT, Chen S, Chou LW. The Impact of Foot Orthoses and Exercises on Pain and Navicular Drop for Adult Flatfoot: A Network Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2021;18(15).
Source: Cheng J, Han D, Qu J, et al. Effects of short foot training on foot posture in patients with flatfeet: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Back and Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation. 2024;37(4):839–851.

### Best apps for Achilles tendinopathy

Look for heel drops or heavy heel raises that get harder over weeks, with a way to adjust to pain. One caution: in a 2026 trial of 68 people, unsupervised home eccentric exercise did no better than sham exercise over three months.

- [ROM Coach](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1485733376) (iPhone, Android). The most rated app we found (4.8 from about 1,600 ratings on iPhone). Made by a kinesiologist. Calls itself “your #1 resource to eliminate pain”.
- [Rehab Science](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6752273938) (iPhone, Android). Made by a named physical therapist, Dr. Tom Walters, DPT. Says “Heal pain”.
- [Tendon Tracker](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6756897904) (iPhone, Android). Names research models but no paper. Asks “READY TO ACTUALLY HEAL?”.
- [GaitLab Coach](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6755685826) (iPhone), for runners. The only app that cited a specific study, and the only one that spelled out warning signs in its listing.
- [Sidekick](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6759810159) (iPhone), [PhysioCare](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id950989316) (iPhone) and [Achilles Rebuild](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.jcs.fitsw.achillesrebuild) (Android) also name Achilles problems.

Source: Janssen T, van Berkel S, Edens M, et al. Effectiveness of eccentric calf muscle exercise therapy in patients with chronic midportion Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2026. Online ahead of print.

### Best apps for ankle sprain rehab

The 2021 ankle sprain guideline grades a structured exercise program and balance training A. On how to deliver a home program, such as written instructions, exercise video games or an app, the guideline gives only a D because the evidence conflicts.

The same program has been tested as an app. In one trial of 220 athletes, reported in two papers, compliance was 73% with the “Strengthen your ankle” app and 77% with a printed booklet, and repeat sprains were similar. A separate e-health program for people seen by their family doctor made no difference to repeat sprains, and only 6.1% stuck with it.

- [AnklePath](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6781827965) (iPhone). Physiotherapist-led videos, no one named. Tells you to know the warning signs, without listing them in the store.
- [Sports Injury Rehabilitation](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1538404666) (iPhone, Android). Made by named physiotherapists Phil Pask and Paul Tanner. The first phase of each program is free.
- [Adapted](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6756030925) (iPhone), for ankle instability. Says “Most users report noticeable improvements in flexibility, range of motion, and recovery within 1-2 weeks”.
- [Sidekick](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6759810159) (iPhone), [PhysioCare](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id950989316) (iPhone) and [Fitivity Ankle Sprain Rehab](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.fitivity.rehab_ankle) (Android, with ads) also cover sprains.

Our [ankle strengthening exercises guide](https://walkito.site/ankle-strengthening-exercises/) has balance and strength exercises.

Source: Martin RL, Davenport TE, Fraser JJ, et al. Ankle Stability and Movement Coordination Impairments: Lateral Ankle Ligament Sprains Revision 2021. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2021;51(4):CPG1–CPG80.
Source: Hupperets MD, Verhagen EA, van Mechelen W. Effect of unsupervised home based proprioceptive training on recurrences of ankle sprain: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2009;339:b2684.
Source: Van Reijen M, Vriend I, Zuidema V, et al. Increasing compliance with neuromuscular training to prevent ankle sprain in sport: does the 'Strengthen your ankle' mobile App make a difference? A randomised controlled trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;50(19):1200–5.
Source: Van Reijen M, Vriend I, Zuidema V, et al. The "Strengthen your ankle" program to prevent recurrent injuries: A randomized controlled trial aimed at long-term effectiveness. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2017;20(6):549–554.
Source: Mailuhu AK, Verhagen EA, van Ochten J, et al. E-health intervention for preventing recurrent ankle sprains: a randomised controlled trial in general practice. British Journal of General Practice. 2024;74(738):e56–e62.

### Apps for bunions

Exercise may ease bunion pain, but there is no reliable evidence that exercise straightens the toe. The [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bunions/) says a GP may refer you for surgery if bunions are very painful or having a big effect on your life, and that surgery is not done just to improve how feet look.

- [Correct Toes](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6793699449) (iPhone). Free, from a foot and ankle clinic that also sells toe spacers. Names bunions, hammertoes, neuromas and metatarsalgia. No clinician named.
- [Neatsy](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1483925852) (iPhone). A 3D foot scan that flags bunions; it says it “does not diagnose diseases or suggest treatment plans”.

See our [bunion exercises guide](https://walkito.site/bunion-exercises/) for what the trials tested.

Source: Hurn SE, Matthews BG, Munteanu SE, et al. Effectiveness of Nonsurgical Interventions for Hallux Valgus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Arthritis Care & Research. 2022;74(10):1676–1688.
Source: Dias CG, Godoy-Santos AL, Ferrari J, et al. Surgical interventions for treating hallux valgus and bunions. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2024;7(7):CD013726.

### Apps for ball of foot pain and Morton’s neuroma

Here exercise is not the main tool. The [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/foot-pain/pain-in-the-ball-of-the-foot/) advises shoes with plenty of room, a low heel and a soft sole, and soft insoles or pads. In a small study, a metatarsal pad lowered pressure under the ball of the foot and improved pain scores. For Morton’s neuroma, first-line care is less of the activity that hurts, orthotics and injections.

The only app we found that names ball of foot pain is [Correct Toes](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6793699449). An exercise-only app is missing the main part of care here. Our guides on [ball of foot pain](https://walkito.site/ball-of-foot-pain/) and [Morton’s neuroma](https://walkito.site/mortons-neuroma/) explain the options.

Source: Kang JH, Chen MD, Chen SC, et al. Correlations between subjective treatment responses and plantar pressure parameters of metatarsal pad treatment in metatarsalgia patients: a prospective study. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2006;7:95.
Source: Cooper MT. Common Painful Foot and Ankle Conditions: A Review. JAMA. 2023;330(23):2285–2294.

### Apps for general foot pain

There is no single exercise program for “foot pain”, because the right care depends on the cause. On its ball of foot pain page, the [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/foot-pain/pain-in-the-ball-of-the-foot/) advises: “Do not try to diagnose the cause of pain yourself.” [How to Do Foot Exercises](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.Fitness.Flexibility.Workout.How.to.Do.Foot.Exercises) (Android, with ads) offers general foot exercises, and Arch covers general foot strengthening.

Our [foot pain identifier](https://walkito.site/foot-pain-identifier/) can help you narrow down where your pain fits before you pick an app.

Source: Cooper MT. Common Painful Foot and Ankle Conditions: A Review. JAMA. 2023;330(23):2285–2294.

### All 16 foot pain apps we checked

“Pain promise” means the listing promises to end pain or gives a quick timeline; “in the name” means only the app’s name does (ArchFix, Run Pain-Free). None of the 16 had a published trial when we searched PubMed.

### How do you choose a foot pain app?

- It names your problem and gives the exercises the research supports for it (see the table above).
- It names who made it, ideally a licensed clinician such as a physical therapist.
- It makes the exercises harder over time and lets you go easier on a bad day.
- It tells you when to stop and see a clinician. Only 1 of 16 spelled out warning signs in its listing.
- It does not promise to end pain or give a quick timeline.
- It tells you what it costs before you start.

### How we checked these apps

On October 11, 2026 we searched the US App Store and Google Play with 2 or 3 terms for each problem, such as “flat feet exercises”, “achilles rehab” and “ankle sprain rehab”. We included an app if its listing named the foot problem and offered exercises. We left out shoe and insole stores, foot scanners without exercises, step trackers, single-clinic portals, general fitness apps, apps only available through an employer or health plan, and apps not updated since 2023.

Every fact comes from the store listing or the developer’s website, not from using the apps, and a second reviewer re-checked each listing. We also searched PubMed for each app’s name. Plantar fasciitis apps are covered in our [heel pain app study](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-apps-study/).

### Where Walkito fits

Walkito is our app, so it is not counted above. Its listing names plantar fasciitis, flat feet, Achilles pain in runners and general foot pain, and it says to see a clinician first if pain came from an injury or comes with swelling, numbness or night pain. Like the others, it has no published trial and names no clinician as its creator. Its listing does not name ankle sprains, bunions or ball of foot pain.

### See a clinician first if

- your foot pain followed an injury, a fall or a pop or snap
- you cannot put weight on the foot
- the foot is swollen, red or hot
- you have numbness, tingling or burning
- it has not improved after about two weeks of home care
- you have diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet

### If your problem is heel pain or flat feet

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) gives you the plantar fascia stretch, calf stretches with the knee straight and bent, and foot and ankle strength work that gets harder over time, on 3, 5 or 7 days a week. It is a weekly or yearly subscription; the price is shown in the store.

#### Is there a free app for foot pain exercises?

Yes. Of the apps we checked, ArchFix (flat feet) showed nothing to buy, Correct Toes (bunions, ball of foot) is free with no subscription though it sells toe spacers in the app, and Sports Injury Rehabilitation gives the first phase of each program free. How to Do Foot Exercises is free with ads.

#### Can exercise change flat feet?

It can ease pain, but it did not realign the foot in a review of 10 trials, and a 2024 review of the short foot exercise found no clear overall change in arch height, except in programs longer than 6 weeks. In the first review, exercise, alone or with insoles, did better for pain than insoles alone.

#### What is the best app for ankle sprain rehab?

No app has been shown to beat a printed program. The 2021 guideline grades structured exercise and balance training A. An app version of a proven program did as well as a booklet, so pick the format you will stick with.

#### Are foot pain apps safe?

An app cannot diagnose you. See a clinician if pain followed an injury, comes with swelling, numbness or tingling, or has not improved after about two weeks of home care.

## Hinge Health alternatives if your employer doesn’t offer it

Language: English · https://walkito.site/hinge-health-alternatives/ · published 2026-10-11 · updated 2026-10-11

If your employer or health plan does not offer Hinge Health, you cannot buy it yourself, and its closest rivals, Sword Health and Kaia, are not sold to individuals either. Options you can get on your own are physical therapy through your insurance, at home or in a clinic, self-pay video visits with a physical therapist (for example $89 for 30 minutes), and exercise apps, from free to about $300 a year. First, check whether your plan covers Sword, Omada or Vori Health.

- Hinge Health is only for people covered through a partner employer or health plan; its own page says you are eligible “as long as Hinge Health is covered by your employer or health insurance plan”.
- Sword Health and Kaia, which agreed to join Sword in January 2026, are also only offered through employers and health plans. Omada and Vori Health go through your plan, and your usual cost share may apply.
- You can book some options yourself: Luna sends a physical therapist to your home ($135 a visit without insurance, or billed to insurance), and Virtual Physical Therapists charges $89 for a 30-minute video visit.
- In a trial of 140 people with low back pain, Sword’s digital program did as well as in-person physiotherapy. No program on this page has a published trial for foot or heel pain.
- Medicare covers telehealth from home through December 31, 2027; CMS says physical therapists can no longer provide Medicare telehealth from January 1, 2028.

### Can you get Hinge Health without your employer?

No. Hinge Health’s [page for individuals](https://www.hingehealth.com/for-individuals/) is an eligibility check: it asks for the name and date of birth on your health insurance card to see whether your employer or plan covers you. There is no price and no way to pay yourself. If you are covered, Hinge says it is $0 to you.

If you lost access, for example after changing jobs, the options below are what is left. Our [Walkito vs Hinge Health](https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-hinge-health/) page compares the two side by side.

### Hinge Health alternatives at a glance

Checked October 11, 2026. We do not list Kaia separately because it is joining Sword. DarioHealth and Limber Health are also not sold to individuals; Limber works only if your physical therapy clinic enrolls you.

### Alternatives through your employer or health plan

Check your benefits portal or call the number on your insurance card and ask about these by name:

- [Sword Health](https://sword.com/individuals). A Doctor of Physical Therapy plus an exercise kit that may include a tablet or sensors. Sword says it “may be offered at no cost through your employer or health plan”, and its [foot pain page](https://sword.com/care-explorer/foot-pain) covers pain “anywhere in the heel, arch, toes, or ankle”. In a trial of 140 people with low back pain, its program did as well as in-person physiotherapy.
- [Kaia Health](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kaia-health/id1100673977). Its App Store listing says it is “currently not available on a self-pay basis”. Sword agreed to buy Kaia in January 2026. Kaia’s app did better than physiotherapy plus online education in a German trial in low back pain.
- [Omada Joint & Muscle](https://www.omadahealth.com/for-individuals/musculoskeletal), formerly Physera. A licensed physical therapist and a free exercise kit. Unlike Hinge, Omada’s [resources page](https://www.omadahealth.com/resources) says the program is “subject to deductibles, copays and co-insurance”. Its published studies are observational, including an insurance claims analysis that found lower costs.
- [Vori Health](https://www.vorihealth.com/). A doctor, a physical therapist and a health coach online, billed to insurance, including Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans. It names “foot & ankle pain”. Its one study followed 100 Medicare Advantage patients without a comparison group.
- [RecoveryOne](https://www.recoveryone.com/). A licensed physical therapist, through doctors, health plans or employers. Names “ankle/foot”. We found no published trial.

None of these has a published trial for foot or heel pain. Their trials are mostly in back and shoulder pain.

Source: Cui D, Janela D, Costa F, et al. Randomized-controlled trial assessing a digital care program versus conventional physiotherapy for chronic low back pain. npj Digital Medicine. 2023;6(1):121.
Source: Toelle TR, Utpadel-Fischler DA, Haas KK, et al. App-based multidisciplinary back pain treatment versus combined physiotherapy plus online education: a randomized controlled trial. npj Digital Medicine. 2019;2:34.
Source: Napoleone JM, Devaraj SM, Noble M, et al. Health Care Cost Savings and Utilization Reductions Associated With Virtual Physical Therapy Care: A Propensity-Matched Claims Analysis. Physical Therapy. 2025;105(8).
Source: O'Connor MI, Dorak Ribaudo M, Peters KC, et al. Clinical Efficacy of Telemedicine for Musculoskeletal Conditions in a Medicare Advantage Population. Telemedicine Reports. 2025;6(1):162–170.

### Alternatives you can sign up for yourself

- [Luna](https://www.getluna.com/). A licensed physical therapist comes to your home. In its [service areas](https://www.getluna.com/locations), you can usually book without a referral, though some insurers require one, and it takes insurance, Medicare and Medicare Advantage. Without insurance it lists $135 a visit. It names heel pain and plantar fasciitis.
- [Virtual Physical Therapists](https://www.virtualphysicaltherapists.com/individual/). One-to-one video visits with licensed physical therapists for $89 per 30 minutes, then $2 a minute. It does not bill insurance; HSA and FSA cards work.
- **Physical therapy in a clinic.** Through your insurance, a visit usually costs your copay or coinsurance. Our [plantar fasciitis cost guide](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-treatment-cost/) has typical prices and the questions to ask your plan.
- **Exercise apps.** No clinician, but you can start today. Prices we checked range from free ([PlantarCare](https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-plantarcare/)) to $299.99 a year (Prehab’s top yearly plan); Exakt Health covers plantar fasciitis and heel spurs. See our [plantar fasciitis app guide](https://walkito.site/best-app-for-plantar-fasciitis/) and [foot pain apps by problem](https://walkito.site/best-apps-for-foot-pain/).

### Does Medicare cover virtual physical therapy?

[Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/telehealth) says telehealth from your home is covered through December 31, 2027, and you pay 20% of the approved amount after the Part B deductible. CMS’s [telehealth FAQ](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/telehealth-faq-updated-10-09-2026.pdf) says that from January 1, 2028, physical therapists “can no longer furnish Medicare Telehealth services”.

Separately, Medicare pays physical therapists for remote monitoring of your home exercise as part of a therapy plan of care. If you have Medicare Advantage, ask your plan about Vori Health; Luna also takes Medicare.

### Which alternative fits foot or heel pain?

For plantar fasciitis, the 2023 guideline supports stretching and strengthening, which you can do at home, and hands-on care such as manual therapy and taping, which need a clinician. A practical order:

- Check whether your plan covers Sword, Omada or Vori Health. If it does, that gets you a physical therapist at little or no cost.
- If not, one visit with a physical therapist, in a clinic, at home with Luna or by video, can confirm the diagnosis and check your exercises.
- Then keep going at home, with a free routine or an app. Our page on [exercise apps vs physical therapy](https://walkito.site/app-vs-physical-therapy-plantar-fasciitis/) covers what the trials show.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

Walkito is an exercise app you can download without an employer or insurance. It gives you a plan of stretching and strengthening for heel pain, flat feet and related foot problems, but no physical therapist, no hands-on care and no diagnosis. If your employer covers Hinge Health or Sword, start there. The full comparison is on [Walkito vs Hinge Health](https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-hinge-health/).

### See a clinician first if

- your pain followed an injury or a fall
- the pain is severe or stops you doing normal activities
- it has not improved after about two weeks of home care, or keeps getting worse
- the pain comes with numbness, tingling or swelling
- you have diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) gives you the plantar fascia stretch, calf stretches with the knee straight and bent, and strength work that gets harder over time, on 3, 5 or 7 days a week. It is a weekly or yearly subscription; the price is shown in the store.

#### Can I use Hinge Health without insurance or an employer?

No. Hinge Health is only for people covered through a partner employer or health plan, and it does not sell its program to individuals. Its page for individuals is an eligibility check, not a sign-up with a price.

#### Is Sword Health free?

Sword says it may be offered at no cost through your employer or health plan. It does not publish a self-pay price in the US, so if your plan does not cover it you cannot buy it directly.

Vori Health works with insurance including Medicare Advantage, and Luna sends a physical therapist to your home and takes Medicare. Medicare covers telehealth from home through December 31, 2027.

## Exakt Health alternatives: which app fits you instead?

Language: English · https://walkito.site/exakt-health-alternatives/ · published 2026-10-12 · updated 2026-10-12

The best Exakt Health alternative depends on why you want one. For a lower price, Injurymap lists $9.49 a month or $40.99 a year with a two-week free trial; for many body areas and a big video library, Prehab; for a free first phase, Sports Injury Rehabilitation; for running form, GaitLab Coach; with an employer plan, Hinge Health; and for heel pain or [flat feet](https://walkito.site/flat-feet/) only, Walkito. For a runner who wants injury rehab and a return-to-running plan in one app, Exakt is still the strongest pick.

- Exakt Health costs $19.99 a month, $39.99 for 3 months or $59.99 for 6 months, with a 7-day free trial (exakthealth.com, checked October 2026).
- Injurymap is the cheapest paid alternative we found: $9.49 a month or $40.99 a year in the US App Store, with a two-week free trial. Like Exakt, it is CE-marked as a medical device.
- Sports Injury Rehabilitation gives phase 1 of every program free; GaitLab Coach is free, with a $4.99 one-time full report.
- Hinge Health costs $0, but only through an employer or health plan; you cannot buy it yourself.
- Walkito covers heel pain, plantar fasciitis and flat feet only, on iPhone and Android. It is a weekly or yearly subscription, with the current price shown in the store.

### Which Exakt Health alternatives are there?

Prices are as each app publishes them in the US, checked in October 2026. They can differ by country and change over time, so check the store before you subscribe.

### Why look for an Exakt Health alternative?

Exakt Health is a good app. It has 15+ injury rehab plans, running plans from 5K to marathon, 600+ exercise videos, a 4.8 rating from 125 ratings on the App Store, and it is certified as a medical device in the EU. People still look elsewhere for a few reasons:

- The price: about $120 a year for the cheapest rehab option (the 6-month plan bought twice).
- Their pain is not from running, and they do not need a run plan.
- They want shorter sessions than Exakt’s typical 15 to 30 minutes.
- Their employer or health plan already covers another program.
- They want an app that focuses on one problem, like heel pain or flat feet.

### Which app is the closest alternative to Exakt Health?

**Prehab** is the closest in breadth. The Prehab Guys app is built by Doctors of Physical Therapy and has 55+ programs, 170+ workouts and 4,000+ exercise videos, including a plantar fasciitis program. It costs more ($49 a month, or about $200 a year), sessions run about 20 minutes, and it is iPhone only and English only.

**Injurymap** is the closest in setup. Like Exakt, it is CE-marked as a medical device. Its listing says its 350+ exercises were selected by medical specialists, that it adjusts your program as you go, and it covers Achilles, ankle, arch, back, elbow, hip, knee, neck and shoulder pain. It has no running plans. It has a 4.2 rating from 80 ratings on the App Store.

**Sports Injury Rehabilitation** is the closest in rehab style. Its programs, by named sports physiotherapists Phil Pask and Paul Tanner, move you through phases when you meet set criteria, for injuries such as ankle sprain, plantar fasciitis, calf strain, shin splints and hamstring strain. Phase 1 of every program is free.

### Is there a cheaper alternative to Exakt Health?

Yes. Over a year, Exakt’s cheapest rehab option comes to about $120. These cost less:

- Injurymap: $40.99 a year or $9.49 a month, after a two-week free trial.

- GaitLab Coach: free for basic running form checks; the full report with a 4-week drill plan is $4.99 once.

- [PlantarCare](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/plantarcare-heel-pain-tracker/id6789899136): free with no in-app purchases, iPhone only, for heel pain only ([Walkito vs PlantarCare](https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-plantarcare/)).

Walkito is a weekly or yearly subscription. The current price for your country is shown in the App Store or Google Play before you subscribe.

If you run, no alternative here replaces Exakt’s return-to-running plans. **GaitLab Coach** does something different: you film yourself running for about 60 seconds, pick up to 4 of 16 running injuries, and it ranks the form habits most likely linked to your pain. Its listing cites a 2018 trial in which new runners who retrained their gait had 62% fewer injuries over a year, and it says it is a coaching tool, not a substitute for a physio.
