## Best app for flat feet: 5 apps compared

Language: English · https://walkito.site/best-app-for-flat-feet/ · published 2026-10-12 · updated 2026-10-12

No flat feet app has been tested in a published trial, so there is no proven best one: the research supports the exercises, not any app. The most focused arch trainer is Arch: Flat Feet Trainer ($9.99 a month or $39.99 a year, iPhone); ArchFix is free and adds a footprint check; Injurymap covers arch pain along with other joints; and Walkito puts arch work into a plan that adjusts to morning pain. Exercise can ease flat feet pain, but in a review of 10 trials it did not realign the foot.

- None of the flat feet apps we found has a published trial; the trials are of the exercises.
- In a trial of 52 people with flexible flat feet, six weeks of short-foot, ankle, hip and stretching work changed arch shape more than in a control group (Brijwasi and Borkar, 2023).
- In a network meta-analysis of 10 trials, exercise and foot orthoses reduced pain in adult flat feet but did not realign foot posture (Hoang and colleagues, 2021).
- Arch: Flat Feet Trainer costs $9.99 a month or $39.99 a year with a 7-day free trial on the yearly plan; ArchFix showed nothing to buy (App Store, checked October 2026).
- Walkito is on iPhone and Android, as a weekly or yearly subscription with the current price shown in the store.

### Which apps are there for flat feet?

Prices are as each app publishes them in the US, checked in October 2026. They can differ by country and change, so check the store before you pay.

### What should a flat feet app include?

First, a check that your flat feet are **flexible**: the arch comes back when you lift the foot or stand on tiptoe. The trials were run on flexible flat feet, and exercise will not change the shape of a rigid one. Then look for:

- The [short foot exercise](https://walkito.site/exercises/short-foot-exercise/) and other arch work that gets harder over weeks.
- Ankle, hip and calf work, since the program that changed arch shape included them.
- A way to go easier on a bad day, and clear advice on when to see a clinician.
- No promise of a new arch: in a 2024 review of the short foot exercise, there was no clear overall change in arch height; only programs longer than 6 weeks showed one.

Source: Brijwasi T, Borkar P. A comprehensive exercise program improves foot alignment in people with flexible flat foot: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2023;69(1):42–46.
Source: Cheng J, Han D, Qu J, et al. Effects of short foot training on foot posture in patients with flatfeet: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Back and Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation. 2024;37(4):839–851.

### Arch: Flat Feet Trainer: the most focused

Arch is built only for flat feet and arch strength. It has 40+ foot exercises with illustrations and audio coaching, custom routines, streaks, a calendar and reminders. It costs $9.99 a month or $39.99 a year, with a 7-day free trial on the yearly plan, and all features need a subscription. It has a 4.3 rating from 6 ratings.

Its listing says “See significant results in just 6 weeks” and “BACKED BY SCIENCE” without naming a study or a clinician. Its App Store privacy label lists purchases, identifiers and usage data as used to track you. It is iPhone only.

### ArchFix: free, with a footprint check

ArchFix lets you make a footprint at home with paper and paint or a wet foot, then checks the photo for signs of flat feet. It adds preventive and corrective exercises with videos and text, your own exercise plans, reminders, and repeat footprint scans to track change. The App Store listing showed it free with nothing to buy.

It says it is not a substitute for a diagnosis. In our heel pain apps study, its website called its exercises “clinically validated” without citing a study. It has too few ratings to show a score.

### Injurymap: arch pain and other joints

Injurymap is a general pain app that lists arch pain among the areas it covers, with Achilles, ankle, knee, hip, back, neck, shoulder and elbow pain. Its listing says its 350+ exercises were selected by medical specialists and that it adjusts your program as you go. It is CE-marked as a medical device in the EU.

It costs $9.49 a month or $40.99 a year after a two-week free trial, and has a 4.2 rating from 80 ratings. It does not have a flat-feet-only program, so it fits best if your arch is one of several sore spots.

### How to Do Foot Exercises: a free list on Android

This Android app offers general foot exercises for free, with ads. It names no clinician and has no plan that changes over time. It is fine as a reminder of what to do; for a plan, our [flat feet exercises guide](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-exercises/) gives doses, how often, and when to stop, for free.

### Walkito: what it does and what it does not

Walkito’s flat feet work starts with towel scrunches and big toe lifts, then moves up through three versions of the short foot, with toe spreads, band turn-ins, a single-leg hold, hip abduction and calf stretches around them. Each morning a check-in makes a bad day lighter, and every 14 days a test measures your arch hold, calf raises and balance and compares left and right.

It is on iPhone and Android, with sessions of 3, 5 or 10 minutes on the 3, 5 or 7 days a week you pick. It is a weekly or yearly subscription; the price is shown in the store. It launched in October 2026 and has no ratings yet.

### Can an app change flat feet?

Not reliably. Exercise and insoles reduced pain in adult flat feet in a review of 10 trials, but did not realign the foot, and exercise, alone or with insoles, did better for pain than insoles alone. One trial of flexible flat feet did find a change in arch shape after six weeks of a full program. So the honest goal of a flat feet app is less pain and stronger, steadier feet, not a new arch.

Source: Hoang NT, Chen S, Chou LW. The Impact of Foot Orthoses and Exercises on Pain and Navicular Drop for Adult Flatfoot: A Network Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2021;18(15).
Source: Brijwasi T, Borkar P. A comprehensive exercise program improves foot alignment in people with flexible flat foot: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2023;69(1):42–46.

### Do you need an app for flat feet at all?

No. The exercises from the trials can be done from a sheet: our [flat feet exercises guide](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-exercises/) has them with doses. An app mostly adds reminders, progression and tracking, which help some people keep going. If you also have heel pain, see our [plantar fasciitis app guide](https://walkito.site/best-app-for-plantar-fasciitis/); for other foot problems, our [foot pain apps by problem](https://walkito.site/best-apps-for-foot-pain/).

### How we checked these apps

On October 12, 2026 we read the US App Store listings of Arch: Flat Feet Trainer, ArchFix and Injurymap. Android availability and How to Do Foot Exercises are from our [foot pain apps check](https://walkito.site/best-apps-for-foot-pain/) of October 11, 2026. We read listings and websites; we did not test the apps from the inside. Walkito facts come from its store listings and the app itself.

### See a clinician first if

- one arch has flattened suddenly as an adult
- the arch stays flat when the foot is off the ground
- you have pain or swelling on the inside of the ankle
- your foot pain followed an injury, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- you have numbness, tingling or burning
- you have diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet

### If you want a plan for your arches

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) builds the arch exercises into a plan for the 3, 5 or 7 days a week you pick, in sessions of 3, 5 or 10 minutes, and tests your arch hold, calf raises and balance every 14 days so you can see what changes.

#### What is the best app for flat feet?

There is no proven best one, because no flat feet app has a published trial. Arch: Flat Feet Trainer is the most focused, ArchFix is free with a footprint check, Injurymap covers arch pain with other joints, and Walkito adjusts arch work to morning pain. Pick one with short foot exercises that get harder over time.

#### Is there a free app for flat feet exercises?

Yes. ArchFix showed nothing to buy in the App Store in October 2026 and is also on Android, and How to Do Foot Exercises is free with ads on Android. Arch and Injurymap offer free trials before a subscription. Our flat feet exercises guide is free and has the exercises from the trials with doses.

#### Can exercises fix flat feet?

Exercises can ease flat feet pain, but they did not realign the foot in a review of 10 trials. A 2024 review of the short foot exercise found no clear overall change in arch height, except in programs longer than 6 weeks. Expect less pain and stronger feet, not a new arch.

#### How long do flat feet exercises take to work?

In the trial of 52 people with flexible flat feet, the program ran for six weeks. In a 2024 review of the short foot exercise, only programs longer than 6 weeks showed a change in arch height. Plan on at least six weeks of regular work before you judge it.

#### Is there a flat feet app for Android?

Yes. ArchFix, Injurymap, How to Do Foot Exercises and Walkito are on Android. Arch: Flat Feet Trainer is iPhone only. Walkito reads steps, exercise sessions, distance and sleep from Health Connect on Android and steps, sleep and walking data from Apple Health on iPhone.

#### Are flat feet apps for kids?

Walkito is built for adults. Flat feet in young children are usually normal: in one study of 835 children, 54 percent of 3-year-olds had flat feet and 24 percent of 6-year-olds did. A child whose foot hurts, is stiff or is flat on one side only should see a clinician. See our [flat feet in kids guide](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-in-kids/).

## Best insoles for plantar fasciitis: what the trials show

Language: English · https://walkito.site/best-insoles-for-plantar-fasciitis/ · published 2026-10-11 · updated 2026-10-23

Going by the trials, the best insole for plantar fasciitis to try first is a firm, contoured store-bought arch support (about $50 to $70) or a silicone heel cup (about $18). No trial crowns a brand, and in trials that compared them, custom insoles did no better than store-bought ones. Use it together with stretching and strengthening: the 2023 guideline advises against relying on insoles alone for short-term pain relief. Relying on insoles alone is one of the [reasons plantar fasciitis does not get better](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-not-getting-better/). Any benefit is modest and may take several weeks.

- The 2023 guideline grades insoles used alone for short-term pain relief B against, and says clinicians may use them combined with other care (grade C), custom or store-bought.
- Custom insoles were no better than store-bought ones: a review of 19 trials found no difference at any time point.
- In a trial of 236 people who all stretched, 95% improved with a silicone heel pad and 68% with a custom orthotic after 8 weeks.
- A firm, supportive insole beat soft foam in a small trial, and soft thin foam was the fake (sham) insole in another.
- “Clinically proven” on the insole product pages we checked came with no linked study, and the APMA seal is not a product test: APMA says it “is not a testing laboratory”.

### Do insoles help plantar fasciitis?

A little, and mostly as an add-on. Compared with fake (sham) insoles, real ones gave a small reduction in pain, not function, between weeks 7 and 12 in one review of 19 trials, which may be too small to notice. Another review found no difference from sham insoles in the short term, and a later trial of 185 adults found none at three months.

In a trial of 103 people, a steroid injection did better at week 4 and arch-contouring insoles did better at week 12, but neither difference was large enough to matter much to patients. So expect insoles to help gradually, if at all, not overnight.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Whittaker GA, Munteanu SE, Menz HB, Tan JM, Rabusin CL, Landorf KB. Foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(5):322–328.
Source: Rasenberg N, Riel H, Rathleff MS, et al. Efficacy of foot orthoses for the treatment of plantar heel pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(16):1040–1046.
Source: Rasenberg N, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, Fuit L, et al. Custom insoles versus sham and GP-led usual care in patients with plantar heel pain: results of the STAP-study - a randomised controlled trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(5):272–278.
Source: Whittaker GA, Munteanu SE, Menz HB, et al. Effectiveness of Foot Orthoses Versus Corticosteroid Injection for Plantar Heel Pain: The SOOTHE Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2019;49(7):491–500.

### Plantar fasciitis insoles compared

List prices on each maker’s own site, checked October 11, 2026. These are the insoles review sites pick most often; we did not test them and do not rank them. “APMA seal” means the product is in the American Podiatric Medical Association’s seal database; “No” means it is not listed, not that it failed anything. Powerstep insoles were used in a published study, and a heel cup from Medi-Dyne, the maker of Tuli’s, was given to everyone in another trial. We found no published studies of the other products, searching abstracts and open full texts.

Source: Ring K, Otter S. Clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness of bespoke and prefabricated foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a prospective cohort study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2014;12(1):1–10.
Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, et al. Does a corticosteroid injection plus exercise or exercise alone add to the effect of patient advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy? A randomised clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57(18):1180–1186.

### Are custom orthotics better than store-bought insoles?

Not in trials. The guideline says the evidence “clearly finds a similarity in outcomes between custom and prefabricated orthoses”. Some related trials:

- In a trial of 135 people, firm-foam store-bought insoles and semirigid custom ones both improved function a little more than soft sham insoles at three months, but not at 12 months.
- In a trial of 142 people, low-cost foam insoles, prefabricated or customized, had similar effects after 8 weeks.
- In a study that was not randomized, with 67 people completing it, custom insoles did no better than prefabricated Powerstep insoles, which were 38% cheaper per patient.
- In a trial of 185 adults, custom insoles did no better than sham insoles, and a cost analysis found them not cost-effective compared with usual care from a family doctor.

Custom orthotics often cost $300 to $800, according to [GoodRx](https://www.goodrx.com/conditions/musculoskeletal/custom-orthotics-cost); see our [cost guide](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-treatment-cost/). One best-practice guide puts custom orthoses as a later step, at about three months, after shockwave therapy, if improvement is still suboptimal.

Source: Whittaker GA, Munteanu SE, Menz HB, Tan JM, Rabusin CL, Landorf KB. Foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(5):322–328.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Landorf KB, Keenan AM, Herbert RD. Effectiveness of foot orthoses to treat plantar fasciitis: a randomized trial. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2006;166(12):1305–1310.
Source: Baldassin V, Gomes CR, Beraldo PS. Effectiveness of prefabricated and customized foot orthoses made from low-cost foam for noncomplicated plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2009;90(4):701–6.
Source: Ring K, Otter S. Clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness of bespoke and prefabricated foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a prospective cohort study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2014;12(1):1–10.
Source: Rasenberg N, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, Fuit L, et al. Custom insoles versus sham and GP-led usual care in patients with plantar heel pain: results of the STAP-study - a randomised controlled trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(5):272–278.
Source: Rasenberg N, van Middelkoop M, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, El Alili M, Bindels P, Bosmans J. Cost-effectiveness of custom-made insoles versus usual care in patients with plantar heel pain in primary care: cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open. 2021;11(11):e051866.
Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.

### Heel cup or full-length arch support?

The evidence points both ways. That older trial favoured simple heel pads. A later review concluded that contoured full-length insoles relieve plantar fasciitis symptoms better than heel cups, and in a pressure study in older adults, a prefabricated contoured insole gave a fivefold greater reduction in heel pressure than the next best insert, including a silicone heel cup.

A heel cup is cheaper and fits more shoes; a full-length arch support has more support behind it in recent research. Either can be a first try alongside exercise.

Source: Pfeffer G, Bacchetti P, Deland J, et al. Comparison of custom and prefabricated orthoses in the initial treatment of proximal plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle International. 1999;20(4):214–21.
Source: Schuitema D, Greve C, Postema K, Dekker R, Hijmans JM. Effectiveness of mechanical treatment for plantar fasciitis: a systematic review. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;29(5):657–674.
Source: Bonanno DR, Landorf KB, Menz HB. Pressure-relieving properties of various shoe inserts in older people with plantar heel pain. Gait & Posture. 2011;33(3):385–9.

### What should you look for in a plantar fasciitis insole?

- **Firm, contoured arch support rather than soft foam.** In a small 3-week trial of 30 adults, a foam-covered rigid insole reduced pain more than a soft supportive foam one, and a thin flat insole had no significant effect. In another trial, soft thin foam was used as the fake insole.
- **A heel cup** that cradles the heel.
- **A fit that works in your shoes.** Full-length insoles usually replace the shoe’s own insole; heel cups fit more shoes.
- **No magnets.** In a trial in JAMA, magnetic insoles gave no extra benefit over the same insoles without magnets.

Source: Walther M, Kratschmer B, Verschl J, et al. Effect of different orthotic concepts as first line treatment of plantar fasciitis. Foot and Ankle Surgery. 2013;19(2):103–7.
Source: Landorf KB, Keenan AM, Herbert RD. Effectiveness of foot orthoses to treat plantar fasciitis: a randomized trial. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2006;166(12):1305–1310.
Source: Winemiller MH, Billow RG, Laskowski ER, et al. Effect of magnetic vs sham-magnetic insoles on plantar heel pain: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003;290(11):1474–8.

### What do “clinically proven” and the APMA seal mean?

Less than they sound. The PowerStep, Dr. Scholl’s and Superfeet product pages say “clinically proven” without linking a study; Superfeet’s line is brand-wide: “clinically proven to decrease fatigue, reduce injury, and improve comfort”. Dr. Scholl’s says its plantar fasciitis insole “Immediately relieves heel pain & prevents it from coming back”; we found no trial support for that claim for any insole.

The [APMA seal](https://www.apma.org/seal-db) means the product has the podiatrists’ association’s Seal of Acceptance, but APMA says it “is not a testing laboratory” and does not compare products against each other.

### How to use insoles with exercise

The guideline supports insoles only alongside other care, and the exercises have stronger grades: plantar fascia and calf stretching A, strengthening B. In one trial in which everyone wore shoe inserts, heel raises with a towel under the toes gave faster improvement than stretching.

Wear the insoles in the shoes you use most, and do the [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) every week. Our page on [insoles vs exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) covers the trials behind combining them.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### When should you see a podiatrist?

See a podiatrist or doctor if the pain has not improved after about two weeks of home care ([NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heel-pain/)), or sooner for the warning signs below. If you have diabetes, get your feet checked: Medicare covers therapeutic shoes and inserts only for people with diabetes and severe diabetes-related foot disease ([Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/therapeutic-shoes-inserts)).

### See a clinician first if

- your heel pain followed an injury or a fall
- the pain is severe or stops you doing normal activities
- it has not improved after about two weeks of home care, or keeps getting worse
- the pain comes with numbness, tingling or swelling
- you have diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet

### Pair your insoles with the exercises

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) gives you the plantar fascia stretch, calf stretches with the knee straight and bent, and strength work that gets harder over time, on 3, 5 or 7 days a week. It is a weekly or yearly subscription; the price is shown in the store.

#### Which insoles have clinical evidence for plantar fasciitis?

No brand has strong trial evidence behind it. Of the 12 insoles we compared, only two makers turned up in the published studies we found: Powerstep insoles were used in one study that was not randomized, and a heel cup from Medi-Dyne, the maker of Tuli’s, was given to everyone in a trial, so that trial does not show what the heel cup alone did. What the trials point to is a type, not a brand: a firm, contoured store-bought arch support or a silicone heel cup, used with stretching and strengthening.

#### Do insoles really work for plantar fasciitis?

Modestly, and best alongside exercise. The 2023 guideline advises against relying on insoles alone for short-term pain relief but allows them combined with other care. Trials against fake insoles are mixed, with at most a small benefit after several weeks.

#### Are expensive insoles better than cheap ones?

Trials have not shown it. Custom insoles did no better than store-bought ones in a review of 19 trials, and prefabricated foam insoles matched customized foam insoles in a trial of 142 people.

#### Should plantar fasciitis insoles be soft or firm?

Firm and supportive did better in a small trial that compared them, and soft thin foam was used as the fake insole in another trial. Comfort still matters, since you have to wear them.

#### Are heel cups good for plantar fasciitis?

They can be. In a 1999 trial, 95% of people with a silicone heel pad improved, but a later review found contoured full-length insoles worked better than heel cups. Either is a reasonable cheap first try with exercise.

## Walkito vs Exakt Health: which one fits you?

Language: English · https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-exakt-health/ · published 2026-10-04 · updated 2026-10-13

Walkito and Exakt Health both offer exercise-based plans for [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/), but they are built for different people. Exakt is a runner's app with 15+ injury rehab plans and a return-to-running program. Walkito is a narrower app focused on heel pain, [flat feet](https://walkito.site/flat-feet/) and daily pain adaptation. This page compares them honestly, says where Exakt is the better choice, and explains what Walkito does differently.

- Exakt Health covers 15+ running injuries and includes running training plans from 5K to marathon. Walkito covers heel pain, flat feet and shin pain only.
- Both apps are on iOS and Android. Walkito arrived on Google Play in October 2026.
- Exakt Health is certified as a medical device in the EU. Walkito is not a medical device.
- Walkito adjusts each session from a morning pain check-in and tests left-right asymmetry every 14 days. Exakt adapts its plan from end-of-session feedback.
- Exakt costs $19.99/month or $59.99 for six months. Walkito is a weekly or yearly subscription, with the current price shown in the store.

### Side-by-side comparison

Every Exakt fact below was checked against the Exakt Health App Store listing, Google Play listing and exakthealth.com in October 2026. Every Walkito fact comes from the Walkito App Store and Google Play listings, walkito.site and the app's own source code.

Looking for a free heel pain tracker rather than a plan? See [Walkito vs PlantarCare](https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-plantarcare/). Want a short fixed routine? See [Walkito vs the Plantar Fasciitis Exercises app](https://walkito.site/walkito-vs-plantar-fasciitis-exercises-app/).

### Who is Exakt Health built for?

Exakt Health is built for runners. That is its core identity, and everything in the app reflects it. If you are a runner recovering from plantar fasciitis, [Achilles tendinopathy](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/), an ankle sprain, a hamstring strain or a meniscus tear, Exakt has a specific rehab plan for your injury. It covers over 15 different conditions.

Each rehab plan ends with a walk-run return-to-running program, which is one of the hardest parts of recovery to get right on your own. The app also has running training plans for every distance from couch to 5K through to marathon.

Exakt was founded in 2021 by Philip Billaudelle, Lucia Payo and Maryke Louw. It is built by licensed sports physiotherapists and running coaches, and it raised about EUR 2.2 million in seed funding in September 2024. The team is based in Berlin.

The app is certified as a medical device in the EU, meaning it has passed regulatory review for its intended use.

**If you are a runner who needs both injury rehab and a structured training plan, Exakt is hard to match.** Its 4.8 rating across 125 iOS reviews and 100K+ Android downloads show that it works for its audience.

### Who is Walkito built for?

Walkito is built for people whose feet hurt and who want a short exercise plan, on 3, 5 or 7 days a week they choose, that adjusts to how they feel each morning. That includes:

- Plantar fasciitis.
- Flexible flat feet.
- Shin pain.

It is also built for people on their feet all day: nurses, retail workers, warehouse staff.

The app is narrower than Exakt. It does not cover knee injuries, hamstring strains or running plans. What it does differently is **adjust each day's session from a morning pain check-in** rather than end-of-session feedback.

A morning of 7/10 or higher switches the day to about three minutes of seated work. A big day on your feet (measured through Apple Health steps on iPhone or Health Connect on Android) turns the next strength session into a lighter recovery one.

Walkito tests progress every 14 days with calf raises, an arch hold and [single-leg balance](https://walkito.site/exercises/single-leg-balance/), and compares your left side with your right. That left-right comparison is something most apps in this space do not track.

Walkito was released on October 2, 2026. It is on iPhone and, since October 2026, on Android. It is new and has few ratings so far. It does not have the track record or breadth that Exakt has built since 2021.

### How does each app build your plan?

Exakt asks about your injury, your experience level, and your weekly schedule, then assigns you a structured rehab plan with levels. You progress through levels based on how each session goes. When rehab is done, you can switch directly to a running training plan without starting over.

Walkito asks about pain location, which side, your activity level, your goal, and how many days and minutes you have. It builds a weekly plan around measured goals:

- Pain-free mornings.
- A 60-second arch hold.
- 25 single-leg calf raises.
- 30-second single-leg balance.
- Left-right symmetry.

Each week it rebuilds the plan from how the previous week went. One goal is the focus at a time. When a goal is reached, it moves to maintaining and the next goal starts.

The main difference: Exakt follows a structured level-based progression. Walkito follows a goal-based progression where each morning's check-in adjusts the day's intensity.

### Which conditions does each app cover?

**This is where Exakt is clearly stronger.** Its rehab plans cover plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, ankle sprains, hamstring strains, meniscus tears, runner's knee and more. If your pain is in your knee, hip or hamstring, Walkito does not have a plan for it.

Walkito covers plantar fasciitis, flat feet (flexible), heel pain from standing, and shin pain. Its exercises follow the 2023 heel pain guideline (stretching grade A, strength grade B) and the Rathleff 2015 trial (loaded heel raises for plantar fasciitis). For those specific conditions, it has exercises, progression logic and pain adaptation. For anything outside that scope, Exakt or a [broader app like Prehab](https://walkito.site/exakt-health-alternatives/) is the right choice.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### How much do Walkito and Exakt Health cost?

Walkito is a free download with a weekly or yearly subscription, billed through the App Store or Google Play. The current price for your country is shown in the store before you subscribe.

Exakt costs $19.99 per month for rehab plans, with 3-month ($39.99) and 6-month ($59.99) options. Running training plans go up to $99.99 per year. Every subscription starts with a 7-day free trial.

If you need only heel or foot pain exercises, Walkito is the narrower, focused option. If you need running injury rehab plus a training plan, Exakt's plans cover more.

### Platforms and languages

Both apps are on iOS and Android, so the platform no longer decides between them. On iPhone, Walkito reads Apple Health. On Android it reads Health Connect (steps, exercise sessions, distance and sleep); walking asymmetry and walking speed are read on iPhone only.

Exakt supports English, French, German and Spanish. Walkito supports English, Russian, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and German. Both cover English, Spanish, French and German. If you need Russian, Portuguese or Italian, Walkito is the only option of the two.

### Privacy

Walkito reads Apple Health data (steps, sleep, walking asymmetry, walking speed, resting heart rate) and keeps it on the device. It is never uploaded. What gets synced to the Walkito account is pain scores, session data and test results. There is no ad tracking.

Exakt Health's App Store privacy label lists Identifiers as data used to track you, and Purchases, Identifiers, Usage Data and Diagnostics as data collected but not linked to your identity. Its Google Play listing states:

- No data is shared with third parties.
- Financial data may be collected.
- Data is encrypted in transit.
- Deletion is available.

Both apps collect standard usage data. **Neither sells health data.** Walkito's on-device approach to Apple Health data is a stricter privacy model.

### What evidence is each app built on?

Exakt Health is certified as a medical device in the EU (Germany), which requires evidence of safety and intended purpose. The app is built by licensed sports physiotherapists. It states that its methods are evidence-based but does not list specific studies on its App Store listing or pricing page.

Walkito lists its evidence sources on its website. Its exercises follow:

- The 2023 clinical guideline for heel pain (Koc et al., JOSPT).
- The Rathleff 2015 trial on heavy heel raises.
- The Brijwasi 2023 trial on flat feet exercises, and others.

Each exercise in the app carries an evidence level (Strong, Moderate, or Early) with a one-line explanation.

**Neither app has published its own clinical trial.** Both rely on existing research applied through their respective programs.

### When is Exakt Health the better choice?

## Plantar fascia stretch: how to do it, sets and reps

Language: English · https://walkito.site/exercises/plantar-fascia-stretch/ · published 2026-10-05 · updated 2026-10-17

The plantar fascia stretch is the single stretch tested head-to-head against Achilles tendon stretching for [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/). In a trial of 82 people with chronic heel pain, those who did the plantar fascia stretch had better pain and function scores at eight weeks than those who stretched the Achilles tendon. This page covers the technique, the dose and when the stretch matters most.

- In a trial of 82 people with chronic plantar fasciitis, the plantar fascia stretch produced better pain and function scores at eight weeks than an Achilles tendon stretch (DiGiovanni and colleagues, 2003).
- At a two-year follow-up, after all participants crossed over to the plantar fascia stretch, 92% reported satisfaction with their outcome (DiGiovanni and colleagues, 2006).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline gives plantar fascia and calf stretching its top grade, A (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- The most important time to do it is before taking the first step in the morning and after sitting for a long period.
- Walkito starts at 10 holds of 10 seconds, each foot. The research protocol was 10 holds of 10 seconds, three times a day.

### How do you do a plantar fascia stretch?

Sit down and cross the foot with heel pain over the opposite knee. With the hand on the same side, pull the toes back toward the shin until you feel a stretch along the arch. Hold for 10 seconds, then release. Repeat 10 times.

To check your position, press your thumb along the arch while holding the stretch. The plantar fascia, the thick band of tissue under the foot, should feel taut and firm. If you only feel it in the calf, you are pulling too far or too fast. Ease off until the stretch sits under the arch.

This is a seated, non-weight-bearing stretch. You do not need to stand up or lean against a wall. It targets the plantar fascia directly, which is why the trial tested it separately from calf stretches.

- **Plantar fascia stretch** (Walkito starts at 10 holds of 10 seconds, each foot. Research protocol: 10 holds of 10 seconds, 3 times daily): Sit and cross the affected foot over the opposite knee. Pull the toes back toward the shin until you feel a stretch along the arch, not the calf. Hold 10 seconds, release, repeat.

Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### When should you stretch the plantar fascia?

**Before your first step in the morning.** That is the single most repeated instruction across both the trial and the 2023 guideline. The plantar fascia shortens overnight while the foot is relaxed. The first steps of the day pull it suddenly and sharply, which is why [morning heel pain](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-in-the-morning/) is the hallmark of plantar fasciitis.

The second most important time is before standing after any long period of sitting. The same shortening happens during rest. Stretching the fascia before loading it reduces that jolt.

In the trial, participants were asked to do 10 holds of 10 seconds, three times a day, for at least eight weeks. The most critical sessions were the morning one and the one after prolonged sitting. More sessions throughout the day were encouraged if possible.

Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Does the plantar fascia stretch actually help plantar fasciitis?

In the original 2003 trial, 82 people with chronic plantar fasciitis lasting more than ten months were randomly assigned to either a plantar fascia stretch or a standard Achilles tendon stretch. At eight weeks, the plantar fascia group scored significantly better on the Foot Function Index, which measures pain and activity limitations. The authors called this a clinically meaningful difference.

A follow-up study tracked the same patients for two years. At the eight-week mark, all participants were switched to the plantar fascia stretch. By two years, 92% of all patients reported satisfaction with their outcome, and the group that originally did Achilles stretching improved markedly once they started the plantar fascia stretch.

The 2023 heel pain guideline reviewed the stretching evidence and gave plantar fascia and calf stretching its highest grade, **A**. That does not mean stretching alone is enough for everyone. The guideline also grades strength training **B** and recommends both. For the strength side, see [calf raises for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/).

Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Malay DP, et al. Plantar fascia-specific stretching exercise improves outcomes in patients with chronic plantar fasciitis: a prospective clinical trial with two-year follow-up. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2006;88(8):1775–1781.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Which stretches help plantar fasciitis?

Three stretches cover the stretching the 2023 heel pain guideline grades **A**: one for the plantar fascia and two for the calf. Walkito starts each at these doses:

- Plantar fascia stretch (this page): sit, cross the foot over the other knee and pull the toes back until you feel it in the arch. 10 holds of 10 seconds, each foot.
- [Calf stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/): hands on a wall, back leg straight, back heel flat on the floor. 3 holds of 30 seconds, each leg.
- [Soleus stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/): the same position with the back knee bent, so the stretch moves lower, toward the heel. 3 holds of 30 seconds, each leg.

Do them together rather than picking one. Limited ankle bend, usually from a tight calf, is a risk factor for plantar fasciitis on its own (Riddle and colleagues, 2003), and the plantar fascia stretch works on the tissue under the arch directly. Stretching is one part of the routine: foot and ankle strength work gets a **B** from the same guideline. The full routine is in [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.

### How is the plantar fascia stretch different from a calf stretch?

They target different structures. The [calf stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/) lengthens the gastrocnemius, the big, more superficial calf muscle, through the Achilles tendon. The plantar fascia stretch pulls the toes back to load the fascia directly under the arch. The two are connected through the heel bone but respond to different positions.

A [tight calf](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/) is a risk factor for plantar fasciitis on its own. In a case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 controls, reduced ankle dorsiflexion, how far the foot bends up toward the shin, was the strongest independent risk factor. That is why the guideline recommends both stretches, not one or the other.

For the deeper calf muscle, the soleus, the stretch changes: you bend the back knee to shift the load from the gastrocnemius to the soleus. That is a separate exercise. See [soleus stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/).

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### What are the common mistakes with the plantar fascia stretch?

- **Pulling the toes too hard.** The stretch should feel firm under the arch, not painful. If you are wincing, you are past the useful range. Ease back until you feel a pull without a sharp edge.
- **Feeling it in the calf instead of the arch.** If the stretch is mostly in the calf, the knee is too straight or the pull is too aggressive. Cross the foot higher on the opposite knee so the ankle relaxes, and focus on the toes bending back rather than the whole foot.
- **Skipping the morning stretch.** This is the single session that has the most effect on the worst moment of the day. Keep a note on the nightstand or set a reminder. The stretch takes about two minutes, and it is worth doing before the foot hits the floor.
- **Bouncing.** Hold still for the full 10 seconds. Bouncing does not give the fascia time to lengthen and can irritate the tissue further.

### Easier and harder versions

If crossing the leg is uncomfortable, keep both feet on the floor and use a towel or belt looped around the ball of the foot. Pull the towel toward you so the toes bend back. The stretch is the same, just from a different angle.

A harder version is a standing plantar fascia stretch: place the ball of the foot against a wall with the heel on the ground and lean in gently. This adds bodyweight into the stretch and is harder to dose precisely. It works once the seated version feels easy and does not provoke pain.

**The seated version from the trial is the one the evidence is behind.** Start there. The full set of stretches and strength exercises for heel pain is in [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/). For rolling the sole after a stretch session, see [foot roll](https://walkito.site/exercises/foot-roll/).

### Stop and see a clinician if

- pain is sharp enough that you cannot put weight on the foot
- the pain followed an injury, a fall or a sudden pop in the arch
- it comes with numbness, tingling or burning, which can point to nerve entrapment
- the heel is red, warm or swollen
- it wakes you at night or is present at rest
- stretching consistently makes the pain worse rather than better
- it has not improved after several weeks of daily stretching and lighter load

### Doing it as a plan

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) schedules the plantar fascia stretch on most sessions and prompts it before your first step each morning. You do not need to remember the timing or the count. The app builds a plan one week at a time, starting with stretching and adding strength work once pain settles.

#### How long should you hold a plantar fascia stretch?

The trial that tested this stretch used 10-second holds, repeated 10 times, at least three times a day (DiGiovanni 2003). That means each session is about two minutes. Walkito starts at 10 holds of 10 seconds per foot. Holding longer is not necessarily better. Consistency through the day matters more than a single long hold.

#### Should you stretch plantar fasciitis before getting out of bed?

Yes. Before the first step of the day is the most important time. The plantar fascia shortens overnight, and the first steps pull it sharply. Stretching it while still seated on the bed reduces that jolt. Both the trial and the 2023 guideline single this out as the key timing.

#### Can stretching make plantar fasciitis worse?

In the DiGiovanni trial, stretching improved outcomes, not worsened them. If a stretch pushes pain past 6/10, ease off. Too much force or bouncing can irritate the tissue. The stretch should feel firm under the arch, never sharp. If stretching consistently makes pain worse, see a clinician before continuing.

#### Is the plantar fascia stretch or the calf stretch better for plantar fasciitis?

The 2023 heel pain guideline grades both plantar fascia stretching and calf stretching A, its top grade, and recommends both. The plantar fascia stretch targets the arch directly. Calf stretches target a tight calf, which is a separate risk factor. Doing both covers more ground than choosing one.

#### How many times a day should you stretch for plantar fasciitis?

The DiGiovanni trial asked participants to stretch three times a day: before the first step in the morning, before standing after prolonged sitting, and at least one more time. Each session was 10 holds of 10 seconds. More sessions were encouraged if practical.

## Calf stretch for plantar fasciitis: technique, sets and hold time

Language: English · https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/ · published 2026-10-05 · updated 2026-10-05

The calf stretch with a straight knee targets the gastrocnemius, the large, more superficial calf muscle. A tight gastrocnemius limits how far the ankle bends, and in a case-control study of 50 people with [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) and 100 controls, reduced ankle dorsiflexion was the strongest independent risk factor. The 2023 heel pain guideline gives calf stretching its top grade, A.

- Reduced ankle dorsiflexion was the strongest independent risk factor for plantar fasciitis in a matched case-control study, at 23.3 times the odds (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).
- In a series of 254 people with plantar fasciitis, 52 to 60 percent had a contracture isolated to the gastrocnemius (Patel and DiGiovanni, 2011).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching A, its top grade (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- A 2020 meta-analysis found a large treatment effect for calf and plantar fascia stretching, though evidence quality ranged from moderate to very low (Siriphorn and Eksakulkla, 2020).
- Walkito starts at 3 holds of 30 seconds, each leg.

### How do you do a calf stretch with a straight knee?

Stand facing a wall with your hands flat against it at about shoulder height. Step one foot back about two feet. Keep the back leg straight, the heel pressed into the floor and the toes pointing forward. Lean your hips toward the wall until you feel a stretch in the upper part of the back calf. Hold for 30 seconds, then switch legs.

**The key is keeping the back knee locked straight.** That isolates the gastrocnemius, which crosses both the knee and the ankle. If you bend the knee, the stretch shifts to the soleus, the deeper calf muscle, and that is a different exercise. See [soleus stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/) for that version.

- **Calf stretch (straight knee)** (Walkito starts at 3 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Hands on a wall. Step one foot back, keep that knee straight and the heel down. Lean the hips forward until you feel a stretch in the upper calf. Hold 30 seconds.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### Why does a tight calf muscle cause heel pain?

The gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel through the Achilles tendon. The plantar fascia picks up where the Achilles leaves off, wrapping under the heel bone and running forward to the toes. When the gastrocnemius is tight, it limits how far the ankle can bend upward. That forces the plantar fascia to absorb more strain with every step.

In a matched case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 controls, reduced ankle dorsiflexion raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 23.3 times. That was stronger than BMI, standing time or any other variable in the study.

Separately, a review of 254 people with plantar fasciitis found that 52 to 60 percent had a contracture isolated to the gastrocnemius, and another 23 to 30 percent had a combined gastrocnemius-soleus contracture. In other words, **a tight calf is not a side issue.** It is present in most people with this condition.

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Patel A, DiGiovanni B. Association between plantar fasciitis and isolated contracture of the gastrocnemius. Foot & Ankle International. 2011;32(1):5–8.

### Does the calf stretch help plantar fasciitis?

The 2023 heel pain guideline reviewed the available stretching studies and gave plantar fascia and calf stretching a grade of **A**, its highest. That grade covers both the plantar fascia stretch and the calf stretch together, because most protocols include both.

A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled the stretching trials and found a large treatment effect for both calf stretching and plantar fascia stretching. The authors rated the evidence quality as moderate to very low and called for higher-quality trials. Even so, the effect size was large and comparable to other interventions.

No single trial isolates the straight-knee calf stretch on its own for plantar fasciitis. It is always tested as part of a program. The guideline recommends it alongside the [plantar fascia stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/plantar-fascia-stretch/) and strength work like [calf raises](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-raises/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Siriphorn A, Eksakulkla S. Calf stretching and plantar fascia-specific stretching for plantar fasciitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies. 2020;24(4):222–232.

### What are the common mistakes with the calf stretch?

- **Bending the back knee.** The moment the knee bends, the gastrocnemius goes slack and the stretch moves to the soleus. Keep the back knee locked straight throughout the hold.
- **Letting the back heel lift.** If the heel comes off the floor, the calf is not being stretched. Press the heel down first, then lean forward until the stretch appears.
- **Turning the back foot outward.** When the foot rotates out, the stretch hits the outside of the calf instead of the full muscle. Keep the toes pointed straight at the wall.
- **Holding too short.** A 10-second hold is not long enough for a sustained stretch to have an effect on tissue length. Hold for at least 30 seconds per rep.

### Who should do this stretch and who should skip it?

This stretch is relevant for anyone with heel pain, plantar fasciitis, [tight calves](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/) from standing all day or a sport that loads the calf, like running. It appears in the exercise lists for [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/), [feet that hurt from standing](https://walkito.site/feet-hurt-standing-all-day/) and [heel pain from running](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/).

Skip it or modify it if you have an Achilles tendon problem that is actively painful during the stretch. In that case, the pain is coming from a different structure, and loading the Achilles through a wall stretch may not be the right starting point. See [Achilles tendonitis exercises](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/) for the Achilles-specific approach.

If you cannot reach the wall or stand comfortably, a seated towel stretch gives a similar pull on the calf. Loop a towel around the ball of the foot, keep the knee straight and pull the toes toward you.

### How the calf stretch fits with the soleus stretch

The gastrocnemius and the soleus together make up the calf. The straight-knee version stretches the gastrocnemius. The bent-knee version stretches the soleus. They are two exercises, not two versions of the same one.

Most programs for plantar fasciitis include both, because a tight calf can be tight in either muscle or both. The guideline does not separate them. Walkito programs both on the same session when stretching is on the schedule.

The [soleus stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/) page covers the bent-knee version. For the full stretching and strength program, see [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Stop and see a clinician if

- the pain is in the Achilles tendon itself, not in the calf muscle
- you feel a sudden pop or tearing sensation during the stretch
- the calf is swollen, red or warm on one side only
- the pain followed an injury or a fall
- numbness, tingling or burning accompanies the calf tightness
- it has not improved after several weeks of daily stretching

### Doing it as a plan

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) schedules the calf stretch alongside the soleus stretch and the plantar fascia stretch on most sessions. You pick 3, 5 or 7 days a week and sessions of 3, 5 or 10 minutes. The app moves from stretching into strength work at your pace.

#### How long should you hold a calf stretch for plantar fasciitis?

Most protocols use 30-second holds, and that is what Walkito starts with. The 2023 guideline recommends calf stretching without specifying a single hold duration, but most of the trials it draws from used 30 seconds per hold, repeated 2 to 3 times per leg.

#### Should you stretch your calves every day for plantar fasciitis?

The 2023 guideline recommends calf and plantar fascia stretching as part of daily self-care for plantar fasciitis. Walkito schedules calf stretches on most sessions. The stretch is low-load and low-risk, so daily is reasonable as long as it stays below 6/10 pain.

#### What is the difference between a calf stretch and a soleus stretch?

The calf stretch with a straight knee targets the gastrocnemius, the large, more superficial calf muscle. The soleus stretch bends the back knee, which lets the gastrocnemius go slack and isolates the deeper soleus. Over half of people with plantar fasciitis had only the gastrocnemius tight, and 23 to 30 percent had both calf muscles tight (Patel and DiGiovanni, 2011).

#### Can tight calves cause plantar fasciitis?

A tight calf limits ankle dorsiflexion, and that was the strongest independent risk factor for plantar fasciitis in a case-control study (23.3 times the odds). Separately, 52 to 60 percent of 254 people with plantar fasciitis had an isolated gastrocnemius contracture. A tight calf does not guarantee plantar fasciitis, but it raises the odds substantially.

## Soleus stretch (bent knee): technique, sets and why it matters

Language: English · https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/ · published 2026-10-05 · updated 2026-10-05

The soleus is the deeper calf muscle that sits underneath the gastrocnemius. It only stretches when the knee is bent, because bending the knee takes the gastrocnemius out of the equation. In a series of 254 people with [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/), 23 to 30 percent had a combined gastrocnemius-soleus contracture. If you only do the straight-knee stretch, you are missing this muscle entirely.

- The soleus crosses only the ankle. The gastrocnemius crosses the knee and the ankle. Bending the knee lets the gastrocnemius go slack so the soleus takes the stretch.
- In 254 people with plantar fasciitis, 23 to 30 percent had a contracture in both the gastrocnemius and the soleus (Patel and DiGiovanni, 2011).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline grades calf stretching A, its top grade, without separating the two calf muscles (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- Walkito starts at 3 holds of 30 seconds, each leg, with the back knee bent.

### How do you do a soleus stretch?

Start in the same wall position as the [calf stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/): hands on a wall, one foot stepped back, heel on the floor. Then bend the back knee. Keep bending until you feel the stretch move lower in the calf, down near the Achilles tendon and the heel. That lower pull is the soleus.

The heel stays on the floor throughout. If the heel lifts, the stretch disappears. You will not feel this one as high in the calf as the straight-knee version. The sensation sits closer to the heel, sometimes just above the back of the ankle. Hold for 30 seconds, then switch.

- **Soleus stretch (bent knee)** (Walkito starts at 3 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Hands on a wall, one foot back, heel down. Bend the back knee until you feel a stretch low in the calf, near the heel. Hold 30 seconds.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Why does the soleus need its own stretch?

The gastrocnemius, the more superficial calf muscle, crosses both the knee and the ankle. When you straighten the knee and lean forward, it takes the stretch. The soleus sits deeper and crosses only the ankle. With a straight knee, the gastrocnemius does all the work and the soleus barely moves.

Bending the knee puts slack into the gastrocnemius so it stops resisting. Now the ankle dorsiflexion pulls on the soleus instead. That is the whole point of the bent-knee version. It is not a modification. **It is a separate exercise for a separate muscle.**

In a review of 254 people with plantar fasciitis, about a quarter had both muscles tight. The straight-knee stretch alone would not have reached the soleus portion of that tightness.

Source: Patel A, DiGiovanni B. Association between plantar fasciitis and isolated contracture of the gastrocnemius. Foot & Ankle International. 2011;32(1):5–8.

### How do you know if the stretch is in the right place?

If you feel the stretch high in the calf, behind the knee, the knee is too straight and the gastrocnemius is taking over. Bend the knee further. The stretch should drop to the lower third of the calf or just above the heel.

If you feel nothing, try stepping the back foot closer to the wall and bending the knee more deeply. Some people need a smaller stance to load the soleus.

If the stretch sits in the Achilles tendon itself and feels sharp rather than like a pull, ease off. **A stretch should feel firm and sustained, not painful.** Pain in the tendon during stretching is different from calf tightness and may point to [Achilles tendonitis](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/).

### What are the common mistakes with the soleus stretch?

- **Not bending the knee enough.** A slight bend is not enough to release the gastrocnemius. You need a real bend, enough that you can see the back knee tracking forward over the toes.
- **Letting the heel lift.** The moment the heel comes off the floor, the stretch vanishes. Press the heel down and let the knee move forward over the foot.
- **Rushing through it.** A 5-second hold is too short for a sustained stretch to affect tissue length. Hold for 30 seconds, and try to relax into the stretch rather than pushing harder.
- **Skipping it because the straight-knee stretch felt like enough.** They are different muscles. If both are tight, you need both stretches.

### How the soleus stretch fits in a program

Walkito pairs the soleus stretch with the [calf stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/) and the [plantar fascia stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/plantar-fascia-stretch/) on most sessions. Together, the three stretches cover the main structures that pull on the heel. The order does not matter much, but doing the plantar fascia stretch first, before the first step of the day, is the most commonly repeated instruction.

For the strength side of the calf, see [calf raises for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/) or the individual [calf raise](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-raises/) page. Strength and stretching are recommended together by the 2023 guideline.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Stop and see a clinician if

- the pain is sharp and localized in the Achilles tendon, not a pull in the muscle
- you feel a sudden pop or tearing during the stretch
- the calf or ankle is swollen, red or warm on one side
- the pain followed an injury or a sudden increase in activity
- numbness or tingling runs down the back of the leg
- it has not improved after several weeks of daily stretching

### Doing it as a plan

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) programs the soleus stretch alongside the calf stretch and the plantar fascia stretch on most sessions. You pick 3, 5 or 7 days a week and sessions of 3, 5 or 10 minutes. The app moves from stretching to strength at your pace, not on a fixed calendar.

#### What does the soleus stretch feel like?

A pull low in the calf, near the Achilles tendon, sometimes just above the back of the ankle. It feels different from the straight-knee calf stretch, which sits higher in the calf. If the stretch is high up, the knee is not bent enough and the gastrocnemius is still doing the work.

#### Is the soleus stretch the same as the calf stretch with a bent knee?

Yes. "Soleus stretch" and "bent-knee calf stretch" are two names for the same exercise. Bending the knee takes the gastrocnemius out of the stretch so that the soleus, the deeper calf muscle, receives the load. The technique is identical.

#### Do you need to stretch both calf muscles for plantar fasciitis?

In 254 people with plantar fasciitis, a quarter had both calf muscles tight (Patel and DiGiovanni, 2011). The guideline grades calf stretching A without separating the two. Most plantar fasciitis programs include both the straight-knee and bent-knee versions, because skipping one leaves half the calf untouched.

#### How often should you do the soleus stretch?

Walkito schedules it on most sessions, alongside the calf stretch. The 2023 guideline recommends calf stretching as part of daily self-care for plantar fasciitis. Three holds of 30 seconds per leg takes about three minutes. It is low-load and safe to repeat daily.

## Foot roll for plantar fasciitis: ball, bottle and technique

Language: English · https://walkito.site/exercises/foot-roll/ · published 2026-10-05 · updated 2026-10-05

Rolling the sole of the foot over a ball or bottle is one of the most common self-care steps for [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/). It feels good, and clinicians recommend it as a way to settle the tissue between sessions. But no randomized trial has tested rolling on its own for plantar fasciitis. This page covers what rolling does, what it does not do, and where a frozen bottle fits in honestly.

- No randomized trial has tested foot rolling as an isolated intervention for plantar fasciitis. It is widely recommended as a comfort and recovery measure, not as a primary intervention.
- The 2023 heel pain guideline recommends stretching (grade A) and strength training (grade B) as the exercise pillars. Rolling is not graded separately.
- A frozen water bottle adds cold to the rolling. Cold can reduce discomfort after a flare, but no trial shows it speeds recovery for plantar fasciitis beyond what rolling alone does.
- Walkito uses the foot roll as a recovery exercise at the end of a session, for 2 minutes.

### How do you do a foot roll?

Sit in a chair with one foot on a ball. A tennis ball, lacrosse ball or massage ball all work. Place the ball under the arch and roll it slowly from the ball of the foot back toward the heel and forward again.

Use firm pressure, not light. The ball should press into the tissue enough that you feel a deep, sustained pressure.

Roll for about 2 minutes per foot. Keep the pressure steady and avoid spots that feel sharp. If a spot makes you wince, ease off or skip over it. The goal is a firm massage, not pain.

- **Foot roll** (Walkito starts at 2 minutes): Sit with a ball under the arch. Roll it slowly from the ball of the foot to the heel, with firm pressure. If you wince, ease off.

### Does rolling a ball under your foot help plantar fasciitis?

Rolling is widely recommended by physical therapists and podiatrists as part of plantar fasciitis care. The idea is that it works as a self-massage: it applies pressure along the fascia, may increase blood flow locally and can reduce perceived tightness. Patients commonly report short-term relief after rolling.

That said, **no randomized trial has tested rolling as a standalone intervention for plantar fasciitis.** It appears in protocols alongside stretching and strengthening, but it is never the variable being measured. The 2023 guideline does not grade it separately. Stretching and strength training carry the evidence.

Rolling sits in the recovery category. It is useful after a long day on your feet, after a session of calf raises, or any time the sole feels tight and sore. It is not a replacement for the [plantar fascia stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/plantar-fascia-stretch/), [calf stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/) or [calf raises](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-raises/) that carry the guideline grades.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Should you use a frozen water bottle?

A frozen water bottle is one of the most popular home remedies for plantar fasciitis. The shape lets you roll the full length of the sole, and the cold numbs the area at the same time. Clinicians often recommend it, and it does feel good.

Here is what the evidence actually says. Cold therapy (ice, frozen bottles) is a general pain management tool. It reduces discomfort by numbing nerve endings and may temporarily reduce swelling.

But no randomized trial has compared a frozen bottle to a room-temperature bottle for plantar fasciitis. The benefit you feel is likely a mix of the rolling (pressure on the fascia) and the numbing (cold on the nerve endings). Whether the cold speeds recovery beyond what rolling alone does is an open question.

If a frozen bottle gives you relief, use it. **Just do not count on the cold as a replacement for stretching and strength work.** And avoid icing for longer than 15 to 20 minutes at a time. Prolonged cold can irritate the skin.

### What kind of ball should you use?

- A tennis ball is the most common starting point. It is soft enough to press into the arch without being sharp.
- A lacrosse ball is firmer and delivers more pressure.
- A golf ball is small and very hard, and can be too much for a sore heel.

Start with whatever you have. If a tennis ball feels too soft after a few sessions, try a lacrosse ball. If you are wincing on any ball, it is too firm or you are pressing too hard. The exercise should feel like a deep massage, never like you are grinding into an injury.

A frozen water bottle works in place of a ball and adds cold. A foam roller under the foot is gentler still. A specialized foot roller from a sports store does the same job. None of these is proven to work better than the others.

### What are the common mistakes with the foot roll?

- **Pressing too hard.** Harder is not better. If you push until the pain hits 6/10 or you are grimacing, you may be irritating the fascia rather than settling it. Back off to firm, steady pressure.
- **Rolling too fast.** Quick back-and-forth movement skips over the tissue. Roll slowly, about one full pass per second, so each spot gets sustained pressure.
- **Using it as the only exercise.** Rolling feels productive, and it is easy to do at a desk. But it does not strengthen the calf or stretch the fascia in the way the guideline-graded exercises do. Pair it with the [plantar fascia stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/plantar-fascia-stretch/) and [calf raises](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/) for the full picture.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### When should you roll your foot, and when should you skip it?

Roll after a long day on your feet, after a session of calf raises, or any time the sole feels tight. In Walkito, the foot roll appears on recovery days and at the end of sessions as a cooldown.

**Skip rolling if the heel is acutely swollen, red or warm.** Those signs can point to something other than plantar fasciitis, and pressing into an inflamed area can make it worse. See a clinician first. For the full set of exercises the guideline recommends, see [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) or [feet that hurt from standing all day](https://walkito.site/feet-hurt-standing-all-day/).

### Stop and see a clinician if

- the sole is acutely swollen, red or warm
- rolling consistently makes the pain worse the next morning
- the pain is sharp and localized to one pinpoint spot that worsens with pressure
- you feel numbness, tingling or burning under the foot
- the pain followed an injury, a fall or a sudden pop in the arch
- it has not improved after several weeks despite the full exercise program

### Doing it as a plan

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) puts the foot roll at the end of sessions and on recovery days. The app handles the timing and the order so you do not have to remember which days to roll and which to stretch or strengthen.

#### Does rolling a frozen water bottle under your foot help plantar fasciitis?

A frozen water bottle combines rolling (pressure on the fascia) and cold (numbing the nerve endings). Both can reduce discomfort in the short term. No trial has compared a frozen bottle to a room-temperature one for plantar fasciitis, so whether the cold adds a recovery benefit beyond the rolling itself is unknown. It is safe to try and many people find it soothing.

#### How long should you roll your foot on a ball?

About 2 minutes per foot is a reasonable starting dose. That is what Walkito uses. You can repeat it a few times a day if it gives relief. There is no specific research dose, because rolling has not been tested as a standalone intervention.

#### Is a tennis ball or a lacrosse ball better for plantar fasciitis?

Start with a tennis ball. It is softer and less likely to cause sharp pain on a sore heel. A lacrosse ball delivers firmer pressure and may feel better once the acute pain has settled. Neither is proven superior. Use whichever gives you firm pressure without making you wince.

#### Can rolling your foot make plantar fasciitis worse?

Yes, if you press too hard. Grinding aggressively into a sore fascia can increase inflammation rather than settle it. The pressure should feel like a deep massage, firm but not sharp. If pain hits 6/10 or the sole is more sore the next morning, ease up.

#### Is foot rolling a substitute for stretching?

No. The 2023 guideline grades stretching A and strength training B. Rolling is not graded at all. It works as a recovery step alongside the exercises that carry the evidence, like the plantar fascia stretch and calf raises. Rolling alone will not give you the same benefit.

## Ankle rocks: how to do them, why ankle mobility matters

Language: English · https://walkito.site/exercises/ankle-rocks/ · published 2026-10-05 · updated 2026-10-05

Ankle rocks are a standing exercise where the knee travels forward over the toes while the heel stays flat on the floor. They build ankle dorsiflexion, how far the ankle bends when the foot is on the ground. In a case-control study of 50 people with [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) and 100 controls, reduced dorsiflexion was the single strongest risk factor, at 23.3 times the odds.

- Reduced ankle dorsiflexion was the strongest independent risk factor for plantar fasciitis in a matched case-control study, at 23.3 times the odds (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).
- Ankle rocks build dorsiflexion by loading the end of the range under bodyweight, unlike a passive wall stretch.
- The knee-to-wall test measures how far the knee travels past the toes with the heel down. Walkito includes a knee-to-wall exercise (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg).
- Walkito starts ankle rocks at 2 sets of 15, each leg.

### How do you do ankle rocks?

Stand in a split stance, one foot forward and one back, with your hands on a wall or door frame for balance. Keeping the front heel flat on the floor, slowly rock the front knee forward over your toes. Let the knee travel as far as it can while the heel stays down. Then rock back to the start. That is one rep.

The movement is slow and controlled. You are not bouncing. Each rock should take about two seconds forward and two seconds back. The back leg is just for balance. All the ankle work is happening in the front leg.

**Keep the front foot pointing straight ahead.** If the foot rotates outward, the ankle finds a shortcut and you miss the range you are trying to build.

- **Ankle rocks** (Walkito starts at 2 sets of 15, each leg): Split stance, hands on a wall. Rock the front knee forward over the toes, heel stays flat. Slow, about two seconds each way. Switch legs after each set.

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### Why does ankle mobility matter for heel pain?

Ankle dorsiflexion is how far the foot can bend upward toward the shin while the heel stays on the ground. Every step you take requires some dorsiflexion. When the ankle cannot bend far enough, the body compensates:

- The foot may roll inward.
- The calf takes more strain.
- The plantar fascia absorbs forces it was not designed for.

In the Riddle 2003 case-control study, **reduced ankle dorsiflexion was the variable with the largest independent effect**, at 23.3 times the odds of developing plantar fasciitis. That was stronger than BMI, standing time or running distance. A [tight calf](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/), specifically the gastrocnemius, was present in 52 to 60 percent of 254 people with plantar fasciitis in a separate review.

Stretching the calf passively (as in the [calf stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/) and [soleus stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/)) addresses one side of the problem: muscle length. Ankle rocks address the other side: active control at end-range. Rocking the knee over the toes under bodyweight teaches the ankle to use the range it has, not just reach it passively.

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Patel A, DiGiovanni B. Association between plantar fasciitis and isolated contracture of the gastrocnemius. Foot & Ankle International. 2011;32(1):5–8.

### Ankle rocks vs. the calf stretch: what is the difference?

The [calf stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-stretch/) is a passive hold. You lean into the wall and wait for the muscle to lengthen. The back leg is straight, which targets the gastrocnemius. The [soleus stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/) does the same with a bent knee.

Ankle rocks are an active, repetitive movement. You push the knee forward, come back, push again. You are loading the ankle through its range rather than holding still at end-range. Ankle rocks build the ability to use dorsiflexion under load, which is what walking and running actually require.

Both are useful. **Stretching opens the range. Ankle rocks train you to use it.** The guideline grades calf stretching A. Ankle rocks are part of the [ankle mobility](https://walkito.site/ankle-mobility-exercises/) work Walkito programs alongside those stretches.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### The knee-to-wall test and how it connects

The knee-to-wall test, also called the weight-bearing lunge test, is a simple way to measure ankle dorsiflexion.

You stand facing a wall, one foot a few centimeters back, and lunge the knee forward until it touches the wall. If the heel lifts before the knee reaches the wall, move the foot closer. The distance from the big toe to the wall at the point where the knee just touches, with the heel still flat, is your score.

Walkito includes a knee-to-wall exercise in the app (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg). Tracking this distance over weeks tells you whether your ankle range is actually improving. An increase of a centimeter or two over a few weeks is meaningful.
