In a randomised trial of 28 people with flat feet, everyone wore orthoses for two months and half also did the [short-foot exercise](https://walkito.site/exercises/short-foot-exercise/) (Jung and colleagues, 2011). The muscle along the inner arch grew in both groups, but more with the exercise, and big-toe strength rose more too. If you wear insoles all day, keep the foot working with a few minutes of [foot strengthening exercises](https://walkito.site/foot-strengthening-exercises/).

Source: Protopapas K, Perry SD. The effect of a 12-week custom foot orthotic intervention on muscle size and muscle activity of the intrinsic foot muscle of young adults during gait termination. Clinical Biomechanics. 2020;78:105063.
Source: Jung DY, Koh EK, Kwon OY. Effect of foot orthoses and short-foot exercise on the cross-sectional area of the abductor hallucis muscle in subjects with pes planus: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Back and Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation. 2011;24(4):225–231.

### Insoles vs exercises at a glance

Source: Whittaker GA, Munteanu SE, Menz HB, Tan JM, Rabusin CL, Landorf KB. Foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(5):322–328.
Source: Landorf KB, Keenan AM, Herbert RD. Effectiveness of foot orthoses to treat plantar fasciitis: a randomized trial. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2006;166(12):1305–1310.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Banwell HA, Mackintosh S, Thewlis D. Foot orthoses for adults with flexible pes planus: a systematic review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2014;7(1):23.
Source: Protopapas K, Perry SD. The effect of a 12-week custom foot orthotic intervention on muscle size and muscle activity of the intrinsic foot muscle of young adults during gait termination. Clinical Biomechanics. 2020;78:105063.

### When do insoles make sense?

- **Long shifts on your feet.** A firm arch support can make the day easier while exercise builds capacity. See [feet that hurt from standing all day](https://walkito.site/feet-hurt-standing-all-day/).
- **A flare.** An insole or heel cup can take the edge off while first steps are sharp. [Taping](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-taping/) is another short-term option, with a higher guideline grade.
- **Painful high arches.** In a trial of 154 adults with painful high arches (pes cavus), custom orthoses eased pain more than a sham at three months (Burns and colleagues, 2006). See [high arches exercises](https://walkito.site/high-arches-exercises/).
- **Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction**, where the tendon that holds up the arch weakens. Trials pair an orthosis with exercise (Houck and colleagues, 2015). See [posterior tibial tendon dysfunction exercises](https://walkito.site/posterior-tibial-tendon-dysfunction-exercises/).
- **Diabetes or reduced feeling in the feet.** Pressure-spreading insoles are often part of foot care here, fitted by a clinician.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Burns J, Crosbie J, Ouvrier R, Hunt A. Effective orthotic therapy for the painful cavus foot: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2006;96(3):205–11.
Source: Houck J, Neville C, Tome J, Flemister A. Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Orthosis Augmented by Either Stretching or Stretching and Strengthening for Stage II Tibialis Posterior Tendon Dysfunction. Foot & Ankle International. 2015;36(9):1006–16.

### How do you combine insoles and exercises?

**Use the insole for comfort and the exercises for change.** In both the Rathleff and STAP trials, everyone had exercise advice alongside whatever went in their shoe. Wear an off-the-shelf arch support on the days that hurt, and start the stretches and heel raises at the same time. As morning pain settles, try short spells without the insole, then longer ones.

Walkito can set out the exercise side as a weekly plan: once a week it moves your main exercise up a step when you rated your last two sessions with it easy and morning pain has not risen.

If a few months of daily stretching and strength work have not helped, see a clinician. That is when a custom orthosis, among other options, is worth discussing with someone who has examined your foot.

Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.
Source: Rasenberg N, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, Fuit L, et al. Custom insoles versus sham and GP-led usual care in patients with plantar heel pain: results of the STAP-study - a randomised controlled trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(5):272–278.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain followed an injury or a fall, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- squeezing the sides of the heel is very painful, which can point to a stress fracture
- there is numbness, tingling or burning in the foot
- the foot is red, hot or swollen, or you have a fever
- one arch has dropped recently, or you cannot rise onto the toes of that foot
- you have diabetes, poor circulation or reduced feeling in your feet
- a child has flat feet with pain, stiffness or a limp
- pain has not improved after a few months of daily stretching and strength work

### Doing the exercises as a plan

An insole goes in your shoe once. Exercise works only if you keep at it. [Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) builds a plan one week at a time for heel pain or flat feet, starting with stretches like the [plantar fascia stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/plantar-fascia-stretch/) (2 holds of 30 seconds) and arch work like the short foot (3 sets of 8 with 5-second holds), then steps your main exercise up when you rate it easy twice in a row and morning pain holds steady.

#### Do I need orthotics for plantar fasciitis?

Most people do not. The 2023 heel pain guideline recommends against orthoses used alone for short-term relief (grade B) and allows them alongside other care (grade C). A review of 19 trials found only a small medium-term benefit over sham inserts. Stretching (grade A) and calf strengthening (grade B) are the core, and an insole can be a comfort add-on.

#### Are custom orthotics better than over-the-counter insoles?

For heel pain, trials have not found a difference. A review of 19 trials found no difference between custom and prefabricated insoles at any time point (Whittaker and colleagues, 2018). In a trial of 185 adults, custom insoles did no better than sham insoles at three months (Rasenberg and colleagues, 2021). A well-fitting off-the-shelf arch support is a reasonable first try.

#### Do orthotics make your feet weaker?

There is a small signal that they can. In a non-randomised study of 18 young adults with flat feet, three months of custom orthoses was followed by a 9.6 to 17.4 percent drop in the size of three small foot muscles. In a 28-person trial, adding the short-foot exercise to orthoses built more muscle and big-toe strength than orthoses alone.

#### Do insoles help flat feet?

The evidence is weak. A review of 13 studies found no high-level evidence that orthoses help adults with flexible flat feet, and only low-level evidence for pain (Banwell and colleagues, 2014). In a trial of 45 adults, foot exercises improved foot posture more than custom arch insoles (Kirmizi and colleagues, 2024). Flat feet that do not hurt need nothing.

#### Does my child with flat feet need orthotics?

Usually not, if the feet do not hurt. A Cochrane review of 16 trials with 1,058 children found low to very low certainty evidence for orthoses, and concluded that costly custom orthoses for children with painless flexible flat feet have no supporting evidence (Evans and colleagues, 2022). A child with foot pain, stiffness or a limp should see a clinician.

## Are barefoot shoes good for your feet? Strength, risks and foot pain

Language: English · https://walkito.site/barefoot-shoes/ · published 2026-10-09 · updated 2026-10-09

Barefoot shoes, also called minimalist shoes, can make your foot muscles stronger. In trials, adults who walked in them gained foot strength over a few months. But switching too fast raises the risk of bone stress and pain, no trial shows they ease [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) on their own, and people with diabetes or numb feet need protective shoes.

- In a 2019 trial of 57 runners, walking in minimalist shoes for about two months made foot muscles bigger and stronger, as much as doing foot exercises (Ridge and colleagues).
- Adults who wore minimal shoes for daily life for six months gained 57.4 percent in toe strength on average, in a controlled study of 22 people who switched (Curtis and colleagues, 2021).
- In runners who moved to minimalist running shoes over about two and a half months, 10 of 19 showed new or worse bone stress on MRI, more than runners who kept their usual shoes (Ridge and colleagues, 2013).
- No trial has shown that barefoot shoes on their own ease plantar fasciitis pain. In one small trial in people with plantar fasciitis, foot exercises raised toe strength whether or not people also wore minimalist shoes (Xu and colleagues, 2026).
- The international diabetic foot guideline advises people with diabetes at risk of foot ulcers not to walk without suitable foot protection (IWGDF, 2023).

### What are barefoot shoes?

Barefoot shoes are shoes built to get in the way of your foot as little as possible. Most share four features:

- A thin sole you can feel the ground through.
- A sole that bends and twists easily.
- Zero drop (the heel sits at the same height as the toes).
- A wide toe box so the toes can spread.

They have no arch support and little cushioning.

Researchers call them minimalist or minimal shoes. The idea is simple: a shoe that supports and cushions the foot does some of the work the small foot muscles would otherwise do. Take that support away and the muscles work harder. For anyone with foot pain, the question is whether that extra work helps or hurts.

### Do barefoot shoes make your feet stronger?

Yes, in adults without foot pain, the evidence points that way. In a 2019 randomized trial, Ridge and colleagues split 57 runners into three groups:

- Walk in minimalist shoes.
- Do foot strengthening exercises.
- Change nothing.

The walking group slowly increased how many steps a day they took in the new shoes. After about two months, every foot muscle the researchers measured was bigger and stronger in both active groups, and unchanged in the control group. Walking in the shoes worked about as well as the exercises.

Curtis and colleagues ran a longer study in 2021. Twenty-two adults wore minimal shoes for daily life (not for running) for six months, and 24 kept their usual shoes. Toe strength rose by 57.4 percent on average in the people who switched. The study was not randomized and only took people with no recent leg or foot problems.

A 2025 review of 28 trials by Peters-Dickie and colleagues found that minimalist shoes increased the strength of the smaller toes. It rated the certainty of the evidence as low to very low.

**Stronger foot muscles are not the same as less foot pain.** None of these studies measured pain or included people with a foot condition. For a full set of exercises that build the same muscles, see [foot strengthening exercises](https://walkito.site/foot-strengthening-exercises/).

Source: Ridge ST, Olsen MT, Bruening DA, et al. Walking in minimalist shoes is effective for strengthening foot muscles. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019;51(1):104–113.
Source: Curtis R, Willems C, Paoletti P, D'Août K. Daily activity in minimal footwear increases foot strength. Scientific Reports. 2021;11(1):18648.
Source: Peters-Dickie JL, Detrembleur C, Guallar-Bouloc M, Rastelli M, Lobet S, Hidalgo B, Deschamps K. The effects of foot core exercises and minimalist footwear on foot muscle sizes, foot strength, and biomechanics: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Biomechanics. 2025;122:106417.

### Are barefoot shoes bad for you? The risk is in the switch

The shoes are not the main risk. **The speed of the switch is.** Your foot bones, muscles, calf and Achilles tendon have adapted to your current shoes and need time to take more load.

Ridge and colleagues showed this in 2013. They scanned the feet of 36 experienced runners. Nineteen moved gradually to minimalist running shoes over about two and a half months and 17 kept their normal shoes.

Afterwards, 10 of the 19 who switched had new or worse bone marrow edema (fluid inside the bone, an early sign of bone stress) in at least one foot bone, significantly more than the runners who did not switch. The authors advised that runners should transition "very slowly and gradually".

Two randomized trials point the same way:

- In Ryan and colleagues' trial of 103 runners training for a 10 km race over three months, the partly minimalist shoe group had 12 injuries against 4 in the normal shoe group, and the full minimalist group reported more shin and calf pain.
- In Fuller and colleagues' six-month trial of 61 runners, running pain was higher in minimalist shoes, clearly so above about 35 km a week, and injury risk rose with body weight. The overall injury difference (16 of 31 against 11 of 30) could have been chance.

These were runners. Walking loads the foot far less, which is one reason the strength studies used walking. If you run and have [heel pain](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/), a sudden shoe change is one more load change your foot does not need.

Source: Ridge ST, Johnson AW, Mitchell UH, Hunter I, Robinson E, Rich BS, Brown SD. Foot bone marrow edema after a 10-wk transition to minimalist running shoes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2013;45(7):1363–1368.
Source: Ryan M, Elashi M, Newsham-West R, Taunton J. Examining injury risk and pain perception in runners using minimalist footwear. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2014;48(16):1257–1262.
Source: Fuller JT, Thewlis D, Buckley JD, Brown NA, Hamill J, Tsiros MD. Body mass and weekly training distance influence the pain and injuries experienced by runners using minimalist shoes: a randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;45(5):1162–1170.

### Are barefoot shoes good for plantar fasciitis?

**There is no good evidence that barefoot shoes ease plantar fasciitis** (pain where the thick band under your foot attaches to the heel). There is also no trial showing they cause it. Strong claims either way online mostly come from shoe and insole sellers.

Here is what has been tested:

- In a 2026 randomized trial, Xu and colleagues gave adults with plantar fasciitis about two months of foot exercises, and 34 finished. About half also wore minimalist shoes. Toe strength went up in both groups, and adding the shoes did not clearly add to it. Balance did not change in either group. This report did not cover pain, and the shoe maker supplied the shoes.
- In a small 2022 trial of 36 women with plantar fasciitis, Ribeiro and colleagues compared flexible minimalist shoes alone, the same shoes plus a custom insole, and usual shoe advice, over six months. Only the insole group had clearly less heel pain than the usual advice group.
- A 2022 case series of 20 runners reported less pain after about a month and a half of barefoot running on grass, but it had no comparison group and one author is funded by a barefoot shoe brand.

The 2023 US heel pain guideline recommends calf and plantar fascia stretching (grade A) and strength training (grade B). It does not recommend minimalist shoes, and it lists footwear that reduces load as part of advice for patients. If your heel hurts now, start with the [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/), and see [insoles vs exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) for what support under the foot can and cannot do.

Source: Xu J, Hertel J, Kuenze C, Jaffri AH, Saliba SA. The effects of performing therapeutic exercises and wearing minimalist shoes on intrinsic foot muscle function and single-leg balance in adults with plantar fasciopathy. Clinical Biomechanics. 2026;137:106869.
Source: Ribeiro AP, João SMA. The effect of short and long-term therapeutic treatment with insoles and shoes on pain, function, and plantar load parameters of women with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial. Medicina (Kaunas). 2022;58(11):1546.
Source: MacGabhann S, Kearney D, Perrem N, Francis P. Barefoot running on grass as a potential treatment for plantar fasciitis: a prospective case series. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19(23):15466.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Is walking barefoot at home OK if your heel hurts?

**Be careful with hard floors, especially first thing in the morning.** No trial has tested barefoot walking at home for heel pain, so this is cautious advice, not a tested rule.

Tile or wood gives the heel no cushion, and the first steps after rest are when plantar fasciitis usually hurts most. Our [morning heel pain](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-in-the-morning/) page suggests a stretch before you stand and something on your feet for those first steps.

Cushioning under the heel may matter. In a 2023 study, Landorf and colleagues compared 50 people with plantar heel pain to 25 matched people without it. Those with heel pain stood for 3.4 hours a day longer and wore shoes with harder heels. That shows a link, not a cause.

A deep, central heel ache that is worse barefoot on hard ground can also come from the heel fat pad (the cushion of fat under the heel bone). See [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/) for that pattern.

Short spells barefoot on grass or sand are gentler. If they raise your heel pain the next morning, it was too much. The same next-morning check works for any walk: see [walking with plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/walking-with-plantar-fasciitis/).

Source: Landorf KB, Kaminski MR, Munteanu SE, Zammit GV, Menz HB. Activity and footwear characteristics in people with and without plantar heel pain: a matched cross-sectional observational study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2023;21(1):35–44.

### Are barefoot shoes good for flat feet?

**There are hints, but no trial.** Holowka and colleagues compared 75 Tarahumara men in Mexico, who wear thin sandals most of their lives, with 26 men from the US who wear regular shoes. The sandal wearers had higher, stiffer arches and bigger muscles along the inner and outer edges of the foot. Only one of the 75 had low arches, against 8 of the 26 US men (31 percent).

An older survey of 2,300 children in India, by Rao and Joseph in 1992, found flat feet in 8.6 percent of children who wore shoes and 2.8 percent of those who did not. Flat feet were most common in children who wore closed shoes.

Both studies compare groups who differ in many ways, so they cannot show that shoes cause flat feet, or that new shoes will raise an adult arch. No trial has tested that.

What matters more is the type of flat foot:

- A flexible flat foot (the arch comes back when you sit or stand on your toes) is usually fine to load and strengthen, and a gradual move to flatter shoes is reasonable if your feet feel good.
- A rigid flat foot, or one that is painful, getting flatter or worse on one side, needs a clinician first.

Our [flat feet](https://walkito.site/flat-feet/) page explains the difference.

Source: Holowka NB, Wallace IJ, Lieberman DE. Foot strength and stiffness are related to footwear use in a comparison of minimally- vs. conventionally-shod populations. Scientific Reports. 2018;8(1):3679.
Source: Rao UB, Joseph B. The influence of footwear on the prevalence of flat foot. A survey of 2300 children. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British). 1992;74(4):525–527.

### Who should not wear barefoot shoes?

Some feet need protection more than a challenge.

- **Diabetes with foot risk, or neuropathy (numb feet).** The 2023 IWGDF guideline says people with diabetes at risk of ulcers should not walk without suitable foot protection, and those at moderate to high risk should wear properly fitting, therapeutic footwear. Numb feet miss small injuries.
- **Poor circulation or skin that is slow to mend.** Same reason: small cuts and blisters matter more.
- **A painful heel or foot right now.** Settle the pain first, then decide.
- **High arches.** A stiff, high-arched foot absorbs shock poorly, so cushioning may suit it better. See [high arches exercises](https://walkito.site/high-arches-exercises/).
- **Heavier runners, or runners with high weekly distances.** A six-month trial found more pain and injury risk in minimalist shoes for them. A past foot stress fracture is also a reason to ask a clinician first.

Source: Bus SA, Sacco ICN, Monteiro-Soares M, et al. Guidelines on the prevention of foot ulcers in persons with diabetes (IWGDF 2023 update). Diabetes/Metabolism Research and Reviews. 2024;40(3):e3651.
Source: Fuller JT, Thewlis D, Buckley JD, Brown NA, Hamill J, Tsiros MD. Body mass and weekly training distance influence the pain and injuries experienced by runners using minimalist shoes: a randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;45(5):1162–1170.

### How do you switch to barefoot shoes safely?

**Slowly, and by how your feet respond, not by a calendar.** No study has found a timetable that suits everyone. The strength studies built up step counts gradually and kept people from running in the new shoes. The running trials saw more pain and bone stress even with gradual plans.

- Walk before you run. Start with short spells of everyday walking, in your usual shoes the rest of the day.
- Add time only when your feet and calves feel normal the next morning.
- Expect tired feet and calves at first. Sharp pain is different.
- Stop and get checked if pain sits on one spot of a bone, often on the top of the foot, and gets worse with walking. That is the pattern of a stress fracture.
- Keep running in your usual shoes until walking in the new ones feels normal, then add running in small amounts.

Source: Ridge ST, Olsen MT, Bruening DA, et al. Walking in minimalist shoes is effective for strengthening foot muscles. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019;51(1):104–113.
Source: Curtis R, Willems C, Paoletti P, D'Août K. Daily activity in minimal footwear increases foot strength. Scientific Reports. 2021;11(1):18648.
Source: Ridge ST, Johnson AW, Mitchell UH, Hunter I, Robinson E, Rich BS, Brown SD. Foot bone marrow edema after a 10-wk transition to minimalist running shoes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2013;45(7):1363–1368.

### Exercises that strengthen your feet without new shoes

You can get the strength benefit without changing shoes. In the 2019 Ridge trial, foot exercises worked as well as minimalist shoes. In a 2020 trial of 118 recreational runners, Taddei and colleagues found that runners in the control group were 2.42 times as likely to get a running injury within a year as those who did a foot core training program. That is one trial, in runners.

The four exercises below cover the arch, toes, calf and balance. Walkito starts at 3 sets of 8 for the short foot with a 5 second hold, 3 sets of 10 for toe spreads and heel raises, and 3 holds of 20 seconds on one leg. If an exercise takes your pain to **6/10 or more**, stop for the day. More options are on the [toe strengthening exercises](https://walkito.site/toe-strengthening-exercises/) page.

- **Short foot, seated** (3 sets of 8, hold each for 5 seconds): Sit with your foot flat on the floor. Without curling your toes, draw the ball of the foot toward the heel so the arch lifts a little. Hold, then relax. More on the [short foot exercise](https://walkito.site/exercises/short-foot-exercise/) page.
- **Toe spread** (3 sets of 10): Sit with your feet flat. Spread all your toes apart as wide as you can, hold for a moment, then relax. This trains the muscle a wide toe box lets you use.
- **Two-foot heel raise** (3 sets of 10): Hold a wall. Rise onto the balls of both feet over about 3 seconds, then lower over 3 seconds. Barefoot shoes load the calf more, so a stronger calf helps the switch. More on the [calf raises](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-raises/) page.
- **Single-leg hold** (3 holds of 20 seconds, each leg): Stand on one foot near a wall and keep your eyes on one spot. Let the foot make small corrections. Once it is easy, try it barefoot on a soft mat. More on the [single-leg balance](https://walkito.site/exercises/single-leg-balance/) page.

Source: Ridge ST, Olsen MT, Bruening DA, et al. Walking in minimalist shoes is effective for strengthening foot muscles. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019;51(1):104–113.
Source: Taddei UT, Matias AB, Duarte M, Sacco ICN. Foot core training to prevent running-related injuries: a survival analysis of a single-blind, randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(14):3610–3619.
Source: Holowka NB, Wallace IJ, Lieberman DE. Foot strength and stiffness are related to footwear use in a comparison of minimally- vs. conventionally-shod populations. Scientific Reports. 2018;8(1):3679.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### See a clinician first if

- you have diabetes, numbness, tingling or burning in your feet, or poor circulation
- you have a cut, blister or sore on the foot that is not getting better
- pain sits on one spot of a foot bone, often on the top of the foot, and gets worse with walking, which can be a stress fracture
- the foot is swollen, red or warm, or you cannot put weight on it
- your arch is getting flatter, one foot is much flatter than the other, or the flat foot is stiff
- heel or foot pain started or got worse after switching shoes and has not settled with a return to your old shoes

### Doing it as a plan

[Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) is an exercise program for heel, foot and leg pain. It includes the short foot exercise, toe spreads, heel raises and balance work from this page and builds them up as they get easier. It does not pick your shoes and does not diagnose. A stronger foot and calf is a sensible base whichever shoes you end up in.

#### Are barefoot shoes good for your feet?

They can be, for people without foot pain who switch slowly. In a 2019 trial of 57 runners, walking in minimalist shoes for about two months made foot muscles bigger and stronger. But a fast switch to running in them brought bone stress in 10 of 19 runners in a 2013 MRI study. They are not a good idea with diabetes, numb feet or a current flare of foot pain.

#### Are barefoot shoes good for plantar fasciitis?

No trial has shown that barefoot shoes on their own ease plantar fasciitis pain. In a small 2026 trial in people with plantar fasciitis, foot exercises raised toe strength with or without minimalist shoes. The 2023 heel pain guideline recommends stretching and strength training and does not recommend minimalist shoes. If your heel hurts now, settle the pain with exercises before you change shoes.

#### Are barefoot shoes good for flat feet?

There is no trial. Studies comparing groups found fewer flat feet in people who grew up barefoot or in thin sandals, for example 2.8 percent against 8.6 percent in a survey of 2,300 children in India. That does not show that switching shoes as an adult raises an arch. A painless, flexible flat foot can usually try them slowly. A rigid or painful one needs a clinician first.

#### Are barefoot shoes good for neuropathy?

Usually not. If your feet are numb from neuropathy or diabetes, a thin sole lets cuts, blisters and pressure spots go unnoticed. The 2023 international diabetic foot guideline advises people with diabetes at risk of ulcers not to walk without suitable foot protection, and to wear properly fitting, therapeutic footwear when risk is moderate or high. Ask your foot care team what shoes suit you.

#### How long does it take to get used to barefoot shoes?

There is no safe timetable that fits everyone. In one study, adults who wore minimal shoes for daily life seemed to reach full foot strength by six months, matching people who had worn them for years. Runners who moved to minimalist running shoes over about two and a half months still showed bone stress on MRI. Build up by how your feet feel the next morning, walk before you run, and keep your old shoes in the rotation.

#### Is walking barefoot good for you?

Short spells barefoot on soft ground are fine for most people without foot pain, and use the foot muscles more than shoes do. With heel pain, be careful with hard floors, especially for your first steps in the morning, when plantar fasciitis usually hurts most. No trial has tested barefoot walking at home for heel pain. With diabetes or numb feet, avoid going barefoot.

#### Can I strengthen my feet without barefoot shoes?

Yes. In a 2019 trial, foot exercises built foot muscle size and strength as well as walking in minimalist shoes. In a 2020 trial of 118 runners, those who did not do a foot core training program were 2.42 times as likely to get a running injury within a year. The [short foot exercise](https://walkito.site/exercises/short-foot-exercise/), toe spreads, heel raises and [single-leg balance](https://walkito.site/exercises/single-leg-balance/) cover most of it.

## Plantar fasciitis vs Achilles tendonitis: how to tell them apart

Language: English · https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-achilles-tendonitis/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

The quickest way to tell them apart is where it hurts. [Plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) hurts under the heel, worst with the first steps in the morning (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Achilles tendonitis hurts at the back of the heel or in the tendon above it, usually 2 to 6 centimetres above the heel bone (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024). Both respond to exercise, but the exercises are not the same.

- Plantar fasciitis pain sits under the heel, on the inner side, and is typically worst with the first steps after sleep or sitting (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- Midportion Achilles tendinopathy hurts in the tendon itself, usually 2 to 6 centimetres above the heel bone. Pain right where the tendon meets the bone is the insertional type (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching **A** and strength work **B**. The 2024 Achilles guideline grades tendon-loading exercise **A** (Koc and colleagues, 2023; Chimenti and colleagues, 2024).
- In a trial of 101 people with chronic heel pain, a plantar fascia stretch beat a calf stretch alone at 8 weeks (DiGiovanni and colleagues, 2003). For the Achilles, the guideline’s top grade goes to loading the tendon, not to stretching (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024).
- The two are connected: in 52 MRI scans, people with Achilles changes had a thicker plantar fascia, and 5 of 27 passed the usual threshold for plantar fasciitis (Stecco and colleagues, 2013).

### Where does it hurt: under the heel or at the back?

**Location is the clearest difference.** The plantar fascia is the thick band under your foot that runs from the heel bone to the toes. Plantar fasciitis hurts where that band attaches, under the heel and toward the inner side. Pressing there with a thumb is usually sore (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

The Achilles tendon joins the calf muscles to the back of the heel bone. There are two types of Achilles pain, and the spot tells them apart (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024; Jonsson and colleagues, 2008):

- **Midportion:** pain and often a thicker, tender tendon 2 to 6 centimetres above the heel bone. You can usually pinch the sore spot between finger and thumb.
- **Insertional:** pain right where the tendon meets the back of the heel bone, often worse when shoes press there.

Pain under the heel that hurts when the sides of the heel are squeezed, burns or tingles, or comes with numbness points to other causes, such as a nerve, a stress fracture or the heel fat pad (Tu, 2018). [Heel pain at night](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-at-night/) covers those.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Chimenti RL, Neville C, Houck J, Cuddeford T, Carreira D, Martin RL. Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision 2024. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;54(12):CPG1–CPG32.
Source: Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Sunding K, Fahlström M, Cook J. New regimen for eccentric calf-muscle training in patients with chronic insertional Achilles tendinopathy: results of a pilot study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2008;42(9):746–749.
Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.

### When does it hurt: first steps or during activity?

**Plantar fasciitis is a first-steps pain.** The guideline describes heel pain that is most noticeable with the first steps in the morning or after sitting, often easing as you walk, and coming back after long periods on your feet (Koc and colleagues, 2023). [Heel pain in the morning](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-in-the-morning/) explains that pattern.

**Achilles tendinopathy is a loading pain.** The tendon can be stiff in the morning too, which is why the two get mixed up. The difference is what makes it worse during the day: loading activities such as running and jumping, and the pain tends to follow how much you did (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024). Hills and fast push-offs load the tendon harder still.

So both can hurt in the morning. Ask yourself where, not only when: a stiff, sore band at the back of the ankle points to the Achilles, a stab under the heel points to the plantar fascia.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Chimenti RL, Neville C, Houck J, Cuddeford T, Carreira D, Martin RL. Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision 2024. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;54(12):CPG1–CPG32.

### Plantar fasciitis vs Achilles tendonitis: the side-by-side table

The table sums up the typical picture. Many people do not fit one column neatly, and only a clinician’s exam can tell you which you have.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: de Jonge S, van den Berg C, de Vos RJ, van der Heide HJ, Weir A, Verhaar JA, Bierma-Zeinstra SM, Tol JL. Incidence of midportion Achilles tendinopathy in the general population. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2011;45(13):1026–1028.

### Which exercises suit plantar fasciitis?

**For plantar fasciitis, stretching comes first.** The 2023 guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretches **A**, its top grade, and strength work **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

The stretch that targets the arch matters. In a trial of 101 people, the group doing the plantar fascia stretch reported better outcomes at 8 weeks than the group doing calf stretching alone (DiGiovanni and colleagues, 2003). For strength, a 2015 trial of 48 people used slow heel raises with a towel under the toes, which eased pain faster than stretching alone at three months, though by twelve months both groups were about even (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015).

These are the starting doses from the [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) guide.

- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel all day, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Heel raises with a towel** (4 sets of 10, each leg, with added weight): Stand on one foot on a step, with a rolled towel under your toes. Take three seconds to rise, hold for two at the top, and take three seconds to lower. At this level Walkito adds weight, such as a backpack. The towel is what makes this exercise work the plantar fascia and not just the calf.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### Which exercises suit Achilles tendonitis?

**For the Achilles, loading comes first, not stretching.** The 2024 guideline grades tendon-loading exercise **A**: heel raises, holds and slow lowering that make the tendon work (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024). The guideline gives calf stretching a lower grade, **C**, and only for people whose ankle does not bend well (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024).

Some pain is allowed. In a trial of 38 people, pain up to about 5 out of 10 during loading was fine as long as it settled by the next morning and did not build week to week, and that group did as well at twelve months as the group that rested first (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007).

If the pain is right at the heel bone (insertional), keep every heel raise and heel drop at floor level, and go easy on calf stretches. Dropping the heel below a step presses the tendon against the bone. In a pilot study of 27 people, floor-level heel drops gave good results in 67% (Jonsson and colleagues, 2008). More detail in [Achilles tendonitis exercises](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/).

- **Heel raise hold** (3 holds of 20 seconds, both feet): Rise onto your toes on both feet, then stay still at the top. Don’t sink back down. Holding at the top loads the tendon without the bounce.
- **Eccentric heel drops (straight knee)** (3 sets of 10, each leg): Stand on a step edge. Rise on both feet, shift to the painful leg, and lower slowly over three seconds. Use both feet to come back up. For pain right at the heel bone, do this on the flat floor and do not let the heel sink below the step.

Source: Chimenti RL, Neville C, Houck J, Cuddeford T, Carreira D, Martin RL. Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision 2024. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;54(12):CPG1–CPG32.
Source: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(6):897–906.
Source: Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Sunding K, Fahlström M, Cook J. New regimen for eccentric calf-muscle training in patients with chronic insertional Achilles tendinopathy: results of a pilot study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2008;42(9):746–749.

### Can you have plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendonitis at the same time?

**Yes, and the two are linked.** In a study of 52 MRI scans of people with foot or ankle pain, the 27 with Achilles changes had a thicker plantar fascia, 3.43 mm on average against 2.09 mm. Five of the 27 had a plantar fascia over 4.5 mm, a common threshold for plantar fasciitis. None of the other 25 went over 4 mm (Stecco and colleagues, 2013).

The same study found the plantar fascia connects to the sheath around the Achilles through the covering of the heel bone. A cadaver study showed that pulling on the Achilles strains the plantar fascia, and more so when the toes are bent up (Carlson and colleagues, 2000). A tight or overloaded calf can therefore pull on both.

No study has counted how often people have both conditions together, so there is no reliable figure. No guideline covers having both. An approach that fits both guidelines: calf strength work that suits the tendon, plus the plantar fascia stretch, which works the arch, not the Achilles. Keep heel drops at floor level if the back of the heel bone hurts.

Source: Stecco C, Corradin M, Macchi V, Morra A, Porzionato A, Biz C, De Caro R. Plantar fascia anatomy and its relationship with Achilles tendon and paratenon. Journal of Anatomy. 2013;223(6):665–676.
Source: Carlson RE, Fleming LL, Hutton WC. The biomechanical relationship between the tendoachilles, plantar fascia and metatarsophalangeal joint dorsiflexion angle. Foot & Ankle International. 2000;21(1):18–25.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Chimenti RL, Neville C, Houck J, Cuddeford T, Carreira D, Martin RL. Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision 2024. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;54(12):CPG1–CPG32.

### What else causes heel pain that looks like these two?

Several problems sit close by and can feel similar (Choo and colleagues, 2020; Tu, 2018):

- A bony bump at the back of the heel with a sore, swollen area at the shoe line: [Haglund’s deformity](https://walkito.site/haglunds-deformity/) or retrocalcaneal bursitis, often together with insertional Achilles pain.
- A heel spur on an X-ray: common, and usually not the cause of the pain. See [plantar fasciitis vs heel spur](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-heel-spur/).
- A deep bruise-like ache in the middle of the heel pad, worse on hard floors: [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/).
- Pain on both sides of the heel when you squeeze it, after a jump in walking or running: possible stress fracture, which needs a clinician.
- Burning, tingling or numbness: possibly a trapped nerve.

Source: Choo YJ, Park CH, Chang MC. Rearfoot disorders and conservative treatment: a narrative review. Annals of Palliative Medicine. 2020;9(5):3546–3552.
Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.

### How long does each take to get better?

For plantar fasciitis, about 90% of people get better with non-surgical care, though it often takes months (Latt and colleagues, 2020). [How long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/) has the detail.

For Achilles tendinopathy, the core loading trials ran for about three months and followed people to twelve months. The 2024 guideline notes function can start to improve within 2 weeks, but fuller recovery takes longer (Chimenti and colleagues, 2024). Insertional pain has been harder to help with the classic heel drops below a step: only 32% had good results in an earlier study, which is why floor-level drops are used (Jonsson and colleagues, 2008).

No study has compared recovery time for the two head to head.

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Chimenti RL, Neville C, Houck J, Cuddeford T, Carreira D, Martin RL. Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision 2024. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;54(12):CPG1–CPG32.
Source: Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Sunding K, Fahlström M, Cook J. New regimen for eccentric calf-muscle training in patients with chronic insertional Achilles tendinopathy: results of a pilot study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2008;42(9):746–749.

### See a clinician first if

- you felt a sudden pop or snap at the back of the ankle, or it felt like being kicked there, and pushing off is now hard
- you cannot rise onto your toes on the painful side, or you feel a gap in the tendon
- you are taking or recently took a fluoroquinolone antibiotic, such as ciprofloxacin, and have new tendon pain
- the heel is red, hot and swollen, or you have a fever
- the heel hurts on both sides when squeezed, or hurts at night or at rest
- you feel burning, tingling or numbness in the heel or sole
- pain started after a fall or injury, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- pain keeps getting worse over weeks despite steady exercise

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app. You tell it where it hurts, under the heel or at the back, and it builds the plan from your answer: plantar fascia stretches and towel heel raises for heel pain, calf loading from holds to slow heel drops for Achilles pain.

#### How do I know if my heel pain is plantar fasciitis or Achilles tendonitis?

Start with where it hurts. Plantar fasciitis hurts under the heel, toward the inner side, and is worst with the first steps after rest. Achilles tendonitis hurts at the back of the heel or in the tendon 2 to 6 centimetres above it, and gets worse with push-off, running and hills. A clinician can confirm which it is.

#### Can plantar fasciitis cause Achilles pain?

They are linked, but no study shows one causes the other. In 52 MRI scans, people with Achilles changes had a thicker plantar fascia, 3.43 mm against 2.09 mm. A cadaver study showed that tension in the Achilles strains the plantar fascia. A tight, overloaded calf may load both.

#### Is Achilles tendonitis worse in the morning like plantar fasciitis?

It can be. Both can feel stiff and sore with the first steps of the day, which is why they get mixed up. Plantar fasciitis is a stab under the heel that eases as you walk. Achilles pain is at the back of the ankle and tends to build with running, jumping, hills and stairs.

#### Should I stretch my calf for Achilles tendonitis?

It is optional. The 2024 Achilles guideline puts tendon-loading exercise first, graded A, and gives calf stretching a C, for people whose ankle does not bend well. If your pain is right at the heel bone, deep calf stretches and heel drops below a step press the tendon against the bone, so keep them gentle and at floor level.

#### Are the exercises for plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendonitis the same?

They overlap but are not the same. Plantar fasciitis starts with plantar fascia and calf stretches, graded A, plus heel raises, graded B. Achilles tendonitis starts with loading: heel raise holds, heel raises and slow heel drops, graded A. Calf strength work fits both.

#### Can you have plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendonitis together?

Yes. In one MRI study of 52 people with foot or ankle pain, 5 of the 27 with Achilles changes also had a plantar fascia thick enough to meet a common threshold for plantar fasciitis. No study has counted how often the two happen together in the general population.

#### Is pain at the back of the heel plantar fasciitis?

Usually not. Plantar fasciitis hurts under the heel. Pain at the back of the heel is more often Achilles tendinopathy, retrocalcaneal bursitis or Haglund’s deformity, a bony bump where the tendon attaches. A sudden pop at the back of the heel needs a clinician the same day.

#### Does a heel spur mean plantar fasciitis or Achilles tendonitis?

Neither on its own. A spur under the heel sits near the plantar fascia, and a spur at the back sits where the Achilles attaches, but spurs are common in people with no pain. The exam, not the X-ray alone, decides what is causing the pain.

## Plantar fasciitis vs a heel stress fracture: how to tell

Language: English · https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-stress-fracture/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

[Plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) hurts most on your first steps after rest and usually eases once you walk for a few minutes. A heel stress fracture does the opposite: the pain builds the more you walk or run, often after a jump in activity, and squeezing the sides of the heel tends to hurt (Tu, 2018). An early X-ray can look normal: in 30 military recruits with a heel stress injury on MRI, it showed on plain X-ray in only 15% (Sormaala and colleagues, 2006).

- Plantar fasciitis pain is "most noticeable with weight bearing first thing in the morning or after a period of rest" and eases with walking (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Stress fracture pain starts with activity and can later be there at rest too (Tu, 2018).
- Pain when the sides of the heel bone are squeezed suggests a stress fracture (Tu, 2018), but we found no study that measured how accurate the squeeze test is for the heel, and it is also painful in Sever’s disease in children.
- Plain X-rays often miss early stress fractures: one review put their first-visit sensitivity at about 10%, rising to 30 to 70% after three weeks (Patel and colleagues, 2011). MRI was the most accurate test in a 2016 systematic review (Wright and colleagues, 2016).
- A sudden rise in training is the classic trigger. Runners who average more than 25 miles a week, women, and people with low energy availability or weak bones are at higher risk (Patel and colleagues, 2011; Mountjoy and colleagues, 2023).
- Stretching and strength exercises are graded **A** and **B** for plantar fasciitis (Koc and colleagues, 2023). They are not a plan for a suspected fracture, which first needs less load and a clinician.

### How can you tell plantar fasciitis from a heel stress fracture?

**The clearest clue is what walking does to the pain.** Plantar fasciitis is worst on the first steps after sleep or sitting, eases after a few minutes, and can come back after a long day on your feet (Tu, 2018). The 2023 heel pain guideline describes it as pain "most noticeable with weight bearing first thing in the morning or after a period of rest" (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

A calcaneal stress fracture is a small crack in the heel bone from repeated load. Its pain usually starts after you increase walking, running or standing, or move to a harder surface. At first it hurts only during activity and builds as you go. Later it can hurt at rest (Tu, 2018). In a review of stress fractures in general, pain with walking was reported by 81% of patients, a sore spot on the bone by 65.9 to 100%, and swelling by 18 to 44% (Patel and colleagues, 2011).

The table sums up the usual patterns. No single row decides it, and some people do not fit either column neatly.

Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.
Source: Sormaala MJ, Niva MH, Kiuru MJ, Mattila VM, Pihlajamäki HK. Stress injuries of the calcaneus detected with magnetic resonance imaging in military recruits. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2006;88(10):2237–2242.

### What is the squeeze test, and how much can it tell you?

**The squeeze test means pressing the inside and outside of the heel bone together, between the palms or between a thumb and fingers.** A clinician does it with the foot relaxed. Pain on squeezing "suggests the diagnosis" of a calcaneal stress fracture, according to a 2018 review in American Family Physician (Tu, 2018). Plantar fasciitis, by contrast, is tender when you press under the inside front of the heel, where the fascia attaches.

Its limits are real:

- **Nobody has measured how accurate it is for the heel.** We found no study that reports how often the squeeze test is positive in people with a confirmed calcaneal stress fracture, or how often it is positive without one. The same review that covers stress fractures notes that the hop test, another common bedside test, has not been validated either (Patel and colleagues, 2011).
- **A negative squeeze does not rule out a fracture.** Some heel stress injuries sit toward the front or the middle of the bone: in one MRI study, 15 of 34 were not in the back part (Sormaala and colleagues, 2006).
- **Other things hurt on squeezing too.** In children and young teens, a painful squeeze is a common sign of [Sever’s disease](https://walkito.site/severs-disease/), an irritated growth plate (Tu, 2018). Other heel bone problems can also hurt, so a clinician needs to check.

If you press the sides of your own heel and it hurts, take that as a reason to get it checked, not as a diagnosis. Do not hop on the foot to test it.

Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.
Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.
Source: Sormaala MJ, Niva MH, Kiuru MJ, Mattila VM, Pihlajamäki HK. Stress injuries of the calcaneus detected with magnetic resonance imaging in military recruits. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2006;88(10):2237–2242.

### Who is more at risk of a heel stress fracture?

A stress fracture happens when bone takes more repeated load than it can repair. Risk goes up when the load rises, when the bone is less able to take it, or both (Warden and colleagues, 2014).

- **A sudden increase in training.** A big jump in walking, running, marching or standing, or repeated hard sessions with little rest, is the classic story (Patel and colleagues, 2011). A change to a harder walking surface is a common trigger for the heel (Tu, 2018).
- **High running volume.** Recreational runners averaging more than 25 miles a week are at higher risk, as are athletes in track and field, basketball, soccer and dance (Patel and colleagues, 2011). More for runners in [heel pain in runners](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/).
- **Low energy availability.** Eating too little for the amount you train can affect hormones and bone. The International Olympic Committee lists poor bone health, including bone stress injuries, among the effects of this pattern, called relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), in both women and men (Mountjoy and colleagues, 2023).
- **Bone health.** Women with the female athlete triad (disordered eating, missed periods and low bone density) are at higher risk, and one study found lower vitamin D levels in recruits with stress fractures (Patel and colleagues, 2011). Bone weakened by osteoporosis can crack under normal loads, which is called an insufficiency fracture.
- **Being a woman.** Women are at higher risk than men, especially in military training, though data in female athletes are mixed (Patel and colleagues, 2011).

Plantar fasciitis has a different risk profile. In a study of 50 people with it and 100 without, people with 0 degrees of ankle bend (dorsiflexion) or less had 23.3 times the odds of those with more than 10 degrees, and standing for most of the working day raised the odds 3.6 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).

Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.
Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.
Source: Warden SJ, Davis IS, Fredericson M. Management and prevention of bone stress injuries in long-distance runners. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2014;44(10):749–765.
Source: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57(17):1073–1097.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### Why can an X-ray look normal with a stress fracture?

**An early stress fracture is often too small to show on an X-ray.** The bone first reacts with swelling inside it, which an X-ray cannot see. Signs of repair show up later. One review put the sensitivity of X-rays at the first visit at about 10%, rising to 30 to 70% after three weeks (Patel and colleagues, 2011).

For the heel specifically, a Finnish study looked at military recruits with exercise-related heel or ankle pain who had an MRI. Of 30 recruits with heel stress injuries, only 15% had a visible injury on plain X-rays. In 22 of the 34 injured heels, nearby foot bones were also affected (Sormaala and colleagues, 2006).

A 2016 systematic review of stress fractures in the lower limb found X-ray sensitivity ranging from 12% to 56%, against 68% to 99% for MRI. The authors named MRI the most sensitive and specific test and warned that X-rays are likely to give false negatives early on (Wright and colleagues, 2016).

So a clinician who suspects a fracture may repeat the X-ray after two to three weeks or go straight to an MRI if a quick answer matters (Patel and colleagues, 2011). For plantar fasciitis, the 2023 guideline says imaging is "usually not indicated for patients that meet clinical examination criteria for plantar fasciitis until they fail conservative interventions" (Koc and colleagues, 2023). The [heel spur page](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-heel-spur/) explains why a spur on an X-ray does not settle it either.

Source: Sormaala MJ, Niva MH, Kiuru MJ, Mattila VM, Pihlajamäki HK. Stress injuries of the calcaneus detected with magnetic resonance imaging in military recruits. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2006;88(10):2237–2242.
Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.
Source: Wright AA, Hegedus EJ, Lenchik L, Kuhn KJ, Santiago L, Smoliga JM. Diagnostic accuracy of various imaging modalities for suspected lower extremity stress fractures: a systematic review with evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;44(1):255–263.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### What should you do while you wait to find out?

**If your pain fits the stress fracture column, take load off the heel and book a clinician.** Do not wait to see whether a few more runs settle it. Starting care early matters: one review notes that a delay has been linked to a longer return to activity (Patel and colleagues, 2011).

- **Cut the load to what is pain-free.** That usually means stopping running, jumping and long walks for now. Some people need crutches or a walking boot for a while (Patel and colleagues, 2011; Tu, 2018).
- **Keep fit without loading the heel,** for example swimming or cycling, if they do not hurt (Patel and colleagues, 2011).
- **Ask about painkillers.** The same review says anti-inflammatory drugs should be used with caution with a stress fracture, because some animal studies suggest they may slow bone repair (Patel and colleagues, 2011).
- **Do not start a stretching or strength plan for the heel yet.** Wait until a clinician has ruled a fracture out or cleared you.

Heel stress fractures tend to recover well in otherwise healthy people (Tu, 2018). Across stress fractures in general, recovery takes from four weeks to three months or longer from the point activity is cut back, and activity then builds back up slowly once you are pain-free (Patel and colleagues, 2011).

If your pain fits the plantar fasciitis column instead, you usually do not need imaging to start the exercises below (Koc and colleagues, 2023). If you are not sure which column you are in, see a clinician first.

Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.
Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Why are exercise plans for plantar fasciitis, not a fracture?

**Stretching and loading help plantar fasciitis because the tissue adapts to load. A cracked bone first needs the load taken away.** Bone stress injuries sit on a scale: a stress reaction can progress to a stress fracture and, with continued load, to a complete fracture (Warden and colleagues, 2014).

The evidence for exercise is specific to plantar fasciitis. The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching **A** and strength training **B** for it (Koc and colleagues, 2023). The heel raise program in the best-known trial was tested in 48 people with plantar fasciitis, not in people with a fracture (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015).

For stress fractures the evidence points the other way. Two cluster randomised trials found that leg stretching during warm-ups did not prevent stress fractures (Patel and colleagues, 2011). What does matter is cutting load, then a gradual return guided by a clinician. Once a fracture has recovered, strengthening the muscles around the bone becomes part of preventing the next one (Warden and colleagues, 2014).

That is why the exercises on this page are for plantar fasciitis only. If you have been told you have a stress fracture, follow your clinician’s return plan instead.

Source: Warden SJ, Davis IS, Fredericson M. Management and prevention of bone stress injuries in long-distance runners. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2014;44(10):749–765.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.
Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.

### Plantar fasciitis only: which exercises fit once a fracture is ruled out?

**Use these only if your pain fits plantar fasciitis, or a clinician has ruled out a fracture.** If squeezing the heel hurts, the pain builds with every walk, or the heel is swollen, skip them and get it checked first.

These are the starting steps from our [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) guide: stretches first, then a seated heel raise that puts almost no load on the heel. The full progression, up to the towel heel raise from the trial, is in that guide.

- **Plantar fascia stretch (plantar fasciitis only)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Calf stretch (plantar fasciitis only)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel all day, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Soleus stretch (plantar fasciitis only)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Seated heel raises (plantar fasciitis only)** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, the deeper calf muscle, with almost no load on the heel.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### See a clinician first if

- the heel pain builds the longer you walk or run instead of easing
- squeezing the sides of the heel bone hurts
- the heel is swollen or bruised, or one spot on the bone is very tender
- the pain started after a sudden jump in training or a move to a harder surface
- it hurts at rest or wakes you at night
- you have had a stress fracture before, missed periods, an eating disorder or low bone density
- you cannot put full weight on the foot, or the pain followed a fall or a twist
- you feel burning, tingling or numbness in the heel or sole

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is an exercise app for heel and foot pain. Its plan is built for plantar fasciitis type heel pain, not for a stress fracture, so if your pain fits the fracture pattern, see a clinician before you start.

#### How do I know if my heel pain is a stress fracture or plantar fasciitis?

Watch what walking does. Plantar fasciitis hurts most on the first steps after rest and eases after a few minutes. A heel stress fracture usually follows a jump in activity, builds the longer you walk or run, and often hurts when the sides of the heel are squeezed. If your pain fits the fracture pattern, see a clinician.

#### Can an X-ray miss a heel stress fracture?

Yes, often. In 30 military recruits with a heel stress injury seen on MRI, plain X-rays showed it in only 15%. One review put X-ray sensitivity at the first visit at about 10%, rising to 30 to 70% after three weeks. A normal early X-ray does not rule out a stress fracture.

#### Do I need an MRI for heel pain?

Not for typical plantar fasciitis: the 2023 guideline says imaging is usually not needed when the exam fits. If a clinician suspects a stress fracture, MRI is the most accurate test. A 2016 systematic review found MRI sensitivity of 68% to 99%, against 12% to 56% for plain X-rays.

#### What does a positive squeeze test mean?

Pain when the inside and outside of the heel bone are pressed together suggests a calcaneal stress fracture, or in children Sever’s disease. It is a reason to see a clinician, not a diagnosis. We found no study that measured how accurate the squeeze test is for heel stress fractures, so a painless squeeze does not rule one out.

#### Can you walk on a heel stress fracture?

You may be able to, but you usually should not keep loading it. Care means cutting activity to what is pain-free, and with severe pain, little to no weight on the foot for up to six weeks, sometimes with crutches or a boot. A clinician should guide how much walking is safe.

#### How long does a heel stress fracture take to get better?

Across stress fractures in general, recovery takes from four weeks to three months or longer from the time activity is cut back. Heel stress fractures tend to recover well in otherwise healthy people. Activity then builds back up gradually once you are pain-free. For plantar fasciitis timelines, see [how long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/).

#### Should I stretch if I might have a stress fracture?

No, not until a clinician has ruled it out. Stretching and strength work are graded A and B for plantar fasciitis, but a suspected fracture first needs less load. Two cluster randomised trials found that leg stretching during warm-ups did not prevent stress fractures, so stretching is not the tool for bone.

#### Can plantar fasciitis turn into a stress fracture?

No study shows plantar fasciitis turning into a fracture. They are different injuries, one in the fascia and one in the bone. They can share a trigger, such as a sudden rise in walking or running, and a bone stress reaction can progress to a fracture if loading continues. Pain that changes pattern is worth checking.

#### Who gets heel stress fractures?

Mostly people who suddenly train more: runners, military recruits and athletes. Runners averaging more than 25 miles a week are at higher risk, and women more than men. Low energy availability, missed periods and low bone density raise the risk, and one study found lower vitamin D levels in recruits with stress fractures.

## How much walking is OK with plantar fasciitis?

Language: English · https://walkito.site/walking-with-plantar-fasciitis/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

You can usually keep walking with [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/), as long as the pain stays moderate while you walk and settles by the next morning. The 2023 heel pain guideline recommends advice on adjusting your weight-bearing load and does not tell people to stop walking, though it grades that advice **E**, meaning it rests on theory, not trials (Koc and colleagues, 2023). No study gives a safe number of steps, so the next-morning check is a better guide than a step target.

- The 2023 heel pain guideline lists advice on changing weight-bearing loads at work, in leisure and in daily life, plus footwear advice, at grade **E**: based on theory, not trials (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- In a trial of 180 adults with plantar fasciopathy, a group given only advice to stay active, cut back on pain-aggravating activities and wear a heel cup improved by a clinically meaningful amount at about three months (Riel and colleagues, 2023).
- One pain-monitoring rule allows pain up to about 5 out of 10 during activity, as long as it settles by the next morning and does not build week to week. It was tested in 38 people with Achilles pain, not plantar fasciitis (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007).
- No study gives a daily step count for plantar fasciitis. In 50 people with heel pain and 25 without, activity levels did not differ, but the heel pain group stood 3.4 hours a day longer (Landorf and colleagues, 2023).
- A 2021 best practice guide for heel pain advises shoes with a small heel-to-toe drop and avoiding barefoot walking and flat, unsupportive shoes until symptoms are gone (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021).

### Is walking good or bad for plantar fasciitis?

**Walking is not the enemy, but too much at once can flare the heel.** The 2023 heel pain guideline does not tell people to stop walking. Its summary lists education on ways to change weight-bearing loads at work, in leisure and in daily life, and on footwear. It grades that advice **E**, which means theory and basic science support it, but no trial has tested it (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

The guideline also lists heel pain that started after a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as a typical feature of plantar fasciitis. So the question is rarely whether to walk. It is how much, and how fast you add more.

A Danish trial compared simple advice with added treatments. 180 adults with plantar fasciopathy (another name for plantar fasciitis) were split into three groups. One got only advice and a heel cup; the other two added heel raise training, and one of those also got a steroid injection. The advice was to cut back on activities that cause flare-ups and then slowly return to former activity levels, guided by symptoms. All three groups improved by a clinically meaningful amount at about three months (Riel and colleagues, 2023).

Walking itself may not be what links to heel pain. In a 2023 study, 50 people with heel pain and 25 matched people without it reported similar physical activity. The difference was standing: the heel pain group stood 3.4 hours a day longer (Landorf and colleagues, 2023). That study shows a link, not a cause. If your day is mostly standing, [feet hurt from standing all day](https://walkito.site/feet-hurt-standing-all-day/) covers that side.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, et al. Does a corticosteroid injection plus exercise or exercise alone add to the effect of patient advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy? A randomised clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57(18):1180–1186.
Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, Jensen MB, Ehlers LH, Rathleff MS. Corticosteroid injection plus exercise versus exercise, beyond advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy: protocol for a randomised clinical superiority trial (the FIX-Heel trial). Trials. 2020;21(1):5.
Source: Landorf KB, Kaminski MR, Munteanu SE, Zammit GV, Menz HB. Activity and footwear characteristics in people with and without plantar heel pain: a matched cross-sectional observational study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2023;21(1):35–44.

### How much walking is OK? A simple pain rule

**Use your pain as the dose meter, and check it twice: during the walk and the next morning.** No study has tested a walking rule for plantar fasciitis. The closest tested rule comes from tendon rehab, so use it as a borrowed guide, not a proven limit for the heel.

In a 2007 trial, 38 people with Achilles tendon pain were split into two groups. One group kept running and jumping, using a pain-monitoring model: pain up to about 5 out of 10 was allowed during activity, as long as it settled by the next morning and did not build from week to week. The other group stopped those activities for the first six weeks. Both groups improved, and keeping active did not lead to worse results at twelve months (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007). More on that trial is in [Achilles tendonitis exercises](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/).

For heel pain, a 2021 best practice guide, built from a review of 51 trials, interviews with 14 experts and a patient survey, says pain-monitoring was strongly recommended and that people should be taught to read their pain response to activity (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021). It does not give a number. The table below applies the tested rule to walking, scored from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain). The next-walk column is a practical reading of that rule, not a tested protocol.

Source: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(6):897–906.
Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.

### How many steps a day is OK with plantar fasciitis?

**There is no evidence-based step number for plantar fasciitis.** We found no trial that set a step count or walking distance for people with heel pain and measured the result. Any page that gives you a set figure for heel pain is guessing.

The well-known 10,000 steps is a general health target, not a foot research figure, and even there the evidence behind it is thin. A 2022 analysis of 15 studies and 47,471 adults found that more daily steps went with a lower risk of death, but the benefit levelled off at about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day in adults aged 60 or over, and 8,000 to 10,000 in younger adults (Paluch and colleagues, 2022). That is about long-term health, not about what an irritated heel can handle this week.

A more useful number is your own. Most phones count steps. Look at a normal week before the heel flared and a normal week now. That gives you a starting point, and the pain rule above tells you whether to hold, add or cut back.

Breaking walking up may help more than the total. The 2021 best practice guide advises breaking up long periods of static loading, such as standing (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021). Several short walks spread over the day put the heel through less continuous load than one long one, though no study has compared the two for plantar fasciitis.

Source: Paluch AE, Bajpai S, Bassett DR, et al. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health. 2022;7(3):e219–e228.
Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.

### How do you build walking back up?

The advice tested in the Danish trial was to cut back on activities that cause flare-ups, then slowly return to former activity levels guided by symptoms (Riel and colleagues, 2020). It did not set a weekly percentage, and no study has tested one for plantar fasciitis. Here is one way to put that advice into practice:

- Find a walk that passes the pain rule: moderate pain at most during it, and a normal next morning. If even a short walk fails, start with less.
- Repeat that walk for a few days. One good day is not enough to judge.
- Add a small amount, such as five more minutes, and keep the rest the same. Change one thing at a time: distance, pace, hills or surface.
- If the next morning is worse, go back to the last walk that passed and stay there longer.

The five minutes is a practical suggestion, not a tested figure. What matters is that each step up is small enough that the next morning tells you clearly whether it worked.

Recovery from plantar fasciitis is usually slow. About 90% of people improve with non-surgical care such as stretching, calf work and load management (Latt and colleagues, 2020), but it can take months. See [how long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/). If you also run, [heel pain in runners](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/) covers mileage and load changes.
