Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, Jensen MB, Ehlers LH, Rathleff MS. Corticosteroid injection plus exercise versus exercise, beyond advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy: protocol for a randomised clinical superiority trial (the FIX-Heel trial). Trials. 2020;21(1):5.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.

### Which shoes help when you walk with plantar fasciitis?

**Comfortable, cushioned shoes with a small heel-to-toe drop are the expert advice, but no trial has tested a specific shoe for walking.** The 2021 best practice guide says shoes should be supportive and comfortable, have a small rearfoot-to-forefoot drop (the heel sits a little higher than the toes), and be something you will actually wear. It also advises avoiding barefoot walking and flat, unsupportive shoes until symptoms have fully gone (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021).

The 2023 guideline includes footwear advice in its grade **E** education recommendation. For insoles it is more specific: do not use them as the only approach (**B** against), but they may help combined with other care (**C**). That includes an over-the-counter heel cushion or shoes that cushion the heel (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

Shoe hardness may matter. In the 2023 study of 50 people with heel pain and 25 without, the heel pain group wore shoes with harder heels and reported more trouble finding suitable shoes (Landorf and colleagues, 2023). Again, a link, not proof that soft shoes help.

For specific products and what the trials show, see [best insoles for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/best-insoles-for-plantar-fasciitis/) and [insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/). Thinking about minimalist shoes? [Barefoot shoes](https://walkito.site/barefoot-shoes/) covers why they are a poor fit while the heel is sore.

Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Landorf KB, Kaminski MR, Munteanu SE, Zammit GV, Menz HB. Activity and footwear characteristics in people with and without plantar heel pain: a matched cross-sectional observational study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2023;21(1):35–44.

### Does the surface you walk on matter?

**Probably, but the evidence is indirect.** The guideline lists work-related weight-bearing activity, particularly under conditions with poor shock absorption, as a risk factor for plantar fasciitis (Koc and colleagues, 2023). That points to hard ground and hard shoes as a load on the heel.

Direct evidence is thin. In the 2023 matched study, people with and without heel pain did not differ in whether they stood on hard floors (Landorf and colleagues, 2023). A case series of 20 runners reported less pain after about a month and a half of barefoot running on grass, but it had no comparison group (MacGabhann and colleagues, 2022). No trial has compared walking surfaces for plantar fasciitis.

Practical options while the heel is sore:

- Choose grass, a park path or a track over concrete for longer walks, if it feels better.
- Keep shoes on at home on tile or wood, especially for the first steps of the day.
- Go easy on long downhill stretches and steep hills until the flat walk passes the pain rule. More on descents, packs and poles in [foot pain after hiking](https://walkito.site/hiking-foot-pain/).

A deep ache right in the center of the heel that is clearly worse on hard ground can come from the heel fat pad rather than the plantar fascia. See [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Landorf KB, Kaminski MR, Munteanu SE, Zammit GV, Menz HB. Activity and footwear characteristics in people with and without plantar heel pain: a matched cross-sectional observational study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2023;21(1):35–44.
Source: MacGabhann S, Kearney D, Perrem N, Francis P. Barefoot running on grass as a potential treatment for plantar fasciitis: a prospective case series. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19(23):15466.

### Which exercises make walking easier?

Exercises may help the heel tolerate more load, so the same walk may pass the pain rule more easily over time, though no study has tested this for walking. The 2023 guideline grades stretching of the plantar fascia and calf **A**, its top grade, and strength training **B**.

A tight calf is part of the picture. In a case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, limited ankle bend was the strongest risk factor, and standing for most of the working day also raised the odds (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). See [tight calves](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/).

In a trial of 48 people, heavy heel raises eased pain and improved daily function faster than stretching, and by twelve months both groups were about even (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015). The cards below are Walkito’s starting doses, not a prescription. The full set is in [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).

- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel all day, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, with almost no load on the heel, which suits days when walking is already near your limit.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Both feet share the load. Hold a wall for balance.
- **Heel raises with a towel** (4 sets of 10, each leg, with added weight): Stand on one foot on a step, with a rolled towel under your toes. Take three seconds to rise, hold for two at the top, and take three seconds to lower. At this level Walkito adds weight, such as a backpack. The towel is what makes this exercise work the plantar fascia and not just the calf. More on the [towel heel raise](https://walkito.site/exercises/towel-heel-raise/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### See a clinician first if

- the heel pain started after a fall, a jump or a twist, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- pain builds with every walk and does not ease with rest, or squeezing the sides of the heel hurts (possible stress fracture)
- the heel hurts at night or at rest, not just with walking
- you have numbness, tingling or burning in the foot
- the heel is red, hot or swollen, or you feel unwell or have a fever
- both heels hurt along with other joints, or you have morning stiffness elsewhere
- you have diabetes or poor circulation and your foot hurts or looks different
- pain is getting worse week after week despite cutting back

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app. It does not set a step target or plan your walks, but it reads your heel the same way this page does: by how your foot feels the next morning.

#### Should I walk with plantar fasciitis?

Usually yes, in amounts your heel can handle. The 2023 heel pain guideline recommends adjusting weight-bearing load and does not advise stopping, though that advice rests on theory (grade E). In a trial of 180 adults, advice to stay active but cut back on pain-aggravating activities, plus a heel cup, came with meaningful improvement at about three months.

#### Is walking good for plantar fasciitis?

Walking in moderate amounts is generally fine, though no study has tested how much walking is best. In one study, people with heel pain were as active as people without it but stood 3.4 hours a day longer. A best practice guide advises learning to monitor your pain response to activity.

#### How many steps a day is OK with plantar fasciitis?

No study gives a step number for plantar fasciitis. The 10,000 figure is a general health target, and in mortality research the benefit levelled off at 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day in adults 60 or over. For an irritated heel, start from your own usual count and let next-morning pain decide whether to add or cut back.

#### How much pain is OK when walking with plantar fasciitis?

One tested rule allows pain up to about 5 out of 10 during activity, as long as it settles by the next morning and does not build week to week. It comes from a trial of 38 people with Achilles pain, not plantar fasciitis, so use it as a guide. Pain above that, or a worse morning, means cut back.

#### Can walking make plantar fasciitis worse?

Yes, if you do much more than your heel is used to. The 2023 guideline lists heel pain after a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as a typical feature of plantar fasciitis. A sudden long walk, a new hilly route or a day on hard floors can [flare it](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-flare-up/). Smaller, steady increases are easier on the heel.

#### Should I stop walking completely to let plantar fasciitis settle?

No study shows complete rest is needed. The 2023 guideline recommends adjusting load and does not advise stopping. In an Achilles pain trial, people who stayed active within a pain limit did as well at twelve months as people who paused running and jumping for six weeks. If even short walks hurt sharply or make you limp, see a clinician.

#### What shoes are best for walking with plantar fasciitis?

Comfortable, cushioned shoes with the heel slightly higher than the toes are the expert advice. A 2021 best practice guide advises avoiding barefoot walking and flat, unsupportive shoes until symptoms are gone. The 2023 guideline says insoles or heel cushions may help when combined with other care, but not on their own.

#### Is it better to walk on grass or concrete with plantar fasciitis?

Softer ground may be easier, but no trial has compared surfaces for walking with plantar fasciitis. The 2023 guideline links weight-bearing work on poorly shock-absorbing surfaces to plantar fasciitis risk. A small case series of runners on grass reported less pain but had no comparison group. Go by how your heel feels next morning.

#### Is walking barefoot at home OK with plantar fasciitis?

It is best avoided while your heel is sore, especially on tile or wood first thing in the morning. A 2021 best practice guide for heel pain advises against barefoot walking and flat, unsupportive footwear until symptoms have fully gone. Supportive shoes or firm slippers for the first steps of the day are the usual advice.

## Flat feet test at home: 4 simple checks, and what they can and cannot tell you

Language: English · https://walkito.site/flat-feet-test/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-23

You can check for flat feet at home in about five minutes: look at a wet footprint, compare your arch sitting and standing, rise on tiptoe or lift your big toe to see if the arch comes back, and try a single-leg heel raise. The footprint is the least exact of the four: in 95 older adults checked against X-rays, a footprint score matched the real arch height only moderately (Menz and Munteanu, 2005). The checks that matter most are whether the arch comes back and whether one side behaves differently.

- A wet footprint is a rough guide. In 95 people aged 62 to 94, the footprint arch index matched X-ray arch height only moderately, while a ruler measure of the arch bone matched it closely (Menz and Munteanu, 2005).
- Body fat under the sole can fill in a footprint: in 24 adults with overweight or obesity, the footprint arch index rose with body fat percentage (Wearing and colleagues, 2004).
- If the arch comes back when you sit, rise on tiptoe or lift your big toe, the flat foot is flexible, the common kind that the exercise trials studied (Brijwasi and Borkar, 2023).
- Trouble rising onto one foot, pain behind the inner ankle and one arch that is getting flatter are signs of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction. In 582 women over 40, 3.3% had early-stage (stage I or II) symptoms and none had been diagnosed (Kohls-Gatzoulis and colleagues, 2009).
- Even clinicians’ measures vary: when two inexperienced testers measured navicular drop, they agreed poorly (Picciano and colleagues, 1993). In a later study of 86 young adults, the same measure was highly repeatable (Zuil-Escobar and colleagues, 2018).

### How can you tell if you have flat feet at home?

**Do four checks, in this order, barefoot on a hard floor.** The first two tell you how low your arch sits. The last two tell you whether it is flexible and whether the tendon that holds it up is doing its job. You need a towel, some water, a piece of brown paper or card, and a wall to hold.

Do both feet every time. A difference between your left and right foot tells you more than either foot on its own, because most people’s feet are roughly alike, and a single flat foot is one of the warning signs at the end of this page.

### How do you do the wet foot test, and how accurate is it?

**How to do it:** wet the sole of one foot, step onto brown paper or dry card with your full weight, stand normally for a second, then step off. Do the other foot. Look at the middle of the print, the part between the heel and the ball of the foot:

- **A clear curve on the inner side**, with the middle band about half as wide as the front of the foot or less: a typical arch.
- **A wide middle band with little or no curve**, so the print looks like a slipper: a low arch.
- **Only the heel and the ball print**, joined by a thin band or not at all: a high arch. See [high arches](https://walkito.site/high-arches-exercises/).

**What it can tell you:** roughly how much of your sole touches the ground. Researchers turn the same print into a number, the arch index, by comparing the middle third of the print with the whole print (Cavanagh and Rodgers, 1987).

**What it cannot tell you:** your real arch height. In 95 people aged 62 to 94 checked against X-rays, the footprint index matched the height of the arch bone only moderately (Menz and Munteanu, 2005). A 1992 study of 115 men found footprints could not predict arch height (Hawes and colleagues, 1992), while a 2009 study of 91 young adults found a weak to moderate match with X-rays (Murley and colleagues, 2009). In 198 clinic patients, three footprint scores picked out a flat foot on X-ray with what the authors called fair accuracy (Paecharoen and colleagues, 2023).

One reason is soft tissue. In a small pilot study of 24 adults with overweight or obesity, the walking footprint index rose with body fat percentage, so a fuller print can mean more padding under the arch, not a lower arch (Wearing and colleagues, 2004). A print also says nothing about pain, which is what decides whether a flat foot needs any attention.

Source: Menz HB, Munteanu SE. Validity of 3 clinical techniques for the measurement of static foot posture in older people. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2005;35(8):479–486.
Source: Cavanagh PR, Rodgers MM. The arch index: a useful measure from footprints. Journal of Biomechanics. 1987;20(5):547–551.
Source: Hawes MR, Nachbauer W, Sovak D, Nigg BM. Footprint parameters as a measure of arch height. Foot & Ankle. 1992;13(1):22–26.
Source: Murley GS, Menz HB, Landorf KB. A protocol for classifying normal- and flat-arched foot posture for research studies using clinical and radiographic measurements. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2009;2:22.
Source: Paecharoen S, Arunakul M, Tantivangphaisal N. Diagnostic Accuracy of Harris Imprint Index, Chippaux-Smirak Index, Staheli Index Compared With Talar-First Metatarsal Angle for Screening Arch of Foot. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2023;47(3):222–227.
Source: Wearing SC, Hills AP, Byrne NM, Hennig EM, McDonald M. The arch index: a measure of flat or fat feet? Foot & Ankle International. 2004;25(8):575–581.

### Does your arch look different sitting and standing?

**Sit on a chair with your feet flat and relaxed, and look at the inner side of each foot.** Note the gap under the arch. Then stand up with your weight on both feet and look again, or have someone take a photo from the side at floor level.

Some drop is normal: every arch lowers a little under your weight. In pooled data from 619 healthy adults, the average foot rested slightly rolled in, which the authors call the normal position (Redmond and colleagues, 2008). What you are looking for is a big change, an arch that is clearly there when you sit and gone when you stand.

**Then look from behind.** Stand normally and have someone look at your heels at floor level. A heel that tilts outward, with the inner ankle bone bulging in, goes with a low arch. If one heel tilts more than the other, note it.

This check tells you how much the arch drops, which is what a clinician measures more exactly as navicular drop (covered below). It does not tell you why: a lax foot you were born with and a tendon that is weakening can look the same standing still. The next two checks start to tell them apart.

Source: Redmond AC, Crane YZ, Menz HB. Normative values for the Foot Posture Index. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2008;1(1):6.

### How do you test for a flexible flat foot?

A flexible flat foot flattens under your weight but gets its arch back when the load changes. Two quick checks show it:

- **Tiptoe check.** Stand holding a wall and rise up onto the balls of both feet. Watch the inner side of each foot, or the heels from behind. In a flexible foot, an arch appears and the heels tilt slightly inward as you rise.
- **Big toe check (Jack’s test).** Stand normally. Lift your big toe up as far as it goes, or have someone lift it for you, while the heel stays down. In a flexible foot, the arch lifts as the toe goes up. The test is named after Jack, who described it in 1953 (Jack, 1953).

**If the arch comes back, the flat foot is flexible.** That is the common kind, and the one studied in the exercise trials: in 52 people with flexible flat feet, six weeks of short-foot, ankle, hip and stretching exercises improved two measures of arch shape more than in a control group (Brijwasi and Borkar, 2023).

**If the arch stays flat and the foot feels stiff**, the flat foot may be rigid. One cause is tarsal coalition, a bridge of bone, cartilage or fibrous tissue between two foot bones, often found in young adults with a stiff, painful flat foot (Mehdi and colleagues, 2024). A rigid flat foot needs a clinician to find the cause before you start any exercise program.

Be honest about what these checks are. We found no study that measured how reliable the tiptoe check or Jack’s test is in adults when people do them at home. They are simple to do and the result is usually clear, but take a stiff result as a reason to get checked, not as a diagnosis.

Source: Jack EA. Naviculo-cuneiform fusion in the treatment of flat foot. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. British Volume. 1953;35-B(1):75–82.
Source: Brijwasi T, Borkar P. A comprehensive exercise program improves foot alignment in people with flexible flat foot: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2023;69(1):42–46.
Source: Mehdi N, Bernasconi A, Lintz F. Tarsal coalition in adults. Orthopaedics & Traumatology: Surgery & Research. 2024;110(1S):103761.

### What does the single-leg heel raise show about flat feet?

The tibialis posterior is the muscle whose tendon runs behind the inner ankle bone and holds up the arch. When the tendon weakens, the arch can slowly drop on that side. This is posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, a common reason an adult’s arch flattens over time. A typical picture is pain on the inner side of the ankle, a flattening foot, and the heel turning out (Deu and colleagues, 2022).

**How to check:** stand on one foot next to a wall, fingertips on the wall for balance only. Rise up as high as you can onto the ball of the foot, then lower. Do a few, then switch feet. Watch for three things:

- you can rise onto one foot as easily as onto the other
- the heel turns inward at the top of the rise, the same way on both sides
- there is no pain behind or below the inner ankle bone

Struggling to rise on one side, a heel that does not turn in, or pain at the inner ankle are the signs that point to the tendon. A clinician uses the same movement as a screening check, and the full picture is in [posterior tibial tendon dysfunction exercises](https://walkito.site/posterior-tibial-tendon-dysfunction-exercises/).

This check is about the shape and side-to-side feel of one rise, not about how many you can do. If you want a number for calf endurance, with the research pace and the counts healthy adults reach, use the [calf raise test](https://walkito.site/calf-raise-test/).

Source: Deu RS, Coslick AM, Dreher G. Tendinopathies of the Foot and Ankle. American Family Physician. 2022;105(5):479–486.
Source: Kohls-Gatzoulis J, Woods B, Angel JC, Singh D. The prevalence of symptomatic posterior tibialis tendon dysfunction in women over the age of 40 in England. Foot and Ankle Surgery. 2009;15(2):75–81.
Source: Ross MH, Smith MD, Mellor R, Vicenzino B. Exercise for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction: a systematic review of randomised clinical trials and clinical guidelines. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2018;4(1):e000430.

### What does a clinician measure for flat feet?

A clinician looks at the same things you did, but scores them in a set way. The two most common measures:

- **Foot Posture Index (FPI).** Six checks of the standing foot, each scored from -2 to +2, including the heel angle, the bulge of the inner ankle and the shape of the arch. The total runs from -12 (high-arched) to +12 (flat). In pooled data from 619 healthy adults, the average was +4, and the authors consider scores below -3 or above +10 clearly outside the normal range (Redmond and colleagues, 2008).
- **Navicular drop.** The clinician marks the bone on the inner side of the arch, measures its height sitting with the foot in a set position, then standing, and records how far it sinks. Healthy adults average about 3.6 to 8.1 millimetres in studies, and no cut-off for "too much" has been confirmed (Nielsen and colleagues, 2009).

**These measures are better than a footprint, but not perfect.** In older adults, a ruler measure of the arch bone’s height matched X-rays closely (r = 0.79), while the FPI matched less well (r = 0.36 to 0.59), because it scores the whole foot, not just the arch (Menz and Munteanu, 2005). The FPI total showed moderate reliability overall, navicular height was the most reliable single measure in adults, and none of the measures tested was reliable enough in young children (Evans and colleagues, 2003).

Practice matters. When two inexperienced testers measured navicular drop in 15 people, their results agreed poorly (Picciano and colleagues, 1993). In 86 young adults in a later study, navicular drop and footprint scores were highly repeatable (Zuil-Escobar and colleagues, 2018). If your arch is being tracked over time, the same person measuring helps.

If a clinician suspects a rigid foot, a coalition or tendon damage, they may order a standing X-ray, a CT scan or an MRI, which no home check can replace (Mehdi and colleagues, 2024).

Source: Redmond AC, Crane YZ, Menz HB. Normative values for the Foot Posture Index. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2008;1(1):6.
Source: Nielsen RG, Rathleff MS, Simonsen OH, Langberg H. Determination of normal values for navicular drop during walking: a new model correcting for foot length and gender. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2009;2:12.
Source: Menz HB, Munteanu SE. Validity of 3 clinical techniques for the measurement of static foot posture in older people. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2005;35(8):479–486.
Source: Evans AM, Copper AW, Scharfbillig RW, Scutter SD, Williams MT. Reliability of the foot posture index and traditional measures of foot position. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2003;93(3):203–213.
Source: Picciano AM, Rowlands MS, Worrell T. Reliability of open and closed kinetic chain subtalar joint neutral positions and navicular drop test. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 1993;18(4):553–558.
Source: Zuil-Escobar JC, Martínez-Cepa CB, Martín-Urrialde JA, Gómez-Conesa A. Medial Longitudinal Arch: Accuracy, Reliability, and Correlation Between Navicular Drop Test and Footprint Parameters. Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics. 2018;41(8):672–679.
Source: Mehdi N, Bernasconi A, Lintz F. Tarsal coalition in adults. Orthopaedics & Traumatology: Surgery & Research. 2024;110(1S):103761.

### What should you do with your result?

Put the four checks together:

- **Low arch, comes back on tiptoe, no pain, both feet alike:** a flexible flat foot, a normal variation. Nothing needs doing. Exercise is optional.
- **Low arch that comes back, with tired or aching arches after long days:** foot and ankle exercises are a reasonable start. See [flat feet exercises](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-exercises/) for the full program.
- **Arch that stays flat, one foot flatter than the other, or pain at the inner ankle:** see a clinician before you start exercises. The list below has the details.

**What exercise can and cannot do.** In 52 people with flexible flat feet, six weeks of short-foot, ankle, hip and stretching work improved arch shape more than ankle up-and-down movements alone (Brijwasi and Borkar, 2023). A 2024 review of short-foot training found no clear change in overall foot posture, and a change in one arch measure only in programs longer than six weeks (Cheng and colleagues, 2024). Both measured shape, not pain.

The cards below are a starting point taken from [flat feet exercises](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-exercises/), with the same doses.

- **Short foot, seated** (3 sets of 8, hold 5 seconds, each foot): Sit with your foot flat on the floor. Pull the ball of the foot toward the heel so the arch lifts, and hold. Keep the outside of the foot on the ground and lift the arch to make a small cave under the foot. Don’t curl the toes. Curling them is the most common way to get this exercise wrong.
- **Big toe lift** (3 sets of 8, hold 5 seconds, each foot): Sit with your feet flat. Lift only the big toe and hold. The other four toes stay flat on the floor. The big toe lift teaches the big toe to move on its own, which is the arch’s first switch.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Both feet share the load while the calf wakes up.
- **Band turn-in** (3 sets of 12, each foot): Sit with a resistance band around the foot and turn the foot in against it. Move the foot, not the leg. The knee stays still. Walkito adds the band turn-in only after six sessions of the standing short foot, so the arch’s own muscles come first.

Source: Brijwasi T, Borkar P. A comprehensive exercise program improves foot alignment in people with flexible flat foot: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2023;69(1):42–46.
Source: Cheng J, Han D, Qu J, et al. Effects of short foot training on foot posture in patients with flatfeet: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Back and Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation. 2024;37(4):839–851.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### See a clinician first if

- the arch stays flat when you sit, stand on tiptoe or lift your big toe, and the foot feels stiff
- one foot has become flatter than the other over months, or you notice it suddenly
- you have pain or swelling behind or below the inner ankle bone
- you cannot rise onto one foot, or rising on that side hurts
- a flat foot started after a fall, a twist or an injury
- you have diabetes and the foot is warm, red or swollen, or its shape is changing
- you feel numbness, burning or tingling in the foot
- a child’s flat foot is stiff, painful or comes with a limp

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is an exercise app for heel and foot pain, on iPhone and Android. It builds a plan from your answers, including where it hurts and which side, and repeats a simple test every 14 days: calf raises, an arch hold, single-leg balance, and left against right.

#### How do I know if I have flat feet?

Look at a wet footprint, then compare your arch sitting and standing. A print with no curve on the inner side and an arch that disappears when you stand suggest a low arch. Then rise on tiptoe: if the arch comes back, the flat foot is flexible, the common kind. A footprint alone matches real arch height only moderately.

#### Is the wet foot test accurate?

Only roughly. In 95 older adults checked against X-rays, the footprint score matched arch height moderately, and a 1992 study of 115 men found footprints could not predict arch height. Body fat under the sole can also fill in the print. Use it as a first look, not as a diagnosis.

#### What is the flexible flat foot test?

It checks whether the arch comes back. Stand on tiptoe, or lift your big toe while the heel stays down (Jack’s test, described in 1953). If an arch appears, the flat foot is flexible. If it stays flat and stiff, a clinician should look for the cause. We found no study of how reliable either check is at home.

#### How do I know if my flat feet are rigid?

A rigid flat foot has no arch when you sit, stand on tiptoe or lift your big toe, and it often feels stiff. One cause is tarsal coalition, a bridge between foot bones reported in 1 to 13% of people. A rigid flat foot that hurts needs a clinician and usually imaging.

#### Can you have one flat foot?

Yes, and it is worth checking. An arch that is getting flatter on one side, especially with pain behind the inner ankle or trouble rising onto that foot, is a typical sign of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction. In 582 women over 40, 3.3% had early signs of it and none had been diagnosed. See a clinician.

#### What is a normal navicular drop?

In studies, healthy adults average about 3.6 to 8.1 millimetres of navicular drop, the distance the arch bone sinks when you stand. Cut-offs of 10, 13 or 15 millimetres have been suggested for too much, but none is confirmed, and results vary between testers, especially inexperienced ones. It is hard to measure accurately on yourself.

#### What is the Foot Posture Index?

It is a six-part check a clinician does while you stand, scoring the heel, ankle and arch from -2 to +2 each, for a total from -12 (high-arched) to +12 (flat). In 619 healthy adults the average was +4, which is normal. It showed moderate reliability overall, and no foot posture measure tested was reliable enough in young children.

#### Do flat feet need treatment if they do not hurt?

Usually not. A flexible flat foot that causes no pain and does not limit what you do is a normal variation. The Framingham Foot Study of about 1,900 adults found no link between flat foot posture and low back pain. Pain, stiffness or a change on one side are the reasons to get it checked.

#### Can I test my child for flat feet the same way?

The tiptoe and big toe checks work for children too, but most young children have low arches that form with age, and foot posture measures were not reliable enough in young children in one study. A stiff foot, pain or a limp are reasons to see a doctor. More in [flat feet in kids](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-in-kids/).

## Foot exercises for runners: a short routine and what the research shows

Language: English · https://walkito.site/foot-exercises-for-runners/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

A good foot routine for runners trains four things: the small muscles of the arch (the short foot exercise), calf and soleus endurance (heel raises), toe strength and single-leg balance. It takes about 10 minutes, two to five times a week, after an easy run or on a rest day. In one trial of 118 recreational runners, those who did not do a foot core program were 2.42 times more likely to get a running injury over 12 months (Taddei and colleagues, 2020). That is one trial, so read it as promising, not settled.

- In a 2020 trial of 118 recreational long-distance runners, the group without foot core training was 2.42 times more likely to get a running injury over 12 months. The effect appeared after about four to eight months of training (Taddei and colleagues, 2020).
- In a 2019 trial of 57 runners, about two months of foot exercises done at least five times a week made every measured foot muscle bigger and stronger (Ridge and colleagues, 2019).
- Healthy adults do a median of about 23 to 24 single-leg calf raises per leg, and 25 has been proposed as a reference for normal (Hebert-Losier and colleagues, 2017; Lunsford and Perry, 1995).
- A self-guided hip, thigh and core strength program for 720 first-time marathon runners did not lower the overuse injuries that kept runners from finishing the race: 7.1% against 7.3% (Toresdahl and colleagues, 2020). Strength work alone did not prevent injuries there.
- Across studies of long-distance runners, between 19.4% and 79.3% got a leg injury, and a previous injury was one of the clearest risk factors (van Gent and colleagues, 2007).

### Do foot exercises help runners avoid injury?

**One good trial says yes, and it is still only one trial.** In 2020, Taddei and colleagues in Brazil randomly split 118 recreational long-distance runners into a foot core group (57 runners) and a control group (61 runners). The foot core group did about two months of supervised training on the foot and ankle muscles, then kept going with remote supervision. Everyone reported their running and any injury each week for a year.

Over 12 months, the control group was 2.42 times more likely to get a running injury. The difference showed up after four to eight months of training, not in the first weeks. Runners whose foot strength went up the most went longer before an injury.

An earlier, smaller trial from the same team, with 28 runners, found that about two months of foot training made the small foot muscles bigger and increased push off force while running (Taddei and colleagues, 2020).

What this does not tell us: both trials come from one research group, in experienced recreational runners who were not injured at the start. The trials did not include beginners or runners who already had pain, so we do not know if the results apply to them.

Source: Taddei UT, Matias AB, Duarte M, Sacco ICN. Foot core training to prevent running-related injuries: a survival analysis of a single-blind, randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(14):3610–3619.
Source: Taddei UT, Matias AB, Ribeiro FIA, Bus SA, Sacco ICN. Effects of a foot strengthening program on foot muscle morphology and running mechanics: a proof-of-concept, single-blind randomized controlled trial. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2020;42:107–115.

### What should a runner’s foot routine include?

Four parts, each with one or two exercises. The doses below are Walkito’s starting doses. Do them barefoot, and stop for the day if pain goes above 6 out of 10.

- **Foot core:** the [short foot exercise](https://walkito.site/exercises/short-foot-exercise/), standing and then on one leg. It trains the small muscles that hold up the arch.
- **Calf and soleus:** heel raises with a straight knee for the calf, and with a bent knee for the soleus, the deeper calf muscle.
- **Toes:** big toe lifts. The big toe is the last part of the foot to leave the ground when you push off.
- **Balance:** standing on one leg, because running is a series of one-leg landings.

This mirrors the idea behind the Taddei program, which trained the small foot muscles first and then used them in standing and loaded positions. It is not a copy of that program. For more toe work, see [toe strengthening exercises](https://walkito.site/toe-strengthening-exercises/).

- **Short foot, standing** (3 sets of 10, hold 5 seconds, both feet): Stand with your weight on both feet. Without curling your toes, pull the ball of the foot toward the heel so the arch lifts a little. Hold, then relax. If the toes grip the floor, ease off.
- **Short foot, one leg** (3 sets of 10, hold 5 seconds, each foot): Stand on one foot, a hand near a wall. Lift the arch as above and hold it while you balance. This is closer to what the foot does when you land.
- **Double-leg calf raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Hold a wall. Rise onto the balls of both feet over about 3 seconds, keeping the weight toward the big toe, then lower over 3 seconds. When this is easy, move to one leg. More on the [calf raises](https://walkito.site/exercises/calf-raises/) page.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of the feet. With the knee bent, the soleus does most of the work. A backpack or weights on the knees add load as it gets easy.
- **Big toe lift** (3 sets of 8, hold 5 seconds, each foot): Keep the four small toes on the floor and lift only the big toe. Then try the reverse: big toe down, small toes up. A small movement is enough at first.
- **Single-leg balance hold** (3 holds of 30 seconds, each side): Stand on one foot, knee soft, near a wall. When 30 seconds is easy, close your eyes or stand on a pillow. More on the [single-leg balance](https://walkito.site/exercises/single-leg-balance/) page.

Source: Taddei UT, Matias AB, Duarte M, Sacco ICN. Foot core training to prevent running-related injuries: a survival analysis of a single-blind, randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(14):3610–3619.
Source: Madeley LT, Munteanu SE, Bonanno DR. Endurance of the ankle joint plantar flexor muscles in athletes with medial tibial stress syndrome: a case-control study. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2007;10(6):356–362.
Source: Gooding TM, Feger MA, Hart JM, Hertel J. Intrinsic foot muscle activation during specific exercises: a T2 time magnetic resonance imaging study. Journal of Athletic Training. 2016;51(8):644–650.

### Why do runners need calf and soleus strength?

**The calf muscles do much of the pushing when you run.** A 2014 review of how leg muscles work in running found that at speeds up to about 7 metres per second, which covers nearly all recreational running, runners go faster mainly by pushing harder into the ground for a longer stride. The two calf muscles, the soleus and the gastrocnemius, have a particularly important role in that push (Schache and colleagues, 2014).

The soleus sits under the gastrocnemius and works most when the knee is bent, which is why the routine has a seated, bent-knee heel raise as well as the standing one. If your calves often feel tight after runs, [tight calves](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/) covers stretching and the [soleus stretch](https://walkito.site/exercises/soleus-stretch/).

Calf endurance also comes up in shin pain. In a case-control study, athletes with shin splints did fewer heel raises to fatigue than athletes without them (Madeley and colleagues, 2007). That shows a link, not that weak calves cause shin splints. More in [shin splints exercises](https://walkito.site/shin-splints-exercises/).

Source: Schache AG, Dorn TW, Williams GP, Brown NA, Pandy MG. Lower-limb muscular strategies for increasing running speed. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2014;44(10):813-824.
Source: Madeley LT, Munteanu SE, Bonanno DR. Endurance of the ankle joint plantar flexor muscles in athletes with medial tibial stress syndrome: a case-control study. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2007;10(6):356–362.

### How many calf raises should a runner be able to do?

There is no runner-specific norm, so use the general adult numbers as a floor. In a study of 566 adults, the median was 24 single-leg heel raises on the right leg and 23 on the left, at a pace of one beat up and one beat down at 60 beats per minute. Counts fall with age, and more active people did more (Hebert-Losier and colleagues, 2017). An older study proposed 25 as the reference for normal (Lunsford and Perry, 1995).

Compare your legs too. A gap of more than 10 percent between sides is the usual threshold for a meaningful difference in leg rehabilitation (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2010). The full protocol, a home version and a calculator are on the [calf raise test](https://walkito.site/calf-raise-test/) page.

Source: Hébert-Losier K, Wessman C, Alricsson M, Svantesson U. Updated reliability and normative values for the standing heel-rise test in healthy adults. Physiotherapy. 2017;103(4):446–452.
Source: Lunsford BR, Perry J. The standing heel-rise test for ankle plantar flexion: criterion for normal. Physical Therapy. 1995;75(8):694–698.
Source: Silbernagel KG, Nilsson-Helander K, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. A new measurement of heel-rise endurance with the ability to detect functional deficits in patients with Achilles tendon rupture. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2010;18(2):258–264.

### When should runners do foot exercises, and how often?

**No study has compared doing foot exercises after a run against doing them on a rest day,** so the timing below is practical, not tested.

- **After an easy run or on a rest day.** The exercises tire the small foot muscles, so they fit better after a short, easy run than before a hard session or a long run.
- **Not right before speed work or a race.** You want fresh calves for those.
- **Calf raises 2 to 3 days a week,** with a day off between them, like any strength work.
- **Foot core, toes and balance 2 to 5 days a week.** In the 2019 trial, runners did foot exercises at least five times a week and gained strength in about two months (Ridge and colleagues, 2019).

Give it time. Muscle size changed within about two months in the trials, but the drop in injuries in the Taddei trial only showed after four to eight months. A routine you keep for months matters more than a hard one you drop after three weeks.

Source: Ridge ST, Olsen MT, Bruening DA, et al. Walking in minimalist shoes is effective for strengthening foot muscles. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019;51(1):104–113.
Source: Taddei UT, Matias AB, Duarte M, Sacco ICN. Foot core training to prevent running-related injuries: a survival analysis of a single-blind, randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(14):3610–3619.

### Can you do foot exercises with a niggle?

Usually yes, if the niggle is mild and stable, and if you adjust. Use the same rule as the rest of this site: some discomfort is fine, but stop for the day if pain goes above 6 out of 10, and go lighter if it is worse the next morning.

A few niggles change the plan:

- **Heel pain on the first steps in the morning** points to plantar fasciitis. Calf raises and stretches matter more there: see [heel pain from running](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/) and [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).
- **Pain at the back of the heel or in the Achilles tendon** needs a more gradual calf plan, often with slow heel drops: see [Achilles tendonitis exercises](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/).
- **Pain along the inner shin** may be shin splints: see [shin splints exercises](https://walkito.site/shin-splints-exercises/).
- **Pain in one spot on a bone** that grows with each run is a stress fracture warning sign. Stop running and get it checked.

### What foot exercises do not do

**They do not replace sensible training.** Across studies of long-distance runners, between 19.4% and 79.3% got a leg injury, and a long weekly distance in men and a previous injury were among the clearest risk factors (van Gent and colleagues, 2007). In a Danish study of 874 novice runners, those who raised their weekly distance by more than 30% seemed more prone to some overuse injuries, though the result fell just short of statistical significance (Nielsen and colleagues, 2014).

**Strength work is not automatic protection.** In a trial with 720 first-time New York City Marathon runners, a self-guided 10-minute program for the hips, thighs and core, three times a week for about three months, did not lower the overuse injuries that stopped runners from finishing the marathon: 7.1% in the strength group against 7.3% in the others (Toresdahl and colleagues, 2020). That program did not train the feet, but it is a reminder that a routine on paper is not the same as a result.

**They change arch shape only a little.** In a small study of 21 people without a control group, the arch sank 1.8 mm less after a month of short foot training (Mulligan and Cook, 2013). Expect a stronger, steadier foot, not a new arch. Shoes and barefoot running are a separate question, covered in [barefoot shoes](https://walkito.site/barefoot-shoes/).

Source: van Gent RN, Siem D, van Middelkoop M, van Os AG, Bierma-Zeinstra SM, Koes BW. Incidence and determinants of lower extremity running injuries in long distance runners: a systematic review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;41(8):469-480.
Source: Nielsen RØ, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sørensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2014;44(10):739–747.
Source: Toresdahl BG, McElheny K, Metzl J, Ammerman B, Chang B, Kinderknecht J. A randomized study of a strength training program to prevent injuries in runners of the New York City Marathon. Sports Health. 2020;12(1):74-79.
Source: Mulligan EP, Cook PG. Effect of plantar intrinsic muscle training on medial longitudinal arch morphology and dynamic function. Manual Therapy. 2013;18(5):425–430.

### See a clinician first if

- pain sits on one spot of a bone in the foot or shin and gets worse with each run, which can be a stress fracture
- you cannot put weight on the foot, or you limp when you walk
- the pain started with a pop, a fall or a twisted ankle
- the foot or ankle is swollen, red or hot, or you have a fever
- you feel numbness, tingling or burning in the foot
- the heel or foot hurts at night or at rest
- pain keeps getting worse over two to three weeks despite easier running

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app with the exercises on this page: the short foot from seated to one leg, heel raises, big toe lifts, toe spreads and single-leg balance. It does not plan your running, so keep your own training plan and fit the sessions on easy days.

#### What are the best foot exercises for runners?

A short set that covers four things: the short foot exercise for the arch, heel raises with a straight and a bent knee for the calf and soleus, big toe lifts for push off, and single-leg balance. A foot core program built on the same idea lowered running injuries in one trial of 118 runners.

#### Do foot strengthening exercises prevent running injuries?

They may. In a 2020 trial of 118 recreational runners, the group without foot core training was 2.42 times more likely to be injured over 12 months, with the effect appearing after four to eight months. It is one trial from one research group, so the evidence is promising but not settled.

#### How often should runners do foot exercises?

Two to five days a week for the foot core, toe and balance work, and two to three days a week for calf raises, with a day off between them. In a 2019 trial, runners who did foot exercises at least five times a week gained strength in about two months.

#### Should I do foot exercises before or after running?

After an easy run or on a rest day is the practical choice, because the exercises tire the small foot muscles. No study has compared timing. Avoid a full routine right before speed work, a long run or a race, when you want fresh feet and calves.

#### How many single-leg calf raises should a runner do?

There is no runner-specific number. Healthy adults do a median of about 23 to 24 per leg at a set pace, and 25 has been proposed as normal. Many active runners do more. A gap of more than 10 percent between legs is worth tracking. The calf raise test page has the full protocol.

#### How long until foot exercises make a difference?

Foot muscles got bigger and stronger in about two months in the trials. The drop in injuries in the runner trial took longer, showing after four to eight months. Plan to keep a short routine going for months, not weeks.

#### Can I keep running while I do foot exercises?

Yes. The routine is meant to sit alongside your running. If you have a niggle, stop an exercise for the day if pain goes above 6 out of 10, and keep runs easy if pain is worse the next morning. Pain that grows with each run, or sits on one spot of bone, needs a clinician.

#### Do barefoot running or minimalist shoes strengthen the feet?

Walking in minimalist shoes built foot strength about as well as exercises in a 2019 trial of runners, with a slow, gradual increase. Switching your running shoes quickly is a different matter and carries its own risks, so build up slowly if you try it.

## Teacher foot pain: what a school day does to your feet, and what helps

Language: English · https://walkito.site/teachers-foot-pain/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

Teacher foot pain mostly comes from hours of standing and walking the room on hard floors, and the options with the best evidence, calf and plantar fascia stretches plus calf strength work, take 3 to 5 minutes and fit between classes. The 2023 heel pain guideline grades those stretches **A**, its top grade, and strength work **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Research on teachers’ feet is limited: in a 2024 review, 27 studies reported pain in the ankle region, mostly counted together with the foot, and the pooled figure was 30% of teachers (Tahernejad and colleagues, 2024).

- In a 2024 review of 44 studies and 15,972 teachers, pain in the ankle region (mostly counted with the foot) was pooled at 30% across 27 studies, below the neck and lower back at 47% each. Results varied widely between studies (Tahernejad and colleagues, 2024).
- In one survey of 1,439 teachers in a single Saudi region, 85.5% reported foot pain in the past 12 months, and it was more common in teachers with 16 or more lessons a week (Alqahtani, 2020). Other surveys found much lower figures, so read it as one region’s result.
- We found no study that measured how many hours a typical teacher stands. In a study of 50 cases and 100 controls, standing for most of the working day raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 3.6 times, and very limited ankle flexibility, usually from a tight calf, raised them 23.3 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching **A** and strength work **B**. Insoles on their own get a **B against** (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- In 50 people with heel pain and 25 without, those with heel pain stood 3.4 hours a day longer and wore shoes with harder heels. That is a link, not proof of cause (Landorf and colleagues, 2023).

### What does a teaching day do to your feet?

**A teaching day mixes standing still with short walks, mostly on hard floors.** You stand at the board or the front desk, walk the rows while students work, then stand again on hall or yard duty. Standing still loads the heel, the plantar fascia (the band under the foot that holds up the arch) and the calf for long stretches without the pumping action of walking.

We found no study that measured how many hours a typical teacher stands, so this page does not give a figure. What is measured is prolonged standing in general. A 2015 review of standing work linked it with leg and foot discomfort, fatigue and leg swelling, and listed floor mats, supportive shoes, compression stockings and sit-stand options among the measures with some evidence (Waters and Dick, 2015).

In a 2017 review of 25 laboratory studies, discomfort in the lower back and legs grew the longer people stood without a break. The authors suggested not standing for more than about 40 minutes at a time (Coenen and colleagues, 2017). That is roughly one lesson.

The calf matters too. In a 2003 study, a [tight calf](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/) was the strongest risk factor for plantar fasciitis, at 23.3 times the odds, and standing for most of the working day raised the odds 3.6 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). A teacher on their feet all day with tight calves has both.

Source: Waters TR, Dick RB. Evidence of health risks associated with prolonged standing at work and intervention effectiveness. Rehabilitation Nursing. 2015;40(3):148–165.
Source: Coenen P, Parry S, Willenberg L, et al. Associations of prolonged standing with musculoskeletal symptoms: a systematic review of laboratory studies. Gait & Posture. 2017;58:310–318.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### How common is foot pain in teachers?

**Common, but less studied than teachers’ backs and necks.** A 2024 review pooled 44 studies of 15,972 teachers. Neck and lower back pain came first, at 47% each. Pain in the ankle region, which most of the studies counted together with the foot, was pooled at 30% across 27 studies of 8,634 teachers. The studies were very different from each other, and the authors found signs of publication bias for the ankle figure, so read 30% as a rough middle, not an exact rate.

An earlier review found that only a few studies had looked at teachers’ legs and feet at all, and that leg and foot pain was reported less often than back, neck and arm pain (Erick and Smith, 2011).

The largest foot-specific survey we found asked 1,439 teachers in one region of Saudi Arabia. 85.5% reported foot pain in the past 12 months. It was more common in teachers with 16 or more lessons a week (88%) than in those with fewer (81.4%), and in those with more than 10 years of teaching (86.8% against 82.6%). It was a self-reported questionnaire in one region, and most of the teachers were women, so it may not match your school (Alqahtani, 2020).

Source: Tahernejad S, Hejazi A, Rezaei E, Makki F, Sahebi A, Zangiabadi Z. Musculoskeletal disorders among teachers: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. 2024;12:1399552.
Source: Erick PN, Smith DR. A systematic review of musculoskeletal disorders among school teachers. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2011;12:260.
Source: Alqahtani TA. The prevalence of foot pain and its associated factors among Saudi school teachers in Abha sector, Saudi Arabia. Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care. 2020;9(9):4641–4647.

### Which exercises fit between classes?

The exercises below come from the plantar fasciitis guideline. They were not tested in teachers, but they target the tissues a standing day loads: the calf, the plantar fascia and the heel. Most need only a wall or a desk, so they fit a passing period or a planning period. These are Walkito’s starting doses, not a prescription. [How these guides are written](https://walkito.site/about/).

Stretches get the guideline’s top grade, **A**. Calf strength work gets a **B**. If any exercise takes your pain to **6/10 or more**, stop for the day.

- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on the wall or the whiteboard frame. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel all day, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position at the wall, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor, and another at your desk before you stand up after a planning period.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit at your desk with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, with almost no load on the heel. It fits under the desk while students do quiet work.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet with a hand on the desk, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Both feet share the load. More on how to build up: [calf raises for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/).
- **Foot roll** (1 minute): Sit and roll the sole of your foot slowly over a massage ball, with firm pressure. If you are wincing, ease off. A ball in your desk drawer makes this an after-school habit. More in [massage ball for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/massage-ball-plantar-fasciitis/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### How do you fit foot exercises into a school day?

You do not need a separate workout. Tie each exercise to a point in the day that already happens. The doses are the same as above; the table only says when they fit.

Source: Coenen P, Parry S, Willenberg L, et al. Associations of prolonged standing with musculoskeletal symptoms: a systematic review of laboratory studies. Gait & Posture. 2017;58:310–318.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### What are the best shoes for teachers on their feet all day?

**No study has compared shoes for teachers, and no trial picks one brand or style.** The 2023 heel pain guideline does not grade shoe types. What evidence there is points to cushioning under the heel and to fit.

In a 2023 study, 50 people with plantar heel pain were compared with 25 matched people without it. Those with heel pain stood 3.4 hours a day longer and wore shoes with harder heels. Shoe style, heel height and standing on hard floors did not differ between the groups (Landorf and colleagues, 2023). That shows a link, not that soft heels prevent pain, but it supports a shoe with a cushioned heel for long days at the board.

A practical checklist, based on fit and comfort rather than a trial:

- a cushioned heel and a firm heel counter (the back of the shoe does not fold when you squeeze it)
- room for your toes to spread, with no pinching at the end of the day
- a low, stable heel rather than a high or very thin one
- a second pair to swap with, so you are not in the same worn pair every day

**Insoles can make a day more comfortable, but do not rely on them alone.** The 2023 guideline grades insoles on their own **B against**, and combined with stretching and strength work a **C** (Koc and colleagues, 2023). [Insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) compares the two, and [best insoles for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/best-insoles-for-plantar-fasciitis/) covers what to look for.

Compression socks are another option for heavy, swollen legs by the end of the day. In a trial of 40 security guards on long standing shifts, 15 to 20 mmHg and 20 to 30 mmHg stockings both avoided the rise in leg discomfort and swelling seen with regular socks (Garcia and colleagues, 2023). It was not a study of teachers.

Source: Landorf KB, Kaminski MR, Munteanu SE, Zammit GV, Menz HB. Activity and footwear characteristics in people with and without plantar heel pain: a matched cross-sectional observational study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2023;21(1):35–44.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Garcia MG, Roman MG, Davila A, Martin BJ. Comparison of physiological effects induced by two compression stockings and regular socks during prolonged standing work. Human Factors. 2023;65(4):562–574.

### Do classroom floors and mats make a difference?

Most classrooms have hard floors: tile, vinyl over concrete, or thin carpet. No study has measured classroom floors and teachers’ feet. The 2015 review of standing work lists floor mats among the measures with some evidence for less discomfort, alongside shoes and sit-stand options (Waters and Dick, 2015).

A mat only helps where you actually stand. If you teach from one spot, such as the board, the projector or a lab bench, an anti-fatigue mat there is worth trying. If you walk the room, the shoe is your mat.

Moving is the other half. The standing studies found discomfort building with time spent standing still (Coenen and colleagues, 2017). Walking between desks, sitting during quiet work and shifting your weight all break up the static load.

At home, avoid going barefoot on hard floors first thing in the morning if your heel hurts. [Heel pain in the morning](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-in-the-morning/) explains why the first steps matter.

Source: Waters TR, Dick RB. Evidence of health risks associated with prolonged standing at work and intervention effectiveness. Rehabilitation Nursing. 2015;40(3):148–165.
Source: Coenen P, Parry S, Willenberg L, et al. Associations of prolonged standing with musculoskeletal symptoms: a systematic review of laboratory studies. Gait & Posture. 2017;58:310–318.

### When is a teacher’s heel pain plantar fasciitis?

General aching at the end of a school day that is gone by the next morning is standing fatigue. **Plantar fasciitis has a typical pattern: sharp pain under the heel on the first steps in the morning or after you have been sitting, that eases as you walk, then comes back after a long day on your feet.** In the Saudi survey, 25.8% of teachers with foot pain said it came early in the morning and after rest (Alqahtani, 2020). That survey did not diagnose anyone, so it is a pattern, not a count of plantar fasciitis.

If that sounds like you, start with [plantar fasciitis exercises and stretches](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/). About 90% of people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care, though it can take three to six months (Latt and colleagues, 2020). [How long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/) has the details.

Other patterns point elsewhere:

- a deep ache in the middle of the heel, worse barefoot on hard floors: [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/)
- pain along the arch that builds through the day: [arch pain](https://walkito.site/arch-pain/)
- pain under the ball of the foot: [ball of foot pain](https://walkito.site/ball-of-foot-pain/)
- pain at the back of the heel, in the tendon: [Achilles tendonitis exercises](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/)

Not sure which one it is? The [foot pain identifier](https://walkito.site/foot-pain-identifier/) asks a few questions about where and when it hurts. **If you are still unsure, see a clinician before you load it with exercise.**

Source: Alqahtani TA. The prevalence of foot pain and its associated factors among Saudi school teachers in Abha sector, Saudi Arabia. Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care. 2020;9(9):4641–4647.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain started after a fall, a twist or a knock, for example on yard duty or the stairs
- you cannot put weight on the foot, or you are limping
- the foot is numb, tingling, burning, swollen or warm
- the heel or foot is red, or you have a fever or feel unwell
- pain wakes you at night or is there at rest
- pain is in one pinpoint spot and gets worse with activity, which can be a stress fracture pattern
- one calf or leg has swollen suddenly and is painful, red or warm
- you have diabetes, reduced feeling in your feet or poor circulation

### Doing it as a plan

You do not have to work out the order, the doses or when to move to a harder version. [Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) builds a plan one week at a time around one goal. If your heel follows the morning pattern of plantar fasciitis, the first goal is morning pain at 1 out of 10 or less for 14 days in a row.

#### Why do my feet hurt so much after teaching all day?

Teaching keeps you standing and walking on hard floors for most of the day, which loads the heel, arch and calf without much rest. Reviews of standing work link long standing with leg and foot discomfort and fatigue, and laboratory studies found discomfort growing the longer people stood still. Breaks to sit, calf stretches and cushioned shoes all help.

#### How common is foot pain in teachers?

A 2024 review pooled pain in the ankle region, mostly counted together with the foot, at 30% of teachers across 27 studies, with very different results between studies. One survey of 1,439 teachers in a single Saudi region found 85.5% with foot pain in the past year. Neck and lower back pain are reported more often than foot pain.

#### What are the best shoes for teachers who stand all day?

No study has tested shoes for teachers. Look for a cushioned heel, a firm heel counter, room for the toes and a low, stable heel. In one study, people with heel pain wore shoes with harder heels and stood longer each day. Insoles alone get a B against in the 2023 heel pain guideline, so pair them with stretching.

#### What stretches can teachers do between classes?

A calf stretch and a soleus stretch at a wall take about a minute each side: 2 holds of 30 seconds per leg. The plantar fascia stretch can be done seated at your desk, 2 holds of 30 seconds per foot. The 2023 heel pain guideline grades these stretches A, though it was written for plantar fasciitis, not teachers.

#### Can standing all day as a teacher cause plantar fasciitis?

It can raise the risk. In a 2003 study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, standing for most of the working day raised the odds 3.6 times, and very limited ankle flexibility, usually from a tight calf, raised them 23.3 times. The study did not look at teachers, and no study has counted plantar fasciitis in teachers specifically.

#### Do anti-fatigue mats help teachers?

They may, if you stand in one spot. A 2015 review of standing work lists floor mats among the measures with some evidence for less discomfort. No study has tested mats in classrooms. If you walk the room most of the lesson, your shoes matter more than a mat.

#### Should teachers wear compression socks?

They are worth trying if your legs feel heavy or swollen by the end of the day. In a trial of 40 security guards on long standing shifts, 15 to 20 mmHg and 20 to 30 mmHg stockings both avoided the rise in leg discomfort and swelling seen with regular socks. The trial did not include teachers.

#### How long should a teacher stand before sitting down?

There is no tested limit for teachers. A 2017 review of laboratory standing studies found discomfort building with time and suggested not standing for more than about 40 minutes at a time. In practice, sit for a few minutes when students start independent work, and walk the room instead of standing still in one place.

## Foot pain for retail and warehouse workers: what helps on hard floors

Language: English · https://walkito.site/retail-warehouse-foot-pain/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

Warehouse and retail feet hurt because hours of standing and walking on hard floors load the heel, arch and calf with little give underneath. Standing for most of the working day raised the odds of [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) 3.6 times in one study (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). Calf and plantar fascia stretches carry the top grade, **A**, in the 2023 heel pain guideline, and a short version fits in about 3 minutes on a break. Mats and cushioned insoles help comfort, but the evidence for them is thinner (Speed and colleagues, 2018).

- Spending most of the workday on your feet raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 3.6 times in a case-control study of 50 cases and 100 controls. Very limited ankle flexibility, usually from a tight calf, raised them 23.3 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline keeps a grade **B** recommendation: clinicians should check for work-related weight-bearing, particularly on surfaces with poor shock absorption, as a risk factor for heel pain (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- A review of 10 studies found moderate evidence that mats and cushioned insoles reduce discomfort and fatigue in standing workers, and only limited evidence that insoles beat mats (Speed and colleagues, 2018).
- In a review of 7 studies of workers in safety footwear, the 4 that measured pain found foot pain in 42.3% to 60.8% of workers, with heat, sweating, weight and stiffness the main complaints (Arceri and colleagues, 2024).
- Calf and plantar fascia stretching get the guideline’s top grade, **A**, and strength work a **B**. Insoles on their own get a **B against** for heel pain (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

### Why do your feet hurt after a warehouse or retail shift?

Retail and warehouse work mixes two loads. On a till or a packing station you stand still for long stretches. On the floor or picking orders you walk, carry, push carts and turn. Both keep weight on the heel and arch for most of the shift, and break times are set by the rota, not by when your feet need them.

A 2003 case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 matched controls found that spending most of the workday weight-bearing raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 3.6 times. Reduced ankle flexibility, a [tight calf](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/), was the strongest factor, at 23.3 times the odds. **A tight calf is something you can work on. The job usually is not.**

A systematic review of 16 studies on chronic heel pain found some evidence of a link with prolonged standing, alongside higher body weight, age and reduced ankle flexibility. The authors called for studies that follow people over time, so this shows an association, not proof that standing causes heel pain (Irving and colleagues, 2006).

How far do you walk? We found no published study that counts steps per shift for warehouse or retail workers. Figures like "12 miles a shift" appear on industry blogs without a study behind them. The closest measured number is from nurses: an average of 9,360 steps per shift in a tracker study (Chang and Cho, 2022).

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Irving DB, Cook JL, Menz HB. Factors associated with chronic plantar heel pain: a systematic review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2006;9(1-2):11–22.
Source: Chang J, Cho E. Nurses' steps, distance traveled, and perceived physical demands in a three-shift schedule. Human Resources for Health. 2022;20:72.

### Is concrete really worse for your feet?

Probably, but nobody has measured concrete on its own. The 2023 heel pain guideline keeps a recommendation from 2014, graded **B**: clinicians should assess work-related weight-bearing activities, particularly under conditions with poor shock absorption, as a risk factor for heel pain and plantar fasciitis. A bare concrete floor is about as low in shock absorption as a work surface gets.

What has been tested is the opposite: adding something soft. In lab and workplace studies, standing on a mat or wearing cushioned insoles reduced discomfort compared with a hard floor (Speed and colleagues, 2018). That fits the idea that the hard surface adds to the load, without proving concrete causes any one condition.

Some heel pain is worse on hard floors for a different reason. If the ache sits deep in the centre of the heel and is clearly worse barefoot on tile or concrete, [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/) is worth reading about.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Speed G, Harris K, Keegel T. The effect of cushioning materials on musculoskeletal discomfort and fatigue during prolonged standing at work: a systematic review. Applied Ergonomics. 2018;70:300–314.

### Do anti-fatigue mats or insoles help more?

**Both help comfort, with no clear winner, and neither has strong evidence.** A 2018 systematic review found 10 studies of mats and cushioned insoles in people who stand for work. It rated the evidence moderate that cushioning reduces discomfort and fatigue, and limited that insoles do better than mats. The studies differed a lot in design, and the authors called for larger trials in real workplaces.

In one workplace study, assembly workers spent one week of 8-hour days in each of four conditions: hard floor, a mat, insoles, and insoles on a mat. The mat, the insoles and the combination were all more comfortable than the hard floor, and there was no clear difference between them (King, 2002).

In a 4-hour lab test, three of four commercial anti-fatigue mats reduced discomfort compared with a hard floor, but no mat beat the others (Wiggermann and Keyserling, 2013). So no one mat has been shown to be better than the others.

The practical split: **a mat only helps where you stand still**, such as a till, a pack bench or a workstation. If you walk the floor or pick orders, the cushioning has to travel with you, in the shoe. For heel pain specifically, the 2023 guideline grades insoles on their own **B against**, so do not rely on them alone. [Insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) compares the two, and [best insoles for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/best-insoles-for-plantar-fasciitis/) covers the types.

Source: Speed G, Harris K, Keegel T. The effect of cushioning materials on musculoskeletal discomfort and fatigue during prolonged standing at work: a systematic review. Applied Ergonomics. 2018;70:300–314.
Source: King PM. A comparison of the effects of floor mats and shoe in-soles on standing fatigue. Applied Ergonomics. 2002;33(5):477–484.
Source: Wiggermann N, Keyserling WM. Effects of anti-fatigue mats on perceived discomfort and weight-shifting during prolonged standing. Human Factors. 2013;55(4):764–775.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Do safety boots cause foot pain?

Safety boots protect your feet, and they also come with complaints. A 2024 systematic review found 7 studies of workers in safety footwear. Every study reported discomfort and pain, and the 4 studies that measured pain found foot pain in 42.3% to 60.8% of workers. The main complaints were heat, sweating, weight and a stiff sole, mostly around the toes and toecap.

In a study of 509 workers in 12 metal-working factories, all wearing safety footwear every day, 81% had at least one foot problem. Their most common complaints about the shoes were hot and wet conditions inside (42%), weight (27.5%) and fit (22.9%) (Mancuso and colleagues, 2017).

These are surveys, so they cannot say the boots cause the pain: long hours on hard floors would hurt in any shoe. The review’s suggestions are practical:

- Get the right size and width, and check whether your employer’s approved models come in wide fits.
- Choose the lightest boot that meets your site’s safety rating.
- Look for breathable materials if your feet get hot and wet.
- Most safety boots have a removable insole, so a cushioned insert can go in if it does not make the boot too tight.

Never swap a required safety boot for a trainer because your feet hurt. Talk to your supervisor or safety officer about other approved models.

Source: Arceri A, Mazzotti A, Liosi SG, Zielli SO, Artioli E, Golinelli D, et al. What's the impact of safety footwear on workers concerning foot-related problems? A systematic review. Healthcare (Basel). 2024;12(15):1522.
Source: Mancuso G, Cavrini G, Berdondini RM, Mancuso M. Skin lesions and other foot problems associated with safety footwear [in Italian]. Giornale Italiano di Medicina del Lavoro ed Ergonomia. 2017;38(4):261–264.

### What exercises can you do on a break?

The exercises below need no equipment and no floor space beyond a wall, a rack or a counter edge. The first three work standing up in a break room or a stock aisle. The rest are for after the shift, sitting down.

The guideline grades calf and plantar fascia stretching **A** and strength work **B**. Those grades are for plantar fasciitis, but these are the same tissues a shift on hard floors loads. Stop for the day if any exercise pushes your pain to 6 out of 10 or more.

- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall, a rack upright or a counter. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. Works in safety boots too.
