- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Ankle rocks** (2 sets of 15, each leg): Split stance, hands on a wall. Rock the front knee forward over the toes while the heel stays flat. Slow, about two seconds each way. More in [ankle rocks](https://walkito.site/exercises/ankle-rocks/).
- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down, boots off, and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. If your first steps out of bed hurt, do one on the edge of the bed before your foot touches the floor.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, hold a wall, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Strength work fits best on days off, so the calf has time to recover before the next shift. More in [calf raises for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/).
- **Foot roll** (1 minute): Sit and roll the sole of your foot slowly over a massage ball, with firm pressure. If you are wincing, ease off.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### How do you fit it into a shift: 3, 5 or 10 minutes?

Most retail and warehouse breaks are short and set by the rota. A laboratory review found that symptoms from uninterrupted standing became clinically relevant after about 42 minutes in people prone to standing pain, and its authors suggested not standing still for more than about 40 minutes (Coenen and colleagues, 2017). You often cannot choose when to sit, but you can change position: walk to the end of the aisle, shift your weight, or do one calf stretch at a rack.

- **3 minutes, on a break:** the calf stretch, 2 holds of 30 seconds each leg, plus one 30-second soleus hold each leg. That targets the tight calf, the strongest risk factor in the 2003 study.
- **5 minutes, on a longer break or at the end of the shift:** add ankle rocks, or the plantar fascia stretch once your boots are off.
- **10 minutes, on a day off:** add heel raises (3 sets of 10) and the foot roll. That covers the strength side, graded **B**.

**Doing a short routine on most shifts matters more than a long one you skip.** Tie it to something you already do, such as the first break or taking your boots off.

Source: Coenen P, Parry S, Willenberg L, et al. Associations of prolonged standing with musculoskeletal symptoms: a systematic review of laboratory studies. Gait & Posture. 2017;58:310–318.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### What the evidence says about each option

Most workplace advice mixes strong and weak evidence. This table puts the main options side by side, with the best study we found for each.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Speed G, Harris K, Keegel T. The effect of cushioning materials on musculoskeletal discomfort and fatigue during prolonged standing at work: a systematic review. Applied Ergonomics. 2018;70:300–314.
Source: Garcia MG, Roman MG, Davila A, Martin BJ. Comparison of physiological effects induced by two compression stockings and regular socks during prolonged standing work. Human Factors. 2023;65(4):562–574.
Source: Arceri A, Mazzotti A, Liosi SG, Zielli SO, Artioli E, Golinelli D, et al. What's the impact of safety footwear on workers concerning foot-related problems? A systematic review. Healthcare (Basel). 2024;12(15):1522.

### Could it be plantar fasciitis or something else?

A general ache and tired feet after a long shift usually settle with a night’s rest. Plantar fasciitis has a clearer pattern: sharp pain near the inside of the heel, worst on the first steps in the morning or after sitting. If that sounds like you, see [heel pain in the morning](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-in-the-morning/) and [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/). About 90% of people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care, though it can take three to six months (Latt and colleagues, 2020).

Other patterns point elsewhere. A burning ache under the ball of the foot points to [ball of foot pain](https://walkito.site/ball-of-foot-pain/). An ache along the arch that gets worse through the shift is covered in [arch pain](https://walkito.site/arch-pain/). Pain on top of the foot can come from boots laced or pressing too tightly; see [top of foot pain](https://walkito.site/top-of-foot-pain/).

Pain in one small spot on a bone that gets worse the more you walk can be a stress fracture, especially after a jump in hours or a new job with more walking. **That needs a clinician, not more exercise.**

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain started with a fall, a dropped load or a twist at work
- you cannot put weight on the foot, or you are limping
- pain sits in one small spot on a bone and gets worse with walking, which can be a stress fracture
- the foot is numb, tingling or burning, or feels cold
- the foot or heel is red, warm or swollen, or you have a fever
- one calf or leg is suddenly painful and swollen
- you have diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet, and a boot has rubbed a sore or blister
- pain wakes you at night or keeps getting worse after several weeks of the changes on this page

### Doing it as a plan

You do not have to work out the order, the doses or when to move to a harder version. [Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) builds the plan from your answers and adjusts it to how your feet feel each day, so a bad morning after a long shift means a lighter session.

#### Why do my feet hurt so much working in a warehouse?

Long hours of standing and walking on hard floors keep load on the heel, arch and calf for most of the shift. Spending most of the workday on your feet raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 3.6 times in one study, and the 2023 heel pain guideline lists work-related weight-bearing on poorly cushioned surfaces as a risk factor.

#### How many steps does a warehouse worker walk in a shift?

We found no published study that counts steps for warehouse or retail shifts. Figures like 12 miles a shift come from industry blogs without a study behind them. The closest measured figure is from hospital nurses, who averaged 9,360 steps per shift in a tracker study. Your own phone or watch is the best guide to your job.

#### Do anti-fatigue mats actually work?

They reduce discomfort for people who stand in one place, but the evidence is moderate, not strong. A review of 10 studies found cushioning helps standing workers. In a 4-hour lab test, three of four mats beat a hard floor, and no mat beat the others. A mat only helps where you stand still.

#### Are insoles or a mat better for standing on concrete?

About the same for comfort. In a workplace study, assembly workers found a mat, insoles and both together all more comfortable than a hard floor, with no clear difference between them. A review rated the evidence that insoles beat mats as limited. If you walk around, insoles travel with you and a mat does not.

#### Can safety boots cause plantar fasciitis?

No study shows safety boots cause plantar fasciitis. A review of 7 studies of workers in safety footwear found foot pain in 42.3% to 60.8% of workers in the 4 that measured it, with heat, weight and stiffness the main complaints. Hours on hard floors matter too, whatever the boot. A good fit and the lightest approved boot are reasonable first steps.

#### What stretches can I do on a break at work?

The calf stretch and the soleus stretch work standing up against a wall or rack, in work boots: two holds of 30 seconds each, each leg, about 4 minutes for both stretches. The 2023 heel pain guideline grades calf stretching A. Save the plantar fascia stretch and heel raises for after the shift or days off.

#### Is it normal for my feet to hurt after a retail shift?

Tired, aching feet after a long standing shift are common, and a 2015 review linked prolonged standing at work with discomfort, fatigue and leg pain across many jobs. Common does not mean you should ignore it. Pain that is sharp, lasts into your days off or is worst on your first steps in the morning is worth acting on.

#### Can I keep working with plantar fasciitis in a standing job?

Many people do, with changes. Short stretches on breaks, better-fitting boots and cushioning where you stand ease the load, and about 90% of people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care, though it can take three to six months. If pain is getting worse despite this, see a clinician.

## Foot pain for chefs and restaurant workers: what helps on long kitchen shifts

Language: English · https://walkito.site/chefs-foot-pain/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

Chef foot pain often comes from long hours standing and walking on hard kitchen floors, and for heel pain the options with the best evidence are calf and plantar fascia stretches, which the 2023 heel pain guideline grades **A**, and calf strength work, graded **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Slip-resistant shoes are about safety, not pain: in a randomized trial across 226 school districts, giving food service workers slip-resistant shoes at no cost lowered slipping injury claims from 3.54 to 1.18 per 10,000 worker-months (Bell and colleagues, 2019). No study has tested whether clogs or any kitchen shoe reduce foot pain itself.

- In a survey of 128 kitchen workers in Cairo, 46.1% reported foot pain in the past 12 months, behind only the lower back and the knee (Abdelsalam and colleagues, 2023).
- In 475 workers from 36 US fast-food restaurants, wearing slip-resistant shoes was linked to a 54% lower rate of slipping (Verma and colleagues, 2011).
- In a randomized trial in school food service, slipping injury claims fell from 3.54 to 1.18 per 10,000 worker-months where workers got free slip-resistant shoes, while they rose from 2.01 to 2.30 in the comparison group (Bell and colleagues, 2019).
- Standing for most of the working day raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 3.6 times in a case-control study of 50 cases and 100 controls, and a tight calf raised them 23.3 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline grades calf and plantar fascia stretching **A** and strength training **B**. Insoles on their own are graded **B against** (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

### Why do chefs’ feet hurt so much after a shift?

**Kitchen work stacks the things feet handle worst: hours of standing, short fast walks, hard floors and little rest.** In a survey of 128 kitchen workers at two large student hostels in Cairo, 90.6% reported a musculoskeletal problem in the past 12 months. The foot was the third most affected area, at 46.1%, just behind the knee at 46.9%.

The numbers vary a lot between studies. In 307 restaurant chefs in Pakistan, most working 9 to 12 hours a day, 26 reported ankle or foot pain, far fewer than the 101 who reported lower back and knee pain (Iqbal and colleagues, 2023). The surveys used different groups and questions, so read them as a rough picture, not a precise rate.

One link shows up clearly. In 415 hotel and restaurant kitchen workers in Ethiopia, prolonged standing came with 3.81 times the odds of a work-related musculoskeletal problem (Abebaw and colleagues, 2024). That study counted pain anywhere in the body, not only the feet.

Source: Abdelsalam A, Wassif GO, Eldin WS, Abdel-Hamid MA, Damaty SI. Frequency and risk factors of musculoskeletal disorders among kitchen workers. Journal of the Egyptian Public Health Association. 2023;98(1):3.
Source: Iqbal MU, Ahmad N, Khan ZSU, et al. Prevalence of musculoskeletal disorders among chefs working in restaurants of twins cities of Pakistan. Work. 2023;74(4):1507–1513.
Source: Abebaw T, Destaw B, Yenealem DG, et al. Work-related musculoskeletal disorders: prevalence, associated factors, and impact on quality of life among kitchen workers in hospitality industry, Bahir Dar City, Northwest Ethiopia, 2023. Frontiers in Public Health. 2024;12:1358867.

### Is kitchen foot pain plantar fasciitis?

Often it is general tiredness and ache that eases with a night’s rest. But kitchen work carries the two biggest risk factors found in a case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without: standing for most of the working day raised the odds 3.6 times, and a [tight calf](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/) that limits how far the ankle bends raised them 23.3 times.

Plantar fasciitis has a typical pattern: sharp pain under the heel on the first steps in the morning or after sitting, which eases as you walk and comes back after a long day. That pattern is covered in [heel pain in the morning](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-in-the-morning/), and the full exercise guide is [plantar fasciitis exercises and stretches](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).

Other patterns point elsewhere:

- burning under the ball of the foot by mid-service: see [ball of foot pain](https://walkito.site/ball-of-foot-pain/)
- a deep, bruised ache in the middle of the heel that gets worse the longer you stand on a hard floor: see [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/)
- arches that ache or feel flat by the end of a shift: see [arch pain](https://walkito.site/arch-pain/)

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### Clogs or slip-resistant shoes: what does the evidence say?

**The strongest kitchen footwear evidence is about slips, not sore feet.** A US study followed 475 workers from 36 fast-food restaurants for three months. Workers whose shoes had a slip-resistant marking on the sole reported a 54% lower rate of slipping than workers without them, after allowing for age, sex, body weight and other factors (Verma and colleagues, 2011).

A randomized trial then tested it as a program. School districts were randomly chosen to give their food service workers slip-resistant shoes at no cost. Slipping injury claims fell from 3.54 to 1.18 per 10,000 worker-months in those districts, and rose from 2.01 to 2.30 in the others (Bell and colleagues, 2019).

Shoes wear out. In the same restaurant workers, those who already wore slip-resistant shoes and changed to a new pair had a 55% lower rate of slipping afterwards, and shoes worn for under six months did moderately better than older ones (Verma and colleagues, 2014). The study could not say exactly when to replace them.

**No study we found compares clogs with sneakers, or any kitchen shoe with another, for foot pain.** For heel pain in general, the 2023 guideline grades [insoles](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) on their own **B against**: the evidence says not to rely on them alone. A sensible order: pick a shoe with a slip-resistant sole that fits your foot now and does not pinch the toes, replace it when the tread is worn, and do the stretching and strength work below for the pain itself.

Source: Verma SK, Chang WR, Courtney TK, et al. A prospective study of floor surface, shoes, floor cleaning and slipping in US limited-service restaurant workers. Occupational and Environmental Medicine. 2011;68(4):279–285.
Source: Bell JL, Collins JW, Chiou S. Effectiveness of a no-cost-to-workers, slip-resistant footwear program for reducing slipping-related injuries in food service workers: a cluster randomized trial. Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health. 2019;45(2):194–202.
Source: Verma SK, Zhao Z, Courtney TK, et al. Duration of slip-resistant shoe usage and the rate of slipping in limited-service restaurants: results from a prospective and crossover study. Ergonomics. 2014;57(12):1919–1926.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Where in the kitchen do most slips happen?

In the US restaurant study, most slips happened by the **sink and the fryer**, the areas workers also rated most slippery, and liquid or grease was on the floor in over 70% of slips (Verma and colleagues, 2010).

A second analysis of the same workers looked at the moment of each slip. The rate of slipping was 14.6 times higher while walking on a contaminated floor, 2.9 times higher while rushing and 1.7 times higher while distracted. Slip-resistant shoes reduced the effect of rushing and of a dirty floor (Verma and colleagues, 2011).

Whether the employer provides the shoes matters too. Where the employer provided slip-resistant shoes, 91% of workers wore them. Where they were neither provided nor encouraged, 53.5% did (Verma and colleagues, 2010). If your kitchen has a shoe program, it is worth using.

Source: Verma SK, Chang WR, Courtney TK, et al. Workers' experience of slipping in U.S. limited-service restaurants. Journal of Occupational and Environmental Hygiene. 2010;7(9):491–500.
Source: Verma SK, Lombardi DA, Chang WR, et al. Rushing, distraction, walking on contaminated floors and risk of slipping in limited-service restaurants: a case-crossover study. Occupational and Environmental Medicine. 2011;68(8):575–581.

### Do anti-fatigue mats and compression socks help in a kitchen?

A 2015 review of research on standing at work lists floor mats, compression stockings and supportive footwear among the options with some evidence for less discomfort and fatigue (Waters and Dick, 2015). None of that research was done in kitchens. A mat at a station where you stand for long periods, like the pass or a prep table, is a reasonable thing to try. Choose one that lies flat and stays put on a wet floor, so it does not become a trip hazard of its own.

Compression stockings have not been tested in kitchens. In a small randomized trial of 40 security guards standing roughly 12-hour shifts, both 15 to 20 mmHg and 20 to 30 mmHg stockings avoided the rise in leg discomfort and swelling seen with regular socks (Garcia and colleagues, 2023). The guards were all men and none were cooks, so read this as a likely fit, not proof for kitchens.

**Mats and socks help with comfort during a shift. They do not replace the stretching and strength work** that the heel pain guideline grades highest.

Source: Waters TR, Dick RB. Evidence of health risks associated with prolonged standing at work and intervention effectiveness. Rehabilitation Nursing. 2015;40(3):148–165.
Source: Garcia MG, Roman MG, Davila A, Martin BJ. Comparison of physiological effects induced by two compression stockings and regular socks during prolonged standing work. Human Factors. 2023;65(4):562–574.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Which exercises help chefs with foot pain?

The exercises are the ones from the [plantar fasciitis guide](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/), at the same starting doses. The stretches need only a wall or a chair, so they fit in a break, before service or after you change out of your work shoes. Keep the strength work for days off or after a shift.

The guideline grades are for plantar fasciitis and were not tested in kitchen workers, but the tissues are the same ones a kitchen shift loads all day. If an exercise takes your pain to 6 out of 10 or higher, stop for the day.

- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall or a steel counter. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. Do it on a dry patch of floor, not by the sink.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, with almost no load on the heel, so it suits a break on an upturned crate or a staff-room chair.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Hold a wall or rail. Do these at home or after a shift, not on a wet kitchen floor.
- **Foot roll** (1 minute): Sit and roll the sole of your foot slowly over a massage ball, with firm pressure. If you are wincing, ease off.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### How do you fit exercises into a kitchen shift?

A split shift or a double leaves little room for a routine, so tie the exercises to something you already do:

- **If you have 3 minutes:** the calf stretch and the soleus stretch, 30 seconds each side, before service or when you change shoes. That covers the tight calf, the strongest risk factor in the case-control study.
- **If you have 5 minutes:** add the plantar fascia stretch. Stretching is the part the 2023 guideline grades **A**.
- **If you have 10 minutes:** on a day off or after a shift, add the heel raises and a minute of foot rolling. Strength work is graded **B**.

Breaks themselves seem to matter. In 1,909 Korean kitchen workers, women who reported insufficient rest breaks had 1.68 times the odds of musculoskeletal problems (Park and colleagues, 2021). The link was reported for women, and a survey like this cannot show cause and effect. Even so, sitting down for a few minutes between rushes is worth defending.

For plantar fasciitis in general, about 90% of people get better with non-surgical care, though it can take months; see [how long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/). The 2023 guideline also suggests adjusting the load on your feet at work, advice graded **E** because it rests on theory, not trials.

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Park S, Lee J, Lee JH. Insufficient rest breaks at workplace and musculoskeletal disorders among Korean kitchen workers. Safety and Health at Work. 2021;12(2):225–229.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain started after a slip, a fall, a twist or something heavy landing on your foot
- you cannot put weight on the foot, or you are limping
- the foot is numb, tingling or burning, or swollen, red or warm
- you have a burn, cut or blister on the foot that is not getting better, especially with diabetes or reduced feeling in your feet
- one calf or leg is suddenly painful and swollen
- pain wakes you at night or is there at rest
- pain is in one pinpoint spot and gets worse with activity, which can be a stress fracture pattern
- the pain has not eased after several weeks of better shoes, more breaks and the exercises on this page

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app on iPhone and Android. It does not know your rota, so you choose when the sessions go: before service, between shifts or on your days off.

#### Why do my feet hurt so much after working in a kitchen?

Kitchen shifts combine hours of standing, short fast walks and hard floors. In a survey of 128 kitchen workers, 46.1% reported foot pain in the past year. Standing for most of the working day also raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 3.6 times in a case-control study. Daily calf and plantar fascia stretches target the tissues under the most strain.

#### Are clogs good for chefs with foot pain?

Nobody knows for sure: no study we found compares clogs with sneakers or other kitchen shoes for foot pain. What matters most for safety is a slip-resistant sole. For heel pain, the 2023 guideline grades insoles on their own B against, so pair whichever shoe fits you best with calf and plantar fascia stretches, which it grades A.

#### Do slip-resistant shoes actually work in restaurants?

For slips, yes. In 475 workers from 36 US fast-food restaurants, slip-resistant shoes were linked to a 54% lower rate of slipping. In a randomized trial in school food service, free slip-resistant shoes lowered slipping injury claims from 3.54 to 1.18 per 10,000 worker-months. These studies measured slips, not foot pain.

#### How often should kitchen shoes be replaced?

There is no tested rule. In a study of 475 restaurant workers, slip-resistant shoes worn under six months were moderately more effective against slips than older ones, and slip-resistant shoe wearers who switched to a new pair slipped 55% less often. Check the tread, and replace shoes once the pattern on the sole is worn smooth.

#### Do anti-fatigue mats help kitchen workers?

Probably, for comfort. A 2015 review of standing at work lists floor mats among the options with some evidence for less discomfort and fatigue, but none of that research was done in kitchens. Use a mat where you stand still for long periods, and choose one that lies flat and does not slide on a wet floor.

#### Do compression socks help chefs on long shifts?

They may. In a trial of 40 security guards standing roughly 12-hour shifts, both 15 to 20 mmHg and 20 to 30 mmHg stockings avoided the rise in leg discomfort and swelling seen with regular socks. The trial was small and not in kitchens, and stockings do not replace stretching or strength work.

#### Can you get plantar fasciitis from working as a chef?

Kitchen work carries known risk factors. In a case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, standing for most of the working day raised the odds 3.6 times and a tight calf raised them 23.3 times. No study has measured plantar fasciitis in chefs specifically.

#### What can I do for sore feet during a busy service?

Shift your weight, sit down in breaks when you can, and do a 30-second calf stretch against a wall on a dry patch of floor. In Korean kitchen workers, women with insufficient rest breaks had 1.68 times the odds of musculoskeletal problems. Keep heel raises and longer sessions for after the shift or days off.

## Hairdresser foot pain: what helps when you stand in one spot all day

Language: English · https://walkito.site/hairdressers-foot-pain/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

Hairdresser foot pain mostly comes from standing still at the chair for hours, not from walking, so the options with some evidence target static standing: a cushioned floor or shoe, low-strength compression stockings, and a minute of calf work between clients. In a study of 384 hairdressers and 384 people in other jobs, 49.5% of hairdressers reported knee or foot pain, against 38.3% of the comparison group (Mishra and Sarkar, 2021).

- Of 384 hairdressers in India, 49.5% reported knee or foot pain in the past 12 months, against 38.3% of 384 people in other jobs. The study counted knee and foot together (Mishra and Sarkar, 2021).
- A 2019 scoping review of 44 studies found only 5 that reported foot pain in hairdressers, ranging from 10% to 44%. Most studies looked at the back, neck, shoulders and hands, and standing was one of the common risk factors (Kozak and colleagues, 2019).
- In a randomized crossover trial of 108 hairdressers, 15 to 20 mmHg compression stockings lowered leg pain and swelling scores by 12% and lower leg volume by 19 mL on average (Blazek and colleagues, 2013).
- A 2018 review of 10 studies found moderate evidence that softer floors and cushioned insoles reduce discomfort and fatigue in people who stand at work (Speed and colleagues, 2018).
- A tight calf was the strongest risk factor for plantar fasciitis in a 2003 case-control study, at 23.3 times the odds, and standing most of the working day raised the odds 3.6 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).

### How common is foot pain in hairdressers?

**Foot and leg pain is common in hairdressers, but it is far less studied than shoulder or back pain.** A 2019 scoping review gathered 44 studies on musculoskeletal problems in hairdressing. Only 5 of them reported foot pain, and the figures ranged from 10% to 44%. The spread is wide because the studies used different questions, countries and time frames.

The largest study with a comparison group surveyed 384 hairdressers and 384 people in other jobs in two Indian cities. Knee or foot pain was the most common complaint in both groups: 49.5% of hairdressers against 38.3% of the others. The study counted knee and foot as one category, so it cannot say how much of that was the feet alone.

A UK study of 147 hairdressers and 67 people in other jobs found work-related leg or foot pain far more often in the hairdressers. The odds were 31 times higher, but the statistical range was very wide, from about 4 to 267 times, so the real size of the gap is uncertain. In a 2023 Turkish study, after the lower back, the most painful areas were the lower legs: 36.9% on the right and 32.5% on the left.

Source: Kozak A, Wirth T, Verhamme M, Nienhaus A. Musculoskeletal health, work-related risk factors and preventive measures in hairdressing: a scoping review. Journal of Occupational Medicine and Toxicology. 2019;14:24.
Source: Mishra S, Sarkar K. Work-related musculoskeletal disorders and associated risk factors among urban metropolitan hairdressers in India. Journal of Occupational Health. 2021;63(1):e12200.
Source: Bradshaw L, Harris-Roberts J, Bowen J, Rahman S, Fishwick D. Self-reported work-related symptoms in hairdressers. Occupational Medicine (London). 2011;61(5):328-334.
Source: İnce Parpucu T, Ercan S, Başkurt Z, Başkurt F. The impact of lower extremity fatigue on lower quadrant dysfunction and health profile in hairdressers. La Medicina del Lavoro. 2023;114(3):e2023019.

### Why does standing in one spot hurt more than walking?

A hairdresser’s day is different from a nurse’s. You do not cover long distances. You stand at the chair, shift a little, lean in, and stand again. When you stand still:

- The calf muscles hold one position, so they stop pumping blood back up the leg.
- Blood and fluid pool in the lower legs and feet, which is why shoes feel tighter by evening.
- The heel pad and the plantar fascia, the band under the arch, carry a steady load with no break.

Lab studies show how fast this builds. A 2017 review of 25 laboratory studies found low-back symptoms became clinically relevant after about 71 minutes of standing on average, and after 42 minutes in people prone to standing pain. A single colour or cut can take longer than that. A 2015 review of standing at work linked prolonged standing to low back and leg pain, discomfort and fatigue across many jobs.

In a 2023 study of Turkish hairdressers, those who reported lower-leg fatigue also had more pain in the knees and lower legs and worse scores for energy and mobility. **The swelling side is measurable too:** in 38 hairdressers, ankle size grew from 21.1 cm in the morning to 22.1 cm by the end of a day without compression.

Source: Coenen P, Parry S, Willenberg L, et al. Associations of prolonged standing with musculoskeletal symptoms: a systematic review of laboratory studies. Gait & Posture. 2017;58:310–318.
Source: Waters TR, Dick RB. Evidence of health risks associated with prolonged standing at work and intervention effectiveness. Rehabilitation Nursing. 2015;40(3):148–165.
Source: İnce Parpucu T, Ercan S, Başkurt Z, Başkurt F. The impact of lower extremity fatigue on lower quadrant dysfunction and health profile in hairdressers. La Medicina del Lavoro. 2023;114(3):e2023019.
Source: Agle CG, de Sá CKC, Amorim DS, Figueiredo MAM. Evaluation of the effectiveness of wearing compression stockings for prevention of occupational edema in hairdressers. Jornal Vascular Brasileiro. 2020;19:e20190028.

### Does posture at the chair affect your feet?

Studies of hairdressers’ posture focus on the back and arms, not the feet. A scoping review reported that hairdressers often bend forward or twist while cutting and washing, and that cutting kept the spine bent forward for 66% of the task time in one measurement study. Leaning in for a long time tends to shift your weight toward the front of the foot.

No study has measured how salon posture changes the load on hairdressers’ feet. What you can control is simple: raise or lower the client’s chair so you are not leaning, keep your weight on both feet, and shift your stance every few minutes. In a lab study of four hours of standing, people who shifted their weight more also reported more discomfort, so frequent shifting can be a sign that discomfort is building, and a reasonable cue for a short break (Wiggermann and Keyserling, 2013).

If your feet hurt with your back, the connection runs both ways. [Flat feet and back pain](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-back-pain/) covers what the research says.

Source: Kozak A, Wirth T, Verhamme M, Nienhaus A. Musculoskeletal health, work-related risk factors and preventive measures in hairdressing: a scoping review. Journal of Occupational Medicine and Toxicology. 2019;14:24.
Source: Wiggermann N, Keyserling WM. Effects of anti-fatigue mats on perceived discomfort and weight-shifting during prolonged standing. Human Factors. 2013;55(4):764–775.

### What are the best shoes for hairdressers?

**No study has compared shoe types for hairdressers.** The shoe advice online comes from shoe brands or clinics, not from trials in salons. What the wider standing research supports is cushioning: a 2018 review of 10 studies found moderate evidence that cushioned insoles and softer floors reduce discomfort and fatigue in people who stand at work, and limited evidence that insoles do more than mats.

In practice, look for:

- A cushioned sole and some arch support, so the heel and arch do not take the full load of a hard floor.
- A closed toe that does not squeeze the toes. Pain between the toes can be [Morton’s neuroma](https://walkito.site/mortons-neuroma/).
- A low, stable heel. High heels put more of your weight on the front of the foot.
- A grippy sole. Salon floors get wet and slippery.

Some people change shoes halfway through a long day. No study has tested this, but a different shoe spreads the load differently. If you already have heel or arch pain, insoles can make the day more comfortable, but they work on comfort, not on the calf and arch themselves. [Insoles vs exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) compares the two.

Source: Speed G, Harris K, Keegel T. The effect of cushioning materials on musculoskeletal discomfort and fatigue during prolonged standing at work: a systematic review. Applied Ergonomics. 2018;70:300–314.

### Do anti-fatigue mats help hairdressers?

A mat at your chair is one of the simplest changes with evidence behind it. In a lab study, people stood for four hours on four different anti-fatigue mats and on a hard floor. Three of the four mats lowered discomfort compared with the hard floor, but the mats did not differ much from each other.

The evidence is not all positive. In a small 1994 study of 5 people, mats reduced muscle fatigue in the lower back only, and only with the softer of two mats. The leg muscles showed no change. **So a mat helps with comfort, but it does not replace moving and stretching.**

At the salon, put the mat where you actually stand, behind the chair, and keep it flat so you do not trip on the edges. Hair and water on a mat can make it slippery, so sweep it often.

Source: Speed G, Harris K, Keegel T. The effect of cushioning materials on musculoskeletal discomfort and fatigue during prolonged standing at work: a systematic review. Applied Ergonomics. 2018;70:300–314.
Source: Wiggermann N, Keyserling WM. Effects of anti-fatigue mats on perceived discomfort and weight-shifting during prolonged standing. Human Factors. 2013;55(4):764–775.
Source: Kim JY, Stuart-Buttle C, Marras WS. The effects of mats on back and leg fatigue. Applied Ergonomics. 1994;25(1):29-34.

### Should hairdressers use a stool or a sit-stand seat?

**No study has tested whether a stool reduces foot pain in hairdressers.** Sitting takes load off the feet, and in office studies, alternating between sitting and standing reduced low-back discomfort with no loss of work output (Karakolis and Callaghan, 2014). That is the best indirect evidence for mixing in some sitting.

A stool has a trade-off. A German posture study, summarised in the 2019 scoping review, found hairdressers who used a rolling stool bent their lower back more steeply and raised their hands above shoulder height more often. A stool that is too low can swap foot pain for back and shoulder strain.

A practical approach: use a stool for tasks where you can reach without stretching, like detail work at the back of the head or foils at the lower sections, and stand for the rest. Set the stool high enough that your arms stay below shoulder level. If you work at a basin, sit when the setup allows it.

Source: Karakolis T, Callaghan JP. The impact of sit-stand office workstations on worker discomfort and productivity: a review. Applied Ergonomics. 2014;45(3):799–806.
Source: Kozak A, Wirth T, Verhamme M, Nienhaus A. Musculoskeletal health, work-related risk factors and preventive measures in hairdressing: a scoping review. Journal of Occupational Medicine and Toxicology. 2019;14:24.

### What exercises can you do between clients?

The exercises are the same ones used for [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) and general standing pain: calf stretches, heel raises and a plantar fascia stretch. What is different for hairdressers is the timing. **You get short gaps between clients, so pick one or two exercises per gap instead of a full routine.** No study has tested exercise breaks for hairdressers’ feet, so the doses here come from the main heel pain guide.

The calf matters most. In a case-control study, a tight calf raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 23.3 times, more than any other factor. If any exercise brings your pain to 6 out of 10 or higher, stop for the day.

- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall or the back of your station. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. Two holds on each leg take about two minutes, so it fits one gap between clients.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Same position, back heel flat, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, is the one that holds you upright when you stand still, and it only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Hold the station for balance. Besides building strength, this makes the calf pump blood back up the leg, which still standing does not.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit on your stool with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, with almost no load on the heel. A good option when your heels are already sore.
- **Ankle rocks** (2 sets of 15, each leg): Split stance, hands on a wall. Rock the front knee forward over the toes while the heel stays flat. Go slowly, about two seconds each way. It moves the ankle after a long stretch of standing still.
- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit and cross one foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back gently until you feel a stretch along the arch. Do it on a break when you can sit, and before your first steps in the morning if your heel hurts most then.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.

### Do compression stockings help hairdressers?

**Compression stockings are one of the few things tested in hairdressers themselves.** In a Swiss randomized crossover trial, 108 hairdressers wore low-strength stockings (15 to 20 mmHg) for one period and no stockings for another. With stockings, the score for leg pain and feeling of swelling fell by 12% on average, and lower leg volume fell by 19 mL. Sleep and mood scores improved too.

A smaller Brazilian study of 38 hairdressers measured the ankle. Without stockings it grew from 21.1 cm in the morning to 22.1 cm by the end of the day. With stockings it was 21.2 cm at the end of the day, about the same as in the morning.

The effects were modest, and the studies measured leg swelling and leg symptoms, not foot conditions like plantar fasciitis. A 2023 trial in security guards found similar results for long standing shifts. **Stockings help with swelling and heavy legs, while the calf and arch still need their own exercise.** If you have diabetes, poor circulation or numb feet, ask a clinician before using compression.

Source: Blazek C, Amsler F, Blaettler W, Keo HH, Baumgartner I, Willenberg T. Compression hosiery for occupational leg symptoms and leg volume: a randomized crossover trial in a cohort of hairdressers. Phlebology. 2013;28(5):239-247.
Source: Agle CG, de Sá CKC, Amorim DS, Figueiredo MAM. Evaluation of the effectiveness of wearing compression stockings for prevention of occupational edema in hairdressers. Jornal Vascular Brasileiro. 2020;19:e20190028.
Source: Garcia MG, Roman MG, Davila A, Martin BJ. Comparison of physiological effects induced by two compression stockings and regular socks during prolonged standing work. Human Factors. 2023;65(4):562–574.

### Could it be plantar fasciitis, varicose veins or something else?

General ache and heavy legs at the end of a salon day are common and usually ease overnight. Some patterns point to something more specific:

- Sharp heel pain on the first steps in the morning or after sitting points to [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/). The full routine is in [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).
- Burning or pain under the ball of the foot fits [ball of foot pain](https://walkito.site/ball-of-foot-pain/), common with thin soles or heels.
- An arch that aches or looks lower by evening fits [arch pain](https://walkito.site/arch-pain/).
- Swollen, twisted or bulging veins on the legs may be varicose veins. In a survey of 182 hairdressers in Taiwan, 24.2% had them, and in those over 45, long monthly standing hours were a risk factor (Chen and Guo, 2014).

If you are not sure what the pain is, the [foot pain identifier](https://walkito.site/foot-pain-identifier/) can help you narrow it down, and a clinician can tell you for sure. **If pain changes, spreads or stops easing with rest, get it checked before loading it with exercise.**

Source: Chen CL, Guo HR. Varicose veins in hairdressers and associated risk factors: a cross-sectional study. BMC Public Health. 2014;14:885.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain started after a fall, a twist or something dropped on your foot
- you cannot put weight on the foot, or you are limping
- the foot is numb, tingling or burning
- one leg has swollen suddenly and is painful, red or warm
- the foot is red or hot, or you have a fever or feel unwell
- pain wakes you at night or is there even when you rest
- you have diabetes, poor circulation or reduced feeling in your feet
- the pain has not eased after several weeks of better shoes, a mat, breaks and the exercises on this page

### Doing it as a plan

You do not have to work out the order, the doses or when to move to a harder version. [Walkito](https://walkito.site/program/) is a heel and foot exercise app that builds your plan one week at a time, and sessions are short enough to fit before work or on a break.

#### Why do hairdressers’ feet hurt so much?

Hairdressers stand in one spot for long periods, which loads the heel and arch without the calf pumping that walking provides. In a study of 384 hairdressers, 49.5% reported knee or foot pain over 12 months, against 38.3% of people in other jobs. Leaning forward, hard floors and unsupportive shoes add to the load.

#### What are the best shoes for hairdressers with foot pain?

No study has compared shoe types for hairdressers, so there is no proven best shoe. Look for a cushioned sole, some arch support, a low heel, room for the toes and a grippy sole. A 2018 review of 10 studies found moderate evidence that cushioned insoles and softer floors reduce discomfort in standing workers.

#### Do anti-fatigue mats work for hairdressers?

They help with comfort. In a lab study of four hours of standing, three of four anti-fatigue mats lowered discomfort compared with a hard floor. A small older study found mats reduced back muscle fatigue but not leg fatigue. A mat is worth having at your chair, but it does not replace stretching and moving between clients.

#### Should hairdressers wear compression socks?

Low-strength compression is one of the few options tested in hairdressers. In a crossover trial of 108 hairdressers, 15 to 20 mmHg stockings lowered leg pain and swelling scores by 12% and lower leg volume by 19 mL. The effect was modest. Ask a clinician first if you have diabetes or poor circulation.

#### Is it better for hairdressers to sit on a stool?

Sitting for part of the day takes load off the feet, but no study has tested stools for hairdressers’ foot pain. One posture study found stool users bent their lower back more and raised their hands above the shoulder more often. Use a stool set high enough to keep your arms low, and stand for the rest.

#### What stretches can hairdressers do between clients?

The calf stretch and soleus stretch, 2 holds of 30 seconds on each leg, fit into one gap between clients. Heel raises, 3 sets of 10, get the calf pumping again after standing still. The 2023 heel pain guideline grades calf and plantar fascia stretching A, its top grade, for plantar fasciitis.

#### Can hairdressing cause plantar fasciitis?

Standing for most of the working day raised the odds of plantar fasciitis 3.6 times in a case-control study of 50 cases and 100 controls, and a tight calf raised them 23.3 times. No study has measured plantar fasciitis in hairdressers specifically, but salon work involves exactly that kind of long standing.

#### How long can a hairdresser stand before taking a break?

There is no tested limit for hairdressers. In a review of lab studies, low-back symptoms became clinically relevant after about 71 minutes of standing on average and after 42 minutes in people prone to standing pain. Breaking long services with a short stretch, a few heel raises or a minute on a stool is a reasonable approach.

## Weight and plantar fasciitis: what the research shows, and what helps now

Language: English · https://walkito.site/weight-and-plantar-fasciitis/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

A higher body weight is one of the clearest risk factors for [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) in people who are not athletes. In a review of 51 studies, a body mass index (BMI) over 27 came with 3.7 times the odds of plantar fasciitis (van Leeuwen and colleagues, 2016). Whether losing weight eases heel pain is less clear: no randomized trial has tested it in people with heel pain, so the stretches and strength work the 2023 guideline grades highest are the place to start, at any weight.

- In a case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, a BMI over 30 came with 5.6 times the odds of plantar fasciitis, compared with a BMI of 25 or under. A stiff ankle was the strongest factor, at 23.3 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).
- A review of 51 studies found that a BMI over 27 was the only clinical factor, among those that could be pooled, clearly linked to plantar fasciitis, with 3.7 times the odds, and the link was strongest in people who are not athletes (van Leeuwen and colleagues, 2016).
- No randomized trial has tested weight loss for heel pain. A 2012 review found only two studies of weight loss and foot pain, both after weight loss surgery, and called the evidence limited (Butterworth and colleagues, 2012).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching **A** and strength work **B**. Advice on keeping a healthy lean body mass is graded **E**, meaning it rests on theory, not trials (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- In a follow-up of 174 people, BMI did not predict who still had heel pain years later. Being a woman and having pain in both heels did (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).

### Does weight affect plantar fasciitis?

**Yes, for people who are not athletes, a higher BMI is linked to plantar fasciitis in study after study.** BMI is weight divided by height squared. It is a rough measure, but it is the one these studies used.

The best known study compared 50 people with plantar fasciitis in one heel with 100 people of the same age and sex without it. A BMI over 30 came with 5.6 times the odds of plantar fasciitis, compared with a BMI of 25 or under (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).

A 2016 review pooled 51 studies. Of all the clinical factors the authors could combine, a BMI over 27 was the only one clearly linked to plantar fasciitis, with 3.7 times the odds, and the link was strongest in people who are not athletes (van Leeuwen and colleagues, 2016). Two earlier reviews reached the same conclusion, and both found no link between BMI and heel pain in athletes (Irving and colleagues, 2006; Butterworth and colleagues, 2012).

The 2023 heel pain guideline lists high BMI in people who are not athletes as a risk factor, next to a stiff ankle, running and long hours on your feet, especially on hard surfaces (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: van Leeuwen KD, Rogers J, Winzenberg T, van Middelkoop M. Higher body mass index is associated with plantar fasciopathy/'plantar fasciitis': systematic review and meta-analysis of various clinical and imaging risk factors. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;50(16):972–981.
Source: Irving DB, Cook JL, Menz HB. Factors associated with chronic plantar heel pain: a systematic review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2006;9(1-2):11–22.
Source: Butterworth PA, Landorf KB, Smith SE, Menz HB. The association between body mass index and musculoskeletal foot disorders: a systematic review. Obesity Reviews. 2012;13(7):630–642.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Is weight the cause, or just one factor?

**One factor among several, and not the strongest.** In the 2003 case-control study, three factors each counted on their own:

- A stiff ankle (the foot barely bending up toward the shin): 23.3 times the odds.
- A BMI over 30: 5.6 times the odds.
- Spending most of the workday on your feet: 3.6 times the odds.

The authors called the stiff ankle the most important of the three (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). That matters, because ankle stiffness often comes from [tight calves](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/), and calf stretching is something you can start today.

Most of these studies are case-control or cross-sectional: they compare people who already have heel pain with people who do not. They show a link, not proof that weight causes plantar fasciitis (van Leeuwen and colleagues, 2016). If you also stand for work, [feet that hurt from standing all day](https://walkito.site/feet-hurt-standing-all-day/) covers that side of the load.

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: van Leeuwen KD, Rogers J, Winzenberg T, van Middelkoop M. Higher body mass index is associated with plantar fasciopathy/'plantar fasciitis': systematic review and meta-analysis of various clinical and imaging risk factors. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;50(16):972–981.

### Why does load matter for the heel?

**The plantar fascia is the band under your foot that holds up the arch, and it takes load with every step.** More body weight means more load per step, so the same walk or the same shift asks more of the tissue. The guideline’s advice for heel pain is built around this idea: adjust the load on your feet at work, in leisure and in daily life. It grades that advice **E**, because it rests on theory, not trials (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

Weight loss does lower pressure under the foot. In a trial of 41 adults with an average BMI near 36, the group on a meal plan lost 5.9 kg in three months against 1.9 kg in the comparison group, and had lower peak pressure under parts of the foot. Foot shape and walking pattern did not change (Song and colleagues, 2015). That trial did not measure heel pain.

Pressure is not the whole story either. In a study of people with foot pain waiting for weight loss surgery, pain fell after surgery, but the drop in foot pressure was not linked to the drop in pain. Mood was: people with more depressive symptoms reported more foot pain, before and after (Walsh and colleagues, 2018). Pain is shaped by more than mechanics, which is one more reason not to blame yourself for it.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Song J, Kane R, Tango DN, Veur SS, Furmato J, Komaroff E, et al. Effects of weight loss on foot structure and function in obese adults: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Gait & Posture. 2015;41(1):86–92.
Source: Walsh TP, Gill TK, Evans AM, Yaxley A, Chisholm JA, Kow L, et al. Changes in foot pain, structure and function following bariatric surgery. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2018;11:35.

### Does losing weight help plantar fasciitis?

**It may, but no randomized trial has tested it in people with heel pain.** That is the honest answer. Everything we have comes from studies without a fair comparison group, mostly after weight loss surgery. Here is what exists:

Source: Butterworth PA, Landorf KB, Smith SE, Menz HB. The association between body mass index and musculoskeletal foot disorders: a systematic review. Obesity Reviews. 2012;13(7):630–642.
Source: Boules M, Batayyah E, Froylich D, Zelisko A, O'Rourke C, Brethauer S, et al. Effect of surgical weight loss on plantar fasciitis and health-care use. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2018;108(6):442–448.
Source: Walsh TP, Gill TK, Evans AM, Yaxley A, Chisholm JA, Kow L, et al. Changes in foot pain, structure and function following bariatric surgery. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2018;11:35.
Source: Song J, Kane R, Tango DN, Veur SS, Furmato J, Komaroff E, et al. Effects of weight loss on foot structure and function in obese adults: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Gait & Posture. 2015;41(1):86–92.
Source: Yang F, Zhou L, Zhang J, Wang Q, Cai Q, Wang J, et al. Association of semaglutide use with outcomes in chronic plantar heel pain: a prospective observational cohort and a pilot interventional study. International Journal of Surgery. 2025;111(12):9333–9341.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Which exercises suit a higher body weight?

The exercises with the best grades in the 2023 guideline, stretching (**A**) and calf strength work (**B**), do not depend on your weight (Koc and colleagues, 2023). What changes is how you start. Seated and supported versions put less load through the heel and are easier on knees and balance, so they come first here.

These are the same starting doses as the main [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) guide. Do the first plantar fascia stretch sitting on the edge of the bed, before you stand: in a trial of 82 people, a plantar fascia stretch done before standing eased first-step morning pain more than calf stretching alone (DiGiovanni and colleagues, 2003). If any exercise takes your heel pain to 6 out of 10, stop for the day.

- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. If crossing the leg is hard, keep the foot on the floor, loop a towel around the ball of the foot and pull gently instead.
- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall or a kitchen counter. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. The wall takes some of your weight, so you can lean only as far as feels steady.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position at the wall, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, the deeper calf muscle, with almost no load on the heel. It is the first step of the calf work, whatever you weigh.
- **Heel raises on both feet, holding a counter** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand facing a counter or the back of a sturdy chair, hands resting on it. Rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Your hands can take some weight on a sore day and less as you get stronger. Both feet share the load.
- **Short foot, seated** (3 sets of 8, hold 5 seconds, each foot): Sit with your foot flat on the floor. Pull the ball of the foot toward the heel so the arch lifts, and hold. Keep the outside of the foot on the ground. Don’t curl the toes. Curling them is the most common way to get this exercise wrong.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### Which activities are easier on the heel?

**Activities where your feet do not take your full weight with every step.** The guideline advises changing the load on your feet rather than stopping activity (Koc and colleagues, 2023). No study has compared activities for people with heel pain and a higher weight, so these are practical options, not tested ones:

- **A stationary bike or recumbent bike.** You keep moving while a seat carries your weight.
- **Swimming or walking in water.** The water takes much of your weight off your feet.
- **Seated or upper body exercise.** Arm cycling, resistance bands or chair workouts keep you active on days the heel is sore.
- **Shorter walks, more often.** Several short walks can be easier on a sore heel than one long one.

A simple check works for any activity: if your first steps the next morning are clearly worse, that day was more than the heel could take, so do a little less next time. [Walking with plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/walking-with-plantar-fasciitis/) explains how to build walking back up step by step.

If you are starting to exercise to feel better or to lose weight, starting with low-impact activity lets you keep going while the heel settles. The guideline lists running and long hours on your feet, especially on hard surfaces, as risk factors for heel pain (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Do shoes and insoles matter more at a higher weight?

No study has tested shoes or insoles for heel pain in people with a higher weight specifically. For heel pain in general, the 2023 guideline grades insoles on their own **B against**: the evidence says not to rely on them alone. Combined with stretching and strength work, they get a **C** (Koc and colleagues, 2023). [Insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) compares the two.

The guideline does recommend footwear advice as part of managing load, and it lists weight-bearing work on hard surfaces with poor shock absorption as a risk factor (Koc and colleagues, 2023). One practical option, not tested in trials, is supportive, cushioned shoes on hard floors, including at home.

After a lot of weight loss, feet can change. In the surgery study, the authors suggested that losing fat under the midfoot may change how shoes and insoles fit, and that this is worth checking after a large weight loss (Walsh and colleagues, 2018).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Walsh TP, Gill TK, Evans AM, Yaxley A, Chisholm JA, Kow L, et al. Changes in foot pain, structure and function following bariatric surgery. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2018;11:35.

### Will plantar fasciitis go away if I don’t lose weight?

**For most people, yes, it eases with time and non-surgical care.** About 90% of people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care such as stretching and insoles, often within 3 to 6 months (Latt and colleagues, 2020).

In a long follow-up of 174 people, the researchers tested whether BMI, age, smoking, physical work and other factors predicted who still had heel pain years later. Only being a woman and having pain in both heels did. BMI did not (Hansen and colleagues, 2018). Why women are affected more around 50 is covered in [plantar fasciitis and menopause](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-menopause/).

So a higher weight may make plantar fasciitis more likely to start, but it does not mean you are stuck with it. The stretches and calf work above are the same ones that help people of any size. [How long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/) has the full timeline.

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.

### See a clinician first if

- you have diabetes and notice numbness, tingling, a wound, or changes in the skin or shape of your foot
- the pain started after a fall, a jump or a twist, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- the heel is swollen, red or warm, or you have a fever
- the pain is worse at night or at rest, or comes with burning or numbness
- it hurts when you squeeze the sides of the heel, or the pain keeps building with activity (possible stress fracture)
- one calf is painful and swollen (possible blood clot): get help the same day
- both heels hurt along with joint pain or stiffness elsewhere
- you are thinking about weight loss medicines or surgery: that is a conversation for your doctor

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app. It does not track your weight or give diet advice. It builds a plan from the stretches and calf strength work on this page and starts with seated and supported versions.

#### Can being overweight cause plantar fasciitis?

A higher weight is linked to plantar fasciitis, but no study proves it causes it. A BMI over 30 came with 5.6 times the odds in one study, and a review of 51 studies found 3.7 times the odds above a BMI of 27, with the link strongest in people who are not athletes. A stiff ankle was an even stronger factor.

#### Does losing weight help plantar fasciitis?

It may, but no randomized trial has tested it in people with heel pain. In a records study of 163 people with plantar fasciitis who had weight loss surgery, 90% had their heel symptoms resolve, but there was no comparison group, and most people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care anyway (Latt and colleagues, 2020). A 2012 review called the evidence limited.

#### How much weight do I need to lose to help plantar fasciitis?

No study has worked out an amount. There is no trial of weight loss for heel pain, so any number you read is a guess. If you want to lose weight for your health, talk to your doctor. For the heel itself, stretching and calf strength work have the strongest evidence, at any weight.

#### Is BMI a risk factor for plantar fasciitis in runners?

Mostly not. Two systematic reviews found that BMI was linked to chronic heel pain in people who are not athletes, but not in athletes. See [heel pain in runners](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/) for the factors that matter more in runners.

#### What exercise can I do with plantar fasciitis if I am overweight?

Seated and supported exercises are a good start: a plantar fascia stretch sitting down, calf stretches at a wall, and seated heel raises. For fitness, a stationary bike, swimming or walking in water keep you moving with less load on the heel. The 2023 guideline advises changing the load on your feet rather than stopping activity.

#### Do weight loss medicines help plantar fasciitis?

There is one observational study. People with long-standing heel pain who took semaglutide reported more improvement than those who did not, but they were not randomly assigned, and the authors call for a randomized trial. It is a decision for you and your doctor, not something to start for heel pain alone.

#### Why do my heels hurt more after I gain weight?

More body weight means more load on the plantar fascia with every step, and heel pain often starts after the load on your feet goes up. In a trial of 41 adults, losing weight lowered pressure under parts of the foot. Heel pain was not measured in that trial, so the link to pain is likely but not proven.

#### Will plantar fasciitis go away without weight loss?

For most people, yes. About 90% get better with non-surgical care such as stretching and insoles, often within 3 to 6 months. In a long follow-up of 174 people, BMI did not predict who still had heel pain years later. Being a woman and having pain in both heels did.

#### Are insoles more important if I am heavier?

No study has tested that. For heel pain in general, the 2023 guideline advises against relying on insoles alone (grade B against) and gives them a C when combined with stretching and strength work. Cushioned shoes on hard floors are a practical option, though trials have not tested them. See [insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/).

## Foot pain after hiking: why your feet hurt and what to do about it

Language: English · https://walkito.site/hiking-foot-pain/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

Sore feet after a long hike are common, and much of it is overload: more distance, more descent or a heavier pack than your feet are used to. In a survey of 1,295 long-distance hikers on the Appalachian Trail, 29% reported foot injury or pain, and 12% reported Achilles pain (Chrusch and Kavin, 2021). Heel pain on the first steps the next morning points to [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/); pain on one spot of a bone that grows with each hike can be a stress fracture and needs a clinician.

- Of 1,295 Appalachian Trail long-distance hikers, 61% reported a muscle, joint or bone complaint, 37% knee pain, 29% foot pain and 12% Achilles pain, and 11% stopped their hike because of it (Chrusch and Kavin, 2021).
- Hikers who did no training before the trail reported foot pain more often, 38% against 28%, and any such injury more often, 80% against 58%. That is a link in a survey, not proof that training prevents injury (Chrusch and Kavin, 2021).
- Foot blisters were the most common complaint among 280 Appalachian Trail hikers, reported by 64% (Boulware and colleagues, 2003).
- Numbness or tingling rose with pack weight in 128 long-distance hikers, from 35% with 10 to 20 pound packs to 69% above 31 pounds. Shoe type and pack weight were not linked to other muscle and joint injuries (Anderson and colleagues, 2009).
- Trekking poles reduced the load on the ankle, knee and hip when 15 experienced hikers walked downhill, with and without a pack (Bohne and Abendroth-Smith, 2007).

### Why do your feet hurt after a hike?

**Mostly because hiking loads the feet more, and for longer, than everyday walking.** You walk for hours, on uneven ground, up and down, often with a pack. Each of those adds work for the heel, the arch, the calf and the Achilles tendon.

The best numbers come from long-distance hikers. In a 2018 to 2019 survey of 1,295 Appalachian Trail hikers, 61% reported a muscle, joint or bone complaint. Knee pain was the most common at 37%, then foot pain at 29%, ankle sprains at 13%, Achilles pain at 12% and shin pain at 11%. These complaints made 11% of them stop their hike (Chrusch and Kavin, 2021).

Overuse problems, which build up over days of repeated load, were more common than sudden injuries: 28% against 18% in the same survey. That matters for day hikers too. A long first hike of the season, or a weekend with two big days in a row, is the same pattern on a smaller scale.

These are self-reported surveys of people walking hundreds of miles. No study has counted foot pain in ordinary day hikers, so the exact figures will not apply to a weekend walker. The pattern of what hurts is the useful part.

Source: Chrusch A, Kavin M. Survey of musculoskeletal injuries, prehike conditioning, and on-trail injury prevention strategies self-reported by long-distance hikers on the Appalachian Trail. Wilderness Environ Med. 2021;32(3):322–331.

### Where does it hurt, and what is it likely to be?

Where the pain sits is the quickest clue. The table is a starting point, not a diagnosis. The [foot pain identifier](https://walkito.site/foot-pain-identifier/) asks a few more questions.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Boulware DR, Forgey WW, Martin WJ 2nd. Medical risks of wilderness hiking. Am J Med. 2003;114(4):288–293.

### Why does downhill hiking hurt your feet more?

**Going down, your legs work as brakes.** Each step down, the calf, the front of the shin and the thigh muscles control the drop while they lengthen. The foot also slides forward in the shoe, so the toes and the ball of the foot take more pressure. That is why many people feel fine on the climb and sore after the descent.

In a lab study, 15 experienced male hikers walked downhill with no pack, a day pack of 15% of their body weight and an expedition pack of 30%. Using poles reduced the turning forces at the ankle, knee and hip and the peak braking work at the ankle and knee, with every pack (Bohne and Abendroth-Smith, 2007). In the Appalachian Trail survey, 70% carried poles or a stick, and poles went with fewer complaints (Chrusch and Kavin, 2021). That survey link does not prove that poles prevent injury.

Practical points, none of them tested as foot pain prevention: take shorter steps on steep descents, lace the shoe firmly over the instep so the foot does not slide forward, and keep toenails short.

Source: Bohne M, Abendroth-Smith J. Effects of hiking downhill using trekking poles while carrying external loads. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(1):177–183.
Source: Chrusch A, Kavin M. Survey of musculoskeletal injuries, prehike conditioning, and on-trail injury prevention strategies self-reported by long-distance hikers on the Appalachian Trail. Wilderness Environ Med. 2021;32(3):322–331.

### Does a heavier pack make foot pain worse?

**A heavier pack means more load on every step, but the studies on hikers only show a clear link with numbness and tingling.** In a 2006 survey of 128 hikers who had walked more than 500 miles on the Appalachian or Pacific Crest Trail, numbness or tingling went up with pack weight: 35% with packs of 10 to 20 pounds, 50% with 21 to 30 pounds and 69% above 31 pounds (Anderson and colleagues, 2009).

The same survey found that pack weight and shoe type were not linked to other muscle and joint injuries, such as sprains, long-lasting pain or muscle injuries. So nobody has shown that a lighter pack means less heel or arch pain. It is still a sensible place to start if your feet hurt only on the days you carry a full pack.

If your toes burn or tingle, loosen the laces over the top of the foot and check the hip belt and shoulder straps, and see a clinician if it does not go away after you take the pack off.

Source: Anderson LS Jr, Rebholz CM, White LF, Mitchell P, Curcio EP 3rd, Feldman JA, Kahn JH. The impact of footwear and packweight on injury and illness among long-distance hikers. Wilderness Environ Med. 2009;20(3):250–256.

### Boots or trail runners: which is better for foot pain?

**No trial has compared boots and trail runners for foot pain, so nobody can say one is better.** What exists are surveys:

- In the 2006 survey of 128 long-distance hikers, numbness or tingling was reported by 29% in sandals, 36% in running shoes, 42% in hiking shoes and 68% in boots. After allowing for pack weight, the shoe type no longer mattered, which suggests the hikers in boots also carried heavier packs (Anderson and colleagues, 2009).
- In the 2018 to 2019 Appalachian Trail survey, 58% wore running or trail shoes and 24% wore boots. Both went with fewer complaints than other footwear such as sandals (Chrusch and Kavin, 2021).

So pick the shoe that fits, that you have already walked in, and that suits the ground. For heel pain in general, the 2023 guideline recommends against insoles used alone for short-term relief, grade B, and allows them alongside other care, grade C (Koc and colleagues, 2023). More in [insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/). If you want to change to lighter or flatter shoes, do it over weeks, not on the first long hike; [barefoot shoes](https://walkito.site/barefoot-shoes/) explains why.

Source: Anderson LS Jr, Rebholz CM, White LF, Mitchell P, Curcio EP 3rd, Feldman JA, Kahn JH. The impact of footwear and packweight on injury and illness among long-distance hikers. Wilderness Environ Med. 2009;20(3):250–256.
Source: Chrusch A, Kavin M. Survey of musculoskeletal injuries, prehike conditioning, and on-trail injury prevention strategies self-reported by long-distance hikers on the Appalachian Trail. Wilderness Environ Med. 2021;32(3):322–331.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### How fast can you build up hiking distance?

**No study gives a safe weekly increase for hikers.** The closest evidence is the Appalachian Trail survey: the 13% of hikers who did no training before the trail reported more injuries overall (80% against 58%), more foot pain (38% against 28%), more Achilles pain (18% against 11%) and more lower leg stress fractures (5% against 2%). Strength training, stretching or yoga, and endurance training each went with fewer injuries (Chrusch and Kavin, 2021). It is a survey, so fitter or more careful people may simply have trained more.

A practical way to build up, not a tested one:

- Add one change at a time: more distance, more climb and descent, or a heavier pack, not all three on the same day.
- Use the next morning as your check. Pain that settles by the next morning and is not creeping up week to week is a reasonable sign the load is fine. That rule comes from an Achilles trial, not from hikers (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007).
- After a big day, plan an easy one. The [Appalachian Trail Conservancy](https://appalachiantrail.org/experience/hike-the-trail/essential-skills/health-hygiene/common-injuries/) gives similar advice to long-distance hikers: stop for the day if your feet start to hurt, swell or feel tight after you have hiked further than normal.

Calf strength is worth building between hikes, because the calf does much of the work on climbs and descents. The heel raises below are the same ones in the [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) guide.
