Source: Chrusch A, Kavin M. Survey of musculoskeletal injuries, prehike conditioning, and on-trail injury prevention strategies self-reported by long-distance hikers on the Appalachian Trail. Wilderness Environ Med. 2021;32(3):322–331.
Source: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(6):897–906.

### What is a good routine before and after a hike?

Keep it short. Before the hike, a minute or two to get the ankles moving. After, the stretches that target the heel and calf. On days between hikes, heel raises for strength. The doses are Walkito’s starting doses from the main guides. Stop an exercise for the day if pain goes above 6 out of 10.

Be honest about what stretching before a hike does. In a trial of 1,538 army recruits over three months of training, stretching six leg muscle groups before every session did not meaningfully reduce injuries (Pope and colleagues, 2000). The stretches here are for heel and calf pain, where the 2023 guideline grades stretching **A**, and strength work for the calf gets a **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

- **Ankle rocks (before)** (2 sets of 15, each leg): Split stance, hands on a wall, a tree or your poles. Rock the front knee forward over the toes, heel stays flat. Slow, about two seconds each way. Switch legs after each set.
- **Calf stretch (after)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Soleus stretch (after)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Plantar fascia stretch (after, and next morning)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. The next morning, do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Foot roll (after)** (1 minute, each foot): Sit and roll the sole of your foot slowly over a massage ball, with firm pressure. If you are wincing, ease off. No ball? Firm thumb strokes from heel to toes work too.
- **Heel raises on both feet (between hikes)** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. When it is easy, move to one leg or the [towel heel raise](https://walkito.site/exercises/towel-heel-raise/). For Achilles pain, slow lowering on a step is the main exercise: see [Achilles tendonitis exercises](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/).

Source: Pope RP, Herbert RD, Kirwan JD, Graham BJ. A randomized trial of preexercise stretching for prevention of lower-limb injury. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2000;32(2):271–277.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### When should you stop hiking and see a clinician?

**Stop and get checked if the pain sits on one spot of a bone and gets worse with each hike.** That is the classic stress fracture pattern, usually in the metatarsals behind the toes or in the heel bone. In a review of stress fractures, 81% of patients had pain with walking, and a sore spot on the bone was found in 65.9 to 100%. An X-ray at the first visit picked up only about 10% of them, so a normal X-ray does not rule one out (Patel and colleagues, 2011). If you are not sure which it is, stop hiking until a clinician has checked it.

Also stop if you cannot put weight on the foot, if pain started with a twist, a fall or a pop, or if the foot is red, hot and swollen. The full list is below.

Most heel pain is less dramatic. For plantar fasciitis, about 90% of people get better with non-surgical care, though it can take months (Latt and colleagues, 2020). See [how long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/).

Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.

### See a clinician first if

- pain sits on one spot of a bone and gets worse with each hike, which can be a stress fracture
- you cannot put weight on the foot, or you are limping
- pain started with a twist, a fall or a pop, especially at the back of the heel
- the foot or ankle is red, hot or swollen, or you have a fever
- a blister or toenail looks infected: spreading redness, pus or red streaks
- numbness, tingling or burning does not go away after you take off your pack and shoes
- the foot hurts at night or at rest
- pain keeps getting worse over two to three weeks despite shorter hikes

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app with the stretches and heel raises on this page. It does not plan your hikes, so keep your own route plan and fit the sessions around it, with lighter sessions after a big day.

#### Is it normal for your feet to hurt after hiking?

Some soreness after a long or steep hike is common and often settles within a day or two. In a survey of 1,295 Appalachian Trail hikers, 29% reported foot pain. Pain that is sharp, sits on one spot of a bone, or is still there after a few easy days is worth getting checked.

#### Why does my heel hurt after hiking?

The most common cause is plantar fasciitis, which hurts under the heel and is usually worst on the first steps the next morning. The 2023 guideline lists a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as a typical trigger, and a tight calf is the strongest known risk factor. Pain at the back of the heel points to the Achilles.

#### Can I keep hiking with plantar fasciitis?

Many people can, on shorter and flatter routes, if the pain stays moderate during the hike and settles by the next morning. That next-morning rule comes from an Achilles trial, not a hiking study. If the heel is worse each morning, cut distance and descent first. Our walking with plantar fasciitis guide explains how to build back up.

#### Are boots or trail runners better for foot pain?

Nobody knows for sure, because no trial has compared them. In surveys of long-distance hikers, both boots and trail shoes went with fewer complaints than sandals, and a link between boots and numbness disappeared once pack weight was taken into account. Pick the pair that fits and that you have already walked in.

#### Does a heavy backpack cause foot pain?

It adds load to every step, but the hiker surveys only show a clear link with numbness and tingling. In 128 long-distance hikers, that went from 35% with 10 to 20 pound packs to 69% above 31 pounds. Pack weight was not linked to other muscle and joint injuries in that survey.

#### Why do my feet hurt more going downhill?

On a descent your leg muscles work as brakes while they lengthen, and the foot slides forward in the shoe, loading the toes and the ball of the foot. In a lab study of 15 hikers walking downhill, trekking poles reduced the load at the ankle, knee and hip, with and without a pack.

#### Do trekking poles help foot pain?

They reduce load on the legs. In 15 experienced hikers walking downhill, poles reduced the forces at the ankle, knee and hip, and in a survey of Appalachian Trail hikers poles went with fewer complaints. No trial has tested whether poles prevent foot pain itself, so see them as a sensible extra, not a sure thing.

#### How long should feet hurt after a long hike?

Ordinary soreness from a big day often fades within a day or two of easy activity. If heel pain on the first steps keeps coming back every morning, or pain is still there after a week of shorter walks, it is more likely an overuse problem such as plantar fasciitis or Achilles pain, and worth a proper check.

#### Should I stretch before a hike?

A short warm-up such as ankle rocks is fine, but do not expect stretching before a hike to prevent injury. In a trial of 1,538 army recruits, stretching before training did not meaningfully reduce injuries. Calf and arch stretches after the hike are more useful if your heel hurts, where the 2023 guideline grades them A.

## Plantar fasciitis flare-up: what triggers it and what to do in the first 48 hours

Language: English · https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-flare-up/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

A [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) flare-up usually follows a jump in how much your heel has to carry: a long walk, a day standing on hard floors, or a new routine. The 2023 heel pain guideline lists pain after a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as a typical feature, and it recommends advice on adjusting load and does not advise stopping, advice it grades **E** because it rests on theory, not trials (Koc and colleagues, 2023). For the first 48 hours, cut back the load that set it off, keep your gentle stretches, and let the next morning tell you how it is going.

- The 2023 heel pain guideline lists heel pain after a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as a typical feature of plantar fasciitis, and recommends advice on changing load, at grade **E**, without advising complete rest (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- In a study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, a stiff ankle (23.3 times the odds), a BMI over 30 (5.6 times) and standing for most of the workday (3.6 times) were risk factors. That study looked at getting plantar fasciitis, not at flares (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).
- One pain-monitoring rule allows pain up to about 5 out of 10 during activity, as long as it settles by the next morning. It was tested in 38 people with Achilles pain, not plantar fasciitis (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007).
- The guideline makes no recommendation on ice or heat, so ice is a comfort tool at most, and no study shows it calms a flare (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- In a trial of 180 adults, advice to cut back on activities that cause flare-ups and then return slowly, plus a heel cup, came with clinically meaningful improvement at about three months (Riel and colleagues, 2023).

### What is a plantar fasciitis flare-up?

**A flare-up is a stretch of days when your usual heel pain is clearly worse than your normal.** First steps in the morning hurt more, the heel aches sooner on your feet, or pain that had faded comes back. There is no agreed medical definition, and we found no study that counts how often flares happen or how long they last.

The tissue under the heel does not like sudden changes in load. The 2023 guideline describes plantar fasciitis pain as most noticeable with the first steps after rest, and lists a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as a typical part of the history (Koc and colleagues, 2023). A flare is probably the same thing in miniature: the heel was asked to do more than it was ready for.

That is why a flare does not have to mean you are back at square one. About 90% of people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care, though it often takes months (Latt and colleagues, 2020). See [how long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/) for what the long follow-ups show.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.

### What triggers a plantar fasciitis flare-up?

**The common thread is a sudden change in load.** No study has tracked what sets off flares in people who already have plantar fasciitis. What exists is research on what makes people get it in the first place, and it points the same way:

- **A sudden jump in activity.** A holiday with long days of walking, a new running plan, a hike or a busy week at work. The guideline lists a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as typical (Koc and colleagues, 2023). If you run, [heel pain in runners](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/) covers mileage changes.
- **Long hours standing.** In a study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, standing for most of the workday came with 3.6 times the odds (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). In another, people with heel pain were as active as people without it but stood 3.4 hours a day longer (Landorf and colleagues, 2023). See [feet hurt from standing all day](https://walkito.site/feet-hurt-standing-all-day/).
- **Barefoot on hard floors.** The guideline lists weight-bearing work on poorly shock-absorbing surfaces as a risk factor (Koc and colleagues, 2023), though one study found people with heel pain were no more likely to stand on hard floors than people without (Landorf and colleagues, 2023). A 2021 best practice guide advises avoiding barefoot walking and flat, unsupportive shoes until symptoms are gone (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021).
- **New or different shoes.** We found no study that tested new shoes as a trigger. What is known: people with heel pain wore shoes with harder heels than people without it (Landorf and colleagues, 2023), and the best practice guide favours supportive shoes with the heel a little higher than the toes (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021). Switching to flat, thin or very flexible shoes, or to [barefoot shoes](https://walkito.site/barefoot-shoes/), is a change your heel will notice.
- **A tight calf.** In the same 2003 study, people with an ankle that bent up 0 degrees or less had 23.3 times the odds of people with more than 10 degrees (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). Skipping your stretches for a while can let that stiffness come back. See [tight calves](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/).

Body weight is a risk factor too: a BMI over 30 came with 5.6 times the odds in the 2003 study. Weight changes slowly, so it is more of a background factor than a trigger for a flare this week. More in [weight and plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/weight-and-plantar-fasciitis/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Landorf KB, Kaminski MR, Munteanu SE, Zammit GV, Menz HB. Activity and footwear characteristics in people with and without plantar heel pain: a matched cross-sectional observational study. Musculoskeletal Care. 2023;21(1):35–44.
Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.

### What should you do in the first 48 hours of a flare-up?

**Cut back the load, keep moving gently, and judge it by the next morning.** No trial has tested a 48-hour plan for plantar fasciitis. The steps below put the guideline and the closest tested advice into practice:

- **Find the trigger and reduce it.** Shorter walks, more sitting breaks, a pause from running or hills. The advice tested in a Danish trial was to cut back on activities that cause flare-ups, then slowly return to former activity levels guided by symptoms (Riel and colleagues, 2020).
- **Do not stop moving altogether.** The guideline recommends adjusting load and does not advise complete rest (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Walking you need for daily life is fine within the pain rule below.
- **Keep the gentle stretches.** Plantar fascia and calf stretches are graded **A** (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Do the first one before your foot touches the floor in the morning.
- **Wear shoes indoors.** Supportive shoes or firm slippers from the first step of the day, rather than bare feet on tile or wood (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021).
- **Break up standing.** The best practice guide advises breaking up long periods of standing still (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021).

In that trial, every one of the 180 adults got this kind of advice plus a heel cup, and two of the three groups also got heel raise training or heel raises plus a steroid injection. All three groups in the trial improved by a clinically meaningful amount at about three months, including the group that got only the advice and the heel cup (Riel and colleagues, 2023). The advice was the foundation, not an afterthought.

Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, Jensen MB, Ehlers LH, Rathleff MS. Corticosteroid injection plus exercise versus exercise, beyond advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy: protocol for a randomised clinical superiority trial (the FIX-Heel trial). Trials. 2020;21(1):5.
Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, et al. Does a corticosteroid injection plus exercise or exercise alone add to the effect of patient advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy? A randomised clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57(18):1180–1186.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.

### How much pain is OK during a flare-up?

**Use the same pain rule as for walking: moderate at most during activity, and back to your normal by the next morning.** The rule comes from a 2007 trial in 38 people with Achilles tendon pain. Pain up to about 5 out of 10 was allowed during activity, as long as it settled by the next morning and did not build from week to week. Staying active this way did not lead to worse results at twelve months than pausing running and jumping for six weeks (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007). It has not been tested in plantar fasciitis, so use it as a borrowed guide.

For heel pain, the 2021 best practice guide strongly recommends pain-monitoring and teaching people to read their pain response to activity, without giving a number (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021). During exercises, Walkito ends a session if pain reaches 6 out of 10.

Source: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(6):897–906.
Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.

### Should you ice a plantar fasciitis flare-up?

**Ice is fine if it makes the heel feel better, but no study shows it calms a flare.** The 2023 guideline found too little evidence to recommend either superficial heat or cold for plantar fasciitis (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

Even for fresh sports injuries, where ice is used most, a review of 22 trials found no evidence for a best way or best length of time to ice (Bleakley and colleagues, 2004). So there is no tested "ice for X minutes" rule for a sore heel. If you use it, keep a cloth between the ice and your skin, stop if the skin goes numb, and skip it if you have diabetes or poor feeling in your feet.

Use it next to your stretches, not instead of them. [Ice or heat for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/ice-or-heat-for-plantar-fasciitis/) covers what the few studies found and how to protect your skin.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Bleakley C, McDonough S, MacAuley D. The use of ice in the treatment of acute soft-tissue injury: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2004;32(1):251–261.

### How do you rebuild after a flare-up?

**Step your strength work back one level, then climb again once the mornings settle.** No study has tested how to rebuild after a flare. The 2023 guideline grades calf strength work **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023), and in a trial of 48 people, heavy heel raises with a towel under the toes helped faster than stretching (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015). Strength work is worth keeping, just at a level your heel can handle this week.

Walkito’s calf work goes up in steps: seated heel raises, then heel raises on both feet, then a held heel raise, and only later the towel heel raise, which loads the plantar fascia the hardest. During a flare:

- Drop one step down. If you were on the towel heel raise, go back to the held raise or raises on both feet. If you were on both feet, go back to seated.
- Keep the stretches going as usual.
- Move back up a step once the last two sessions at the lower level felt easy and your mornings are back to normal.
- Bring back the activity that set off the flare in small pieces, changing one thing at a time: distance, pace, hills or surface.

These are Walkito’s starting doses, not a prescription. The full set and table are in [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/), and the strength ladder is explained in [calf raises for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/).

- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel all day, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, the deeper calf muscle, with almost no load on the heel.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Both feet share the load. Hold a wall for balance.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### What is the worst thing you can do during a flare-up?

**No study ranks the worst thing, but two opposite mistakes are the most common: pushing straight through it, and stopping everything.** Here is what the evidence says about each:

- **Pushing through rising pain.** Keeping the same long walks or runs while the heel gets worse each morning ignores the one signal the tested pain rule relies on (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007). The experts behind the 2021 best practice guide named a change in overall load as a risk factor for flares, so more load is the wrong direction (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021).
- **Stopping all activity and all exercises.** The guideline recommends adjusting load and does not advise complete rest (Koc and colleagues, 2023), and in the Achilles trial staying active within a pain limit did as well as pausing running and jumping for six weeks (Silbernagel and colleagues, 2007). Dropping your stretches and calf work also throws away the options graded **A** and **B**.
- **Going barefoot on hard floors,** especially for the first steps of the day (Morrissey and colleagues, 2021).
- **Counting on an insole alone.** Insoles used on their own for short-term relief are graded **B against** by the guideline, though they may help combined with exercise (Koc and colleagues, 2023). See [insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/).

A flare is not proof that your plan failed. If flares keep coming back or each one is worse than the last, that is the time to see a clinician, not to try harder.

Source: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(6):897–906.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Morrissey D, Cotchett M, Said J'Bari A, et al. Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(19):1106–1118.

### When is it not a flare-up?

**If the pain behaves differently from your usual plantar fasciitis, do not assume it is a flare.** Plantar fasciitis pain is worst with the first steps after rest, often eases once you get going, and can return after long periods on your feet (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Other patterns point elsewhere:

- **Pain that builds the more you walk,** often after a jump in activity, or pain when you squeeze the sides of the heel, can be a stress fracture (Tu, 2018). See [plantar fasciitis or stress fracture](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-stress-fracture/).
- **Pain at night or at rest,** or burning, tingling and numbness, suggest something other than the plantar fascia. See [heel pain at night](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-at-night/).
- **A sudden pop or sharp pain** under the foot during activity, or new bruising or swelling, needs a clinician, not a flare plan.
- **A deep ache in the centre of the heel** that is worse on hard ground can come from the heel fat pad. See [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/).

Not sure where your pain fits? The [foot pain identifier](https://walkito.site/foot-pain-identifier/) walks through the common patterns, though it does not diagnose.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.
Source: Patel DS, Roth M, Kapil N. Stress fractures: diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. American Family Physician. 2011;83(1):39–46.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain started after a fall, a jump or a twist, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- you felt a pop or sudden sharp pain under the foot, or there is new bruising or swelling
- pain builds the more you walk, or squeezing the sides of the heel hurts (possible stress fracture)
- the heel hurts at night or at rest, not just with your first steps
- you have numbness, tingling or burning in the foot
- the heel is red, hot or swollen, or you feel unwell or have a fever
- you have diabetes or poor circulation and your foot hurts or looks different
- the pain keeps getting worse for more than a few days despite cutting back, or flares keep coming back

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app. It reads a flare the way this page does: by how your heel feels in the morning.

#### What causes plantar fasciitis to flare up?

Usually a sudden rise in load on the heel: more walking or running than usual, long hours standing, or bare feet on hard floors. The 2023 guideline lists a recent increase in weight-bearing activity as typical. In one study, standing for most of the workday came with 3.6 times the odds of getting plantar fasciitis.

#### How long does a plantar fasciitis flare-up last?

No study has measured how long a flare lasts, so any set number of days is a guess. Use your mornings as the guide: if first-step pain eases over a few days once you cut back, you are on track. Plantar fasciitis itself often takes months, and about 90% of people improve with non-surgical care.

#### What should I do when plantar fasciitis flares up?

Cut back the activity that set it off, keep gentle plantar fascia and calf stretches, wear supportive shoes indoors, and judge it by next-morning pain. The 2023 guideline recommends adjusting load and does not advise complete rest. In a trial of 180 adults, that kind of advice plus a heel cup came with meaningful improvement at about three months.

#### Should I rest completely during a plantar fasciitis flare-up?

No study shows complete rest is needed. The 2023 guideline recommends adjusting load and does not advise stopping. In an Achilles pain trial, people who stayed active with pain up to about 5 out of 10, settling by morning, did as well at twelve months as those who paused running and jumping for six weeks. If even short walks hurt sharply or make you limp, see a clinician.

#### What is the worst thing you can do for plantar fasciitis?

No study ranks it, but pushing through pain that gets worse each morning is the clearest mistake, since experts in a 2021 best practice guide named changes in load as a risk factor for flares. Stopping all activity and your exercises is the opposite mistake. Going barefoot on hard floors is also best avoided until symptoms settle.

#### Should I keep doing my exercises during a flare-up?

Yes, at a lighter level. Keep the plantar fascia and calf stretches, which the 2023 guideline grades A, and drop your calf strength work one step, for example from standing to seated heel raises. Strength work is graded B, and heavy heel raises helped faster than stretching in a 48-person trial. Stop if pain reaches 6 out of 10.

#### Is ice good for a plantar fasciitis flare-up?

Ice is fine for comfort, but there is no evidence it calms a flare. The 2023 heel pain guideline makes no recommendation on ice or heat, and a review of 22 trials in fresh injuries found no best way or length of time to ice. Protect your skin, and skip it if your feet have poor feeling.

#### Can new shoes cause a plantar fasciitis flare-up?

They can, though no study has tested new shoes as a trigger. People with heel pain wore shoes with harder heels than people without it, and a best practice guide advises supportive shoes with the heel slightly higher than the toes. A switch to flat, thin or very flexible shoes is a change your heel may notice.

## Can plantar fasciitis cause knee, hip or back pain?

Language: English · https://walkito.site/can-plantar-fasciitis-cause-knee-pain/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

It can contribute, but nobody has proven it. A sore heel changes how you walk: studies of [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/) show people put less weight through the heel and more through the front of the foot (Phillips and McClinton, 2017), and that shift can load the knee, hip and back differently. No study has followed people with heel pain to see whether knee, hip or back pain starts later, so the evidence is associations, not proof of cause.

- In a review of 19 gait studies, people with plantar heel pain put less load through the heel and more through the midfoot and forefoot, while time on each foot stayed about the same (Phillips and McClinton, 2017).
- In 18 people with no foot pain, a painful bead under the heel was enough to shorten the time they stood on that leg with each step (Levins and colleagues, 1998).
- Among 40 people with knee osteoarthritis, 52% had heel pain and 62% had a thickened plantar fascia on ultrasound. The study had no comparison group, so it cannot show which caused which (Miladi and colleagues, 2023).
- In a trial of 83 people with plantar fasciitis, adding foot and hip strengthening to stretching did not reduce heel pain more than stretching alone over eight weeks. All three groups improved (Kamonseki and colleagues, 2016).
- A tight calf is the best-studied link: people with 0 degrees of ankle bend or less had 23.3 times the odds of plantar fasciitis compared with people above 10 degrees (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).

### Can plantar fasciitis cause pain in other parts of the leg?

**Probably sometimes, through the way you walk.** Plantar fasciitis does not spread up the leg. What changes is your walking. When the heel hurts, you land more softly on it, push off less firmly and lean on the front of the foot. A 2017 review of 19 studies found exactly that pattern: less load through the heel at first contact, and more time and load on the midfoot and forefoot.

The change can be small enough that you do not notice it. In that review, the total time each foot spent on the ground was about the same as in people without heel pain. In a lab study, 18 people with no foot pain walked with a bead under the heel, and with the larger beads they spent less time standing on that leg (Levins and colleagues, 1998). That is a mild limp, at least in a short lab test with a sudden pain.

Here is where the evidence stands for each area:

Source: Phillips A, McClinton S. Gait deviations associated with plantar heel pain: a systematic review. Clinical Biomechanics. 2017;42:55–64.
Source: Levins AD, Skinner HB, Caiozzo VJ. Adaptive gait responses to plantar heel pain. Journal of Rehabilitation Research and Development. 1998;35(3):289–293.

### Can plantar fasciitis cause knee pain?

**The two often show up together, but no study shows the heel causes the knee pain.** The closest study looked at 40 people with knee osteoarthritis. 21 of them (52%) had heel pain, and an ultrasound showed a thickened plantar fascia in 25 (62%). People with plantar fasciitis more often had a stiff ankle that did not bend up well (Miladi and colleagues, 2023).

That study had no comparison group of people without knee arthritis, so it cannot say heel pain is more common than usual. The authors point out that both problems share risk factors: getting older, weight, the kind of work you do and poorly fitting shoes. A stiff ankle may be the shared link rather than one joint causing the other.

If your knee started to ache on the same side after the heel pain began, and it eases as the heel settles, a changed walk is a reasonable guess. If the knee swells, locks, catches or gives way, it has its own problem and needs its own check.

For pain around the kneecap, the 2019 patellofemoral pain guideline recommends exercise that combines the hip and the knee (Willy and colleagues, 2019). If you also have flat feet, the foot side of the knee story is on [flat feet and knee pain](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-knee-pain/).

Source: Miladi S, Bouzid S, Fazaa A, et al. Is there an association between plantar fasciitis and knee osteoarthritis? Musculoskeletal Care. 2023;21(4):1045–1052.
Source: Willy RW, Hoglund LT, Barton CJ, et al. Patellofemoral Pain: Clinical Practice Guidelines Linked to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health From the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2019;49(9):CPG1–CPG95.

### Can plantar fasciitis cause hip pain?

**There is a hip link, but which comes first is unknown.** A 2025 lab study compared 15 long-distance runners with plantar fasciitis and 15 without. The runners with heel pain used their gluteus medius and gluteus maximus, the side and back hip muscles, less at certain points of the stride. Their pelvis dropped more on the other side, and their knee and heel tilted inward more (Kongtong and Khongprasert, 2025).

That fits two stories, and the study cannot pick between them. Weak hip control may let the leg roll inward and load the arch more. Or heel pain may change how you run, and the hip follows. No study has measured hip pain in people with plantar fasciitis.

A 2009 study of 25 female runners with a history of plantar fasciitis and 25 matched runners found the plantar fasciitis group landed with a faster rise in force and had lower arches, but no difference in rearfoot motion and, unlike the calf studies, more ankle bend (Pohl and colleagues, 2009). Runners can find more on [foot exercises for runners](https://walkito.site/foot-exercises-for-runners/).

Source: Kongtong W, Khongprasert S. Hip muscle activity and frontal plane lower extremity kinematics in long-distance runners with plantar fasciitis. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2025;41(4):367–373.
Source: Pohl MB, Hamill J, Davis IS. Biomechanical and anatomic factors associated with a history of plantar fasciitis in female runners. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2009;19(5):372–376.

### Can plantar fasciitis cause back pain?

**We found no study that tests whether plantar fasciitis leads to back pain.** Some clinic pages say a limp from heel pain "commonly" causes back pain. That is a possible chain, not a measured one.

The nearest evidence is about foot shape, not heel pain. In the Framingham Foot Study, flat foot posture was not linked to low back pain, and only a foot that rolled inward while walking showed a small link, in women (Menz and colleagues, 2013). The details are on [flat feet and back pain](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-back-pain/), so we do not repeat them here.

Low back pain is very common, and for most people no single cause can be found (Hartvigsen and colleagues, 2018). So if your back hurts, the heel is one possible contributor among many. Exercise is the best-supported approach for long-lasting back pain: a 2021 Cochrane review of 249 trials found it lowered pain by about 15 points on a 100-point scale (Hayden and colleagues, 2021).

Source: Menz HB, Dufour AB, Riskowski JL, Hillstrom HJ, Hannan MT. Foot posture, foot function and low back pain: the Framingham Foot Study. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2013;52(12):2275–2282.
Source: Hartvigsen J, Hancock MJ, Kongsted A, et al. What low back pain is and why we need to pay attention. The Lancet. 2018;391(10137):2356–2367.
Source: Hayden JA, Ellis J, Ogilvie R, Malmivaara A, van Tulder MW. Exercise therapy for chronic low back pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2021;9(9):CD009790.

### Can plantar fasciitis cause calf or ankle pain?

**The calf is the best-studied link, and it may run from the calf to the heel.** A tight calf limits how far the ankle bends. In a case-control study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, people with 0 degrees of ankle bend or less had 23.3 times the odds of plantar fasciitis compared with people above 10 degrees (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). In 254 people with plantar fasciitis, 52 to 60 percent had an isolated tight gastrocnemius (Patel and DiGiovanni, 2011).

So a tight calf with heel pain is common, and stretching it is part of the heel pain plan. More on that in [tight calves](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/).

The plantar fascia and the Achilles tendon are also linked. In 52 MRI scans, people with Achilles changes had a thicker plantar fascia, 3.43 mm on average against 2.09 mm (Stecco and colleagues, 2013). If the pain sits at the back of the heel rather than underneath, read [plantar fasciitis vs Achilles tendonitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-achilles-tendonitis/).

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Patel A, DiGiovanni B. Association between plantar fasciitis and isolated contracture of the gastrocnemius. Foot & Ankle International. 2011;32(1):5–8.
Source: Stecco C, Corradin M, Macchi V, Morra A, Porzionato A, Biz C, De Caro R. Plantar fascia anatomy and its relationship with Achilles tendon and paratenon. Journal of Anatomy. 2013;223(6):665–676.

### Does hip strengthening help plantar fasciitis?

**For the heel itself, adding hip work did not do better than stretching in the one trial that tested it.** In 2016, Kamonseki and colleagues split 83 people with plantar fasciitis into three groups for eight weeks:

- Stretching alone.
- Stretching plus foot strengthening.
- Stretching plus foot strengthening and hip strengthening (the muscles that lift the leg out to the side and turn it out).

All three groups improved in heel pain, daily function and a reach-and-balance test, and no group did better than the others.

What this means in practice:

- Stretching stays the base. The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching **A**, its top grade, and strength work **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- Hip work is not a shortcut for the heel. One trial, eight weeks and 83 people is not enough to rule out a benefit, but it did not show one.
- The trial did not measure knee, hip or back pain. If those hurt, hip strengthening is still a sensible addition, and for kneecap pain the guideline for that condition supports hip and knee exercise (Willy and colleagues, 2019).

Source: Kamonseki DH, Gonçalves GA, Yi LC, Júnior IL. Effect of stretching with and without muscle strengthening exercises for the foot and hip in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled single-blind clinical trial. Manual Therapy. 2016;23:76–82.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Willy RW, Hoglund LT, Barton CJ, et al. Patellofemoral Pain: Clinical Practice Guidelines Linked to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health From the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2019;49(9):CPG1–CPG95.

### Which exercises help when heel pain spreads up the leg?

Start with the heel: the stretches and calf work from the [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) guide. Then add hip and balance work for the leg above it. Doses below are Walkito’s starting doses from the heel pain and flat feet guides.

Keep it to a level where the heel is no worse the next morning. If walking itself is the trigger, [walking with plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/walking-with-plantar-fasciitis/) covers how to keep moving without a flare.

- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel all day, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Both feet share the load while the calf wakes up.
- **Hip abduction** (3 sets of 10, each leg): Stand with a resistance band and lift one leg out to the side against it. Push through the heel, not the toes. Keep the body upright and do not lean away. A hip that gives way lands the load on the arch.
- **Single-leg hold** (3 holds of 20 seconds, each leg): Stand on one foot and look at one spot ahead. Let the foot wobble. It is meant to, because that wobble is the foot doing the balancing. Keep the pelvis level, so the hip on the standing side works too. Lightly touch a counter or wall with your fingertips if you need to. More on [single-leg balance](https://walkito.site/exercises/single-leg-balance/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Kamonseki DH, Gonçalves GA, Yi LC, Júnior IL. Effect of stretching with and without muscle strengthening exercises for the foot and hip in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled single-blind clinical trial. Manual Therapy. 2016;23:76–82.

### How can you tell if the knee, hip or back pain is not from the heel?

A changed walk is only one explanation. These signs point to a separate problem that needs its own check:

- **The other pain came first,** or it has nothing to do with how much you walk.
- **The knee swells, locks, catches or gives way.** Those are signs of a problem inside the knee.
- **The pain is in the groin,** or the hip is stiff when you put on socks or shoes.
- **Pain runs down the leg below the knee, with numbness, tingling or weakness.** That can come from a nerve in the back, and heel pain with burning or tingling may be nerve pain too.
- **Pain at night or at rest** that does not ease when you change position. See also [heel pain at night](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-at-night/).

Clinicians use a short list of warning signs to rule out rare serious spine problems (Finucane and colleagues, 2020). They are in the list below.

Source: Finucane LM, Downie A, Mercer C, et al. International framework for red flags for potential serious spinal pathologies. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2020;50(7):350–372.

### See a clinician first if

- the knee, hip or back pain came first, or does not change with how much you walk
- the knee swells, locks, catches or gives way, or you cannot fully bend or straighten it
- pain runs down the leg below the knee, or you have numbness, tingling, burning or weakness in the leg or foot
- pain wakes you at night or is there at rest and does not ease with a change of position
- you have back pain with fever, unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer
- you have numbness around the groin or buttocks, or new trouble controlling your bladder or bowels: go to an emergency department
- pain started after a fall, a twist or a crack, or you cannot put weight on the leg

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app with the exercises on this page: calf and soleus stretches, heel raises, hip abduction and single-leg balance. It works on the heel and the leg above it. It does not assess your knee, hip or back, so get those checked if they have their own warning signs.

#### Can plantar fasciitis cause knee pain?

It may contribute, but it is not proven. Heel pain shifts load toward the front of the foot as you walk, which changes how the knee is loaded. Among 40 people with knee arthritis, 52% had heel pain, but with no comparison group the study cannot show that one caused the other.

#### Can plantar fasciitis cause hip pain?

Possibly, but no study has measured hip pain in people with plantar fasciitis. A 2025 study of 15 runners with plantar fasciitis and 15 without found lower activity in the side hip muscles and more pelvic drop in the heel pain group. It could not tell which came first.

#### Can plantar fasciitis cause lower back pain?

There is no study testing it. A limp from heel pain could add strain, but that chain has not been measured. For most people with low back pain no single cause is found, and in the Framingham Foot Study, flat foot posture was not linked to back pain.

#### Can plantar fasciitis cause calf pain?

A tight calf often goes with plantar fasciitis, and the link may run from the calf to the heel. The studies measured tightness, not calf pain. People with 0 degrees of ankle bend or less had 23.3 times the odds of plantar fasciitis, and 52 to 60 percent of 254 people with it had a tight gastrocnemius.

#### Can heel pain cause pain on the other leg?

It can, in theory. When one heel hurts, you may spend less time standing on that leg, as a short lab test in 18 people with a painful bead under the heel showed. No study has measured pain in the other leg in people with plantar fasciitis.

#### Will hip exercises help my plantar fasciitis?

Not for the heel itself, as far as the one trial shows. In 83 people over eight weeks, adding foot and hip strengthening to stretching did not reduce heel pain more than stretching alone, and all groups improved. Hip work can still make sense if your knee or hip also hurts.

#### Should I work on the heel or the knee first?

You can work on both at once. Heel stretches and calf strength are graded A and B in the 2023 heel pain guideline, and hip and knee exercise is recommended for kneecap pain. If the knee swells, locks or gives way, get it checked rather than waiting for the heel to settle.

#### Can plantar fasciitis cause ankle pain?

Pain at the back of the heel or around the Achilles tendon can go with plantar fasciitis. In 52 MRI scans, people with Achilles changes had a thicker plantar fascia, 3.43 mm on average against 2.09 mm. Pain on the sides of the ankle after a twist is a different problem.

## Heel pain that isn’t plantar fasciitis: look-alikes and how they differ

Language: English · https://walkito.site/heel-pain-not-plantar-fasciitis/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

If your heel pain does not follow the usual pattern of [plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis/), worst with the first steps in the morning and easing as you warm up, something else may be going on. Under the heel, the common look-alikes are a bruised or thin heel fat pad, an irritated nerve, including one pinched in the lower back, a heel stress fracture and inflammatory arthritis (Latt and colleagues, 2020). Pain at the back of the heel has its own causes, such as the Achilles tendon. In 250 people with pain under the heel, plantar fasciitis explained 53.2% of cases and fat pad atrophy 14.8% (Yi and colleagues, 2011).

- Typical plantar fasciitis pain sits near the inner heel, is worst with the first step in the morning or after sitting, gets better with activity and then worse as activity goes on (Latt and colleagues, 2020).
- In 250 people with plantar heel pain, plantar fasciitis accounted for 53.2%, fat pad atrophy for 14.8%, and both together for 9.2% (Yi and colleagues, 2011).
- Burning, electric or tingling heel pain often points to a nerve. One review estimates Baxter’s nerve entrapment may explain up to 20% of chronic heel pain (Tedeschi, 2025).
- A heel stress fracture usually aches with activity, not with the first step, and in 30 military recruits it showed on plain X-ray in only 15% (Latt and colleagues, 2020; Sormaala and colleagues, 2006).
- Pain in both heels together with other painful or stiff joints, or a stiff back, suggests an inflammatory cause that needs a doctor, not just stretches (Latt and colleagues, 2020).

### What else can cause heel pain besides plantar fasciitis?

**Plantar fasciitis is the most common cause of heel pain, but it is far from the only one.** A US foot surgeons’ guideline describes heel pain as mostly mechanical, but says nerve, arthritis, injury, tumour, infection and blood vessel causes must also be considered (Thomas and colleagues, 2010). A 2020 review groups the causes of pain under the heel into nerve problems, injuries such as a stress fracture or a torn fascia, inflammatory arthritis, and wear of the fat pad or the fascia itself (Latt and colleagues, 2020).

The table puts the nine most common look-alikes next to plantar fasciitis. Read it as a map of patterns, not a checklist: the cells describe what is typical, and your heel does not have to read the textbook.

Source: Yi TI, Lee GE, Seo IS, Huh WS, Yoon TH, Kim BR. Clinical characteristics of the causes of plantar heel pain. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2011;35(4):507–13.
Source: Thomas JL, Christensen JC, Kravitz SR, et al. The diagnosis and treatment of heel pain: a clinical practice guideline, revision 2010. Journal of Foot and Ankle Surgery. 2010;49(3 Suppl):S1–S19.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.

### What does plantar fasciitis usually feel like?

**Knowing the usual pattern is the easiest way to spot when your heel does not fit it.** Typical plantar fasciitis is a dull ache or throbbing around the inner front of the heel, where the fascia attaches. It is worst with the first step in the morning and when you get up after sitting, often gets better once you are moving, and then worsens again as standing or walking goes on (Latt and colleagues, 2020). More on that pattern in [heel pain in the morning](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-in-the-morning/).

The same review says that when someone does not describe these classic features, a clinician should look for other causes. It also notes that plantar fasciitis usually affects one foot, though about 30% of people have it in both (Latt and colleagues, 2020). So two sore heels do not rule plantar fasciitis out, but they are one reason to look more widely.

Plantar fasciitis is also the most common cause, so a heel that fits most of the pattern is still most likely to be plantar fasciitis. In the 250 people above, it explained about half of cases on its own and was present in another 9.2% together with fat pad atrophy (Yi and colleagues, 2011).

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Yi TI, Lee GE, Seo IS, Huh WS, Yoon TH, Kim BR. Clinical characteristics of the causes of plantar heel pain. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2011;35(4):507–13.

### Could it be a nerve, or pain coming from your back?

**Pain described as burning or like an electric shock is often coming from a nerve** (Latt and colleagues, 2020). Three nerve sources are the usual suspects:

- **Baxter’s nerve**, a small branch that runs under the heel. When it is squeezed, it gives a chronic, burning pain across the heel pad (Latt and colleagues, 2020). One review estimates it may explain up to 20% of chronic heel pain and says it is often mistaken for plantar fasciitis (Tedeschi, 2025), while another calls it uncommon (Latt and colleagues, 2020).
- **Tarsal tunnel syndrome**, where the tibial nerve is squeezed behind the inner ankle bone. It usually brings burning or shooting pain along the sole, often with numbness (Latt and colleagues, 2020). More on arch nerve pain in [arch pain](https://walkito.site/arch-pain/).
- **A pinched nerve in the lower back**, at the L5 or S1 level. It is relatively common and usually comes with back pain, pain down the leg, or numbness in the foot or leg (Latt and colleagues, 2020).

A review of nerve related heel pain found that nerve entrapment may play a part both early on and in heel pain that does not get better, but that how it works and how best to test for it are still debated (Alshami and colleagues, 2008). Night or rest pain with tingling is covered in [heel pain at night](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-at-night/).

This is one group where self-help exercises are not the first step. A clinician examines the foot, for example by tapping along the tibial nerve, and may use ultrasound, nerve tests or MRI (Latt and colleagues, 2020; Tedeschi, 2025).

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Tedeschi R. Baxter's nerve: the hidden culprit of chronic heel pain. Neurological Sciences. 2025;46(9):4685–4689.
Source: Alshami AM, Souvlis T, Coppieters MW. A review of plantar heel pain of neural origin: differential diagnosis and management. Manual Therapy. 2008;13(2):103–111.

### Could it be a stress fracture or the fat pad?

**Both tend to ache with activity rather than with the first step of the morning.** A heel stress fracture typically causes aching across the back part of the heel bone that is tied to activity, not to getting out of bed. It is more likely if you have had low bone density or a stress fracture before (Latt and colleagues, 2020). It usually follows a jump in walking, running or a move to a harder surface (Tu, 2018).

A normal X-ray does not rule it out: in 30 recruits with a heel stress injury on MRI, plain X-rays showed it in only 15% (Sormaala and colleagues, 2006). The side by side comparison is in [plantar fasciitis vs stress fracture](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-stress-fracture/).

Fat pad pain is usually described as a deep, bruise-like ache in the middle of the heel pad, worse on hard floors and barefoot. Like a stress fracture, it tends to be activity related (Latt and colleagues, 2020), and in one clinic it more often affected both heels and was made worse by standing (Yi and colleagues, 2011). It was the second most common cause in the 250 people above, at 14.8% (Yi and colleagues, 2011). A 2022 review found only seven original studies on it, so much of the advice is based on experience, not trials (Chang and colleagues, 2022). More in [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/), and on how a spur fits in, [plantar fasciitis vs heel spur](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-heel-spur/).

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.
Source: Sormaala MJ, Niva MH, Kiuru MJ, Mattila VM, Pihlajamäki HK. Stress injuries of the calcaneus detected with magnetic resonance imaging in military recruits. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2006;88(10):2237–2242.
Source: Yi TI, Lee GE, Seo IS, Huh WS, Yoon TH, Kim BR. Clinical characteristics of the causes of plantar heel pain. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2011;35(4):507–13.
Source: Chang AH, Rasmussen SZ, Jensen AE, Sørensen T, Rathleff MS. What do we actually know about a common cause of plantar heel pain? A scoping review of heel fat pad syndrome. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2022;15(1):60.

### What if the pain is at the back of the heel?

**Plantar fasciitis hurts under the heel. Pain at the back of the heel usually comes from the Achilles tendon, the bone where it attaches, or, in children, the growth plate.** Three look-alikes live here:

- **Insertional Achilles tendinopathy**, pain right where the Achilles tendon meets the heel bone, rather than higher up the tendon (Jonsson and colleagues, 2008). See [plantar fasciitis vs Achilles tendonitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-achilles-tendonitis/) and [Achilles tendonitis exercises](https://walkito.site/achilles-tendonitis-exercises/).
- **Haglund’s deformity**, a bony bump on the upper back of the heel that shoes rub against, which can irritate the bursa and the tendon (Yuen and colleagues, 2022). See [Haglund’s deformity](https://walkito.site/haglunds-deformity/).
- **Sever’s disease** in children who are still growing: the growth plate at the back of the heel gets sore with running and jumping. In children, pain when the heel is squeezed from both sides points to it (Tu, 2018). See [Sever’s disease](https://walkito.site/severs-disease/).

Insertional Achilles pain changes how you exercise: heel drops are kept at floor level rather than dropping the heel below the step, because deep stretching can press the tendon against the bone (Jonsson and colleagues, 2008).

Source: Jonsson P, Alfredson H, Sunding K, Fahlström M, Cook J. New regimen for eccentric calf-muscle training in patients with chronic insertional Achilles tendinopathy: results of a pilot study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2008;42(9):746–749.
Source: Yuen WLP, Tan PT, Kon KKC. Surgical Treatment of Haglund's Deformity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Cureus. 2022;14(7):e27500.
Source: Tu P. Heel Pain: Diagnosis and Management. American Family Physician. 2018;97(2):86–93.

### What if both heels hurt, or other joints are stiff too?

**Pain in both heels, heel pain together with several painful or stiff joints, or a stiff back suggest an inflammatory cause** such as psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis or spondyloarthritis (Latt and colleagues, 2020). The spondyloarthritis group is most common in young men, while plantar fasciitis is most common in middle age and more often in women (Latt and colleagues, 2020).

The same review lists the clues that make a doctor order blood tests: symptoms elsewhere in the body, both feet affected, several joints involved, especially small ones, and morning stiffness that lasts more than 30 minutes (Latt and colleagues, 2020).

Both heels can hurt with plantar fasciitis too. In a 5 to 15 year follow-up of 174 people with plantar fasciitis, pain in both heels was linked to symptoms that lasted longer (Hansen and colleagues, 2018). That is why two sore heels are a reason to get checked, not proof of arthritis.

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.

### What if it hurts on the inside of the ankle and arch?

**Pain that sits behind or below the inner ankle bone and along the arch, rather than under the heel, can come from the posterior tibial tendon.** It is the main moving support of the inner arch, and people with a problem here have pain on the inner ankle and a foot that slowly flattens (Deu and colleagues, 2022). In a survey of 582 women over 40 in England, 3.3% had early stage PTTD, and none of them had been diagnosed (Kohls-Gatzoulis and colleagues, 2009).

An arch that is flattening on one side, or trouble rising onto the toes of that foot, is a reason to see a clinician. Exercise has some support in the early stages, but only three small trials with 93 people in total have tested it (Ross and colleagues, 2018). More in [posterior tibial tendon dysfunction exercises](https://walkito.site/posterior-tibial-tendon-dysfunction-exercises/).

Source: Deu RS, Coslick AM, Dreher G. Tendinopathies of the Foot and Ankle. American Family Physician. 2022;105(5):479–486.
Source: Kohls-Gatzoulis J, Woods B, Angel JC, Singh D. The prevalence of symptomatic posterior tibialis tendon dysfunction in women over the age of 40 in England. Foot and Ankle Surgery. 2009;15(2):75–81.
Source: Ross MH, Smith MD, Mellor R, Vicenzino B. Exercise for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction: a systematic review of randomised clinical trials and clinical guidelines. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2018;4(1):e000430.

### What should you do next, and when do the exercises fit?

**If your heel fits the plantar fasciitis pattern and none of the warning signs below apply, stretching and calf strength work are the first-line options.** The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching **A** and strength work **B** for plantar fasciitis (Koc and colleagues, 2023). These exercises are for plantar fasciitis only. They are not meant for a suspected fracture, a nerve problem or arthritis.

If your pain fits another row of the table, or you are not sure, see a GP, physiotherapist or podiatrist. Bring a short note: where it hurts, when it is worst, what makes it worse, whether one or both feet are affected, and anything that came with it, such as numbness, swelling or back pain. That is what a clinician uses to sort the look-alikes.

If you have been doing plantar fasciitis exercises for several weeks and nothing has changed, that is also worth a visit. Non-surgical care brings full relief for about 90% of people with plantar fasciitis, though it can take three to six months, so pain that does not budge is a reason to check the diagnosis (Latt and colleagues, 2020). See [how long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/) and the full [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).

- **Plantar fascia stretch (plantar fasciitis only)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Calf stretch (plantar fasciitis only)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward. A tight calf pulls on the heel all day, so this stretch matters even though you feel it higher up.
- **Soleus stretch (plantar fasciitis only)** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Seated heel raises (plantar fasciitis only)** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, the deeper calf muscle, with almost no load on the heel. The heel raise trial on this site tested a harder standing version (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### See a clinician first if

- you feel burning, tingling, electric shocks or numbness in the heel or sole
- heel pain comes with back pain, pain down the leg, or weakness in the foot
- the pain builds the longer you walk or run, or squeezing the sides of the heel bone hurts
- the heel is swollen, red, warm or bruised, or you have a fever
- both heels hurt and other joints are painful or stiff, or morning stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes
- the pain started after a fall, a twist or a sudden pop, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- the heel hurts at rest or wakes you at night
- a child has heel pain that does not settle with less sport

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is an exercise app for heel and foot pain. Its plan is built for plantar fasciitis type heel pain, not for the look-alikes on this page, so if your pain fits another pattern, see a clinician before you start.

#### What is commonly mistaken for plantar fasciitis?

The most common look-alikes are heel fat pad syndrome, nerve entrapment such as Baxter’s nerve or tarsal tunnel syndrome, a heel stress fracture, and insertional Achilles pain. It can also be inflammatory arthritis or a nerve pinched in the lower back. In 250 people with pain under the heel, fat pad atrophy explained 14.8% of cases.

#### How do I know if my heel pain is not plantar fasciitis?

You cannot know for sure without an examination, but some features do not fit. Plantar fasciitis is usually worst with the first morning steps and eases as you move. Burning or tingling, pain that builds with activity, pain at the back of the heel, or both heels with stiff joints suggest something else. A clinician can sort it out.

#### Can heel pain come from your back?

Yes. A nerve pinched in the lower back at the L5 or S1 level can cause pain, numbness or tingling in the heel and sole. It is relatively common and usually comes with back pain or pain running down the leg. Weakness in the foot or numbness that spreads needs a doctor promptly.

#### What does nerve pain in the heel feel like?

Nerve pain in the heel is often burning, shooting or like an electric shock, sometimes with tingling or numbness in the sole. Baxter’s nerve entrapment gives a burning pain across the heel pad, and one review estimates it may explain up to 20% of chronic heel pain. It needs a clinician’s assessment.

#### Is heel pain in both feet plantar fasciitis?

It can be: about 30% of people with plantar fasciitis have it in both feet. But pain in both heels, especially with other painful or stiff joints, a stiff back or morning stiffness that lasts more than 30 minutes, can point to inflammatory arthritis. That combination is a reason to see a doctor.

#### Can an X-ray show what is causing my heel pain?

Sometimes, but a normal X-ray rules out less than people think. In 30 recruits with a heel stress injury on MRI, plain X-rays showed it in only 15%. For typical plantar fasciitis, the 2023 guideline says imaging is usually not needed. A clinician decides whether ultrasound, MRI or nerve tests are worth doing.

#### Why is my plantar fasciitis not getting better?

There are several possible reasons, and one is that it may not be plantar fasciitis. About 90% of people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care, so pain that has not changed after several weeks of steady stretching and strength work is a good reason to have the diagnosis checked by a clinician.

#### What causes heel pain in children if not plantar fasciitis?

In children who are still growing, the most common cause is Sever’s disease, an irritated growth plate at the back of the heel bone. It hurts during and after running and jumping sports, and a heel that is sore when squeezed from both sides points to it. A clinician should check heel pain in a child that does not settle.

#### Can I do plantar fasciitis exercises if I am not sure what it is?

The 2023 guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretches A for plantar fasciitis, and they are gentle. But if you have burning or numbness, swelling, pain that builds with activity, or pain after an injury, see a clinician first. Stop any exercise that makes the heel sharply worse.

## Plantar fasciitis not getting better? Reasons and what to change

Language: English · https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-not-getting-better/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

When plantar fasciitis is not getting better, the usual reasons are a plan that is only stretching, a load that never goes up, stopping when it eases, or something that keeps setting it off. Sometimes it is not plantar fasciitis at all. It is rarely a sign that nothing can change: in a study that followed 174 people for about ten years, 54% were free of symptoms and most of the rest had only minor pain (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).

- In 174 people followed for a mean of 9.7 years from the start of symptoms, 54% were symptom-free and 46% still had some symptoms, mostly minor. Almost all (93%) had a steroid injection at some point, so these were harder cases (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).
- Ups and downs are normal: 31.9% of the people who got better had at least one relapse first, and 77.5% of those still in pain had had a pain-free period at some point (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).
- In a trial of 48 people, loaded heel raises brought improvement forward compared with stretching at three months. By one year both groups were about even (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline grades stretching, manual therapy, taping and night splints **A**, and strength work, dry needling and low-level laser **B**. It recommends against insoles on their own for short-term relief (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- The same guideline says to look for other diagnoses when symptoms are not settling, such as inflammatory arthritis, fat pad atrophy or a lump in the fascia (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

### Is plantar fasciitis permanent if it is not getting better?

**For most people, no.** A 2020 review reports that more than 90% of people get better with non-surgical care, though it can take three to six months (Latt and colleagues, 2020). The harder question is what happens to the people who are still stuck after that.

The best long-term data come from a Danish study that followed 174 people with plantar fasciitis confirmed on ultrasound. At a mean of 9.7 years after their symptoms started, 54% had no symptoms at all. The other 46% still had some, but most described them as minor. On average, people had tried 3.8 different treatments (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).

Two things make this study more hopeful than it first looks. It was a specialist clinic group with hard-to-manage pain: 93% had a steroid injection at some point, which is not a first step. And "still has symptoms" meant any score above 0 out of 10, so it includes people with occasional mild aches.

The study also found the fascia got thinner over time whether people still had pain or not, and only 24% of the pain-free group had a fascia that looked fully normal on ultrasound. So a scan that still looks abnormal does not mean you cannot feel better. For the full timeline, see [how long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/).

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.

### Which reason fits you?

Most stalled cases fit one or two of these patterns. Read down the middle column and see which sounds like you, then go to that section.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.

### Are you only stretching?

**Stretching is worth keeping, but on its own it may not be enough.** The 2023 heel pain guideline grades plantar fascia and calf stretching **A**, its top grade. It also grades strength work for the foot and ankle **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Many home plans only include the first.

In a trial of 48 people, one group did slow, heavy heel raises with a towel under the toes and the other stretched the plantar fascia. At three months, the heel raise group scored 29 points better on the Foot Function Index. By one year the two groups were about even (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015). So doing heel raises in place of stretching did not change where people ended up at one year, but it got them there sooner.

What it looks like: you have stretched faithfully for a month or more, the stretch feels easier, but the first steps of the day are still sharp. What to change: keep the stretches and add the calf work in the next section. [Calf raises for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/) explains the trial routine in detail.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.

### Has the load ever gone up?

**Strength work only helps if it gets harder over time.** Ten easy heel raises on two feet, done for months, is a warm-up, not a load. The steps below move from both feet to one foot and then add weight. The trial routine itself was one-leg heel raises with a towel under the toes, a slow tempo and a backpack for added weight (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015).

How you set the load matters less than people think. A 2019 trial gave 70 people either a set, step-by-step heel raise plan or told them to choose their own sets and weight, as heavy as they could manage. Both groups improved by a similar amount. Choosing your own dose did not lead people to do more (Riel and colleagues, 2019).

The same trial is a useful reality check: after three months of heel raises, 44 of the 65 people who answered said they were better, but only 4 of 70 felt they needed no further treatment. If you are better but not done at three months, you are in the common group, not the failed one.

What to change: move up one step when the current one feels easy for two sessions in a row and your next morning is no worse. The cards below are the steps, in order.

- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, the deeper calf muscle, with almost no load on the heel. Start here if standing raises hurt.
- **Heel raises on both feet** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Stand on both feet, rise straight up over the big toes, then lower slowly. Both feet share the load while the calf gets used to the work.
- **Heel raise hold** (3 holds of 20 seconds, both feet): Rise onto your toes on both feet, then stay still at the top. Don’t sink back down. A useful step on days when moving reps feel too much.
- **Heel raises with a towel** (4 sets of 10, each leg, with added weight): Stand on one foot on a step, with a rolled towel under your toes. Take three seconds to rise, hold for two at the top, and take three seconds to lower. At this level, add weight such as a backpack. The towel is what makes this exercise work the plantar fascia and not just the calf.
