Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.
Source: Riel H, Jensen MB, Olesen JL, et al. Self-dosed and pre-determined progressive heavy-slow resistance training have similar effects in people with plantar fasciopathy: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2019;65(3):144–151.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Did you stop when it started to feel better, or after a flare?

**Relapses are part of the normal path, not proof that nothing works.** In the long-term Danish study, 31.9% of the people who ended up symptom-free had at least one relapse before the pain went for good. Among those who still had symptoms, 77.5% had had a pain-free period at some point (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).

Two patterns come out of that:

- **Stopping too early.** The pain eases, the exercises go, and a few weeks later the heel is back to where it started. What to change: when mornings are good, drop to a lighter maintenance dose, for example fewer strength days, instead of stopping.
- **Flare, then stop.** A long day on your feet or a new pair of shoes sets off a bad morning, and you stop everything for a week. What to change: go back one step on the cards above and keep going. Stopping completely loses the strength you built.

A simple rule helps you tell a flare from a setback: pain during the exercise up to about 6 out of 10 is fine if it settles and your next morning is no worse. This is the rule Walkito uses. It has not been tested as a rule on its own, so if your mornings get worse week after week, see a clinician.

No study has tested how long to keep a maintenance dose going after plantar fasciitis settles. The 2023 guideline does not set an end date for strength work (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### Is something still setting it off?

**Exercises can be outpaced by the load you put on the foot the rest of the day.** In a matched study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, a stiff ankle was the strongest risk factor: an ankle that bent 0 degrees or less raised the odds 23.3 times. A body mass index over 30 raised them about 5.6 times, and spending most of the workday on your feet about 3.6 times (Riddle and colleagues, 2003).

The 2023 guideline lists the same factors, plus running, and adds that hard surfaces with poor shock absorption make standing and walking at work more of a risk (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Some of these you can change, some you cannot:

- **A stiff ankle or tight calf.** Keep the calf and soleus stretches going; [tight calves](https://walkito.site/tight-calves/) has the full set.
- **Long shifts on hard floors.** Cushioned shoes, a mat where you stand, and sitting breaks where you can. See [feet hurt from standing all day](https://walkito.site/feet-hurt-standing-all-day/).
- **Walking or running volume.** Cut the distance or the pace instead of stopping. If your first steps the next morning are clearly worse, it was too much. See [walking with plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/walking-with-plantar-fasciitis/).
- **Body weight.** Weight was not linked to how long symptoms lasted in the long-term study (Hansen and colleagues, 2018), so this is not about blame. [Weight and plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/weight-and-plantar-fasciitis/) covers what is known.

Insoles can take some pressure off the heel while you build strength, but the guideline recommends against relying on them alone for short-term relief (grade **B**) and allows them alongside other care (grade **C**). [Insoles or exercises](https://walkito.site/insoles-vs-exercises/) compares the two.

Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.

### Could it be something other than plantar fasciitis?

**Yes, and the guideline tells clinicians to check when symptoms are not settling.** The 2023 heel pain guideline says clinicians should look for other diagnoses, including inflammatory arthritis of the spine and joints (spondyloarthritis), thinning of the heel fat pad, and a benign lump in the fascia (plantar fibroma), when the picture does not fit or symptoms are not resolving with care (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

A 2020 review lists other causes of pain under the heel, including a trapped nerve (tarsal tunnel syndrome or Baxter’s nerve), a stress fracture of the heel bone, a torn fascia, and inflammatory arthritis (Latt and colleagues, 2020). Clues that point away from plantar fasciitis:

- **Burning, tingling or numbness**, or pain that spreads into the arch or toes: possible nerve problem.
- **Pain that builds the longer you walk**, rather than easing after the first steps, and hurts when you squeeze the sides of the heel: see [plantar fasciitis or stress fracture](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-stress-fracture/).
- **Pain at the back of the heel** rather than underneath: see [plantar fasciitis or Achilles tendonitis](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-achilles-tendonitis/).
- **A deep bruise-like ache in the middle of the heel pad**, worse on hard floors and barefoot: see [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/).
- **Pain at night or at rest**: see [heel pain at night](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-at-night/).
- **Both heels, with long morning stiffness or other sore joints.** In the long-term study, pain in both heels went with slower recovery, and the authors suggested it could point to an inflammatory condition that was not tested for (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.

### What does the guideline list when exercise alone has not helped?

These are options to discuss with a clinician, not things to try at home. All grades are from the 2023 heel pain guideline, where **A** is its strongest recommendation (Koc and colleagues, 2023):

- **Manual therapy** (hands-on joint and soft tissue work): **A**.
- **Taping**, rigid or elastic, alongside other care, for short-term relief: **A**. See [plantar fasciitis taping](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-taping/).
- **Night splints for one to three months**, if first steps keep hurting: **A**. See [night splints](https://walkito.site/night-splints-plantar-fasciitis/).
- **Dry needling** of the calf and foot muscles: **B**.
- **Low-level laser** as part of a rehab program, for short-term pain: **B**.
- **Insoles combined with other care**: **C**.

The guideline recommends **against** insoles as the only thing you do for short-term relief (**B**) and against adding therapeutic ultrasound to stretching (**A**). The 2023 version makes no recommendation on shockwave therapy.

**Steroid injections** ease pain for some people in the short term, but the evidence for adding them is weak. In a trial of 180 people, everyone got advice and a heel cup; one group added heel raises and one added heel raises plus an injection. The differences between groups never reached the size patients would notice, at any point up to a year (Riel and colleagues, 2023). The same trial found no clear extra benefit from adding the heel raises, which is a reminder that no single add-on is a sure thing.

A 2020 review says people who still have pain after at least six months of non-surgical care may be offered minimally invasive options, such as injections or shockwave, or in some cases surgery (Latt and colleagues, 2020). These are decisions for you and a specialist. A physical therapist can also check your form and load in person: see [app or physical therapy](https://walkito.site/app-vs-physical-therapy-plantar-fasciitis/).

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Riel H, Vicenzino B, Olesen JL, et al. Does a corticosteroid injection plus exercise or exercise alone add to the effect of patient advice and a heel cup for patients with plantar fasciopathy? A randomised clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57(18):1180–1186.
Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.

### When should you get reassessed?

**Get checked again if a few months of steady, progressing exercise have not moved your morning pain, or sooner if the pattern changes.** A 2020 review says imaging is kept for unusual cases and for people who do not respond to first-line care (Latt and colleagues, 2020), and the guideline says clinicians should look for other diagnoses when symptoms are not resolving (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

To get the most out of the visit, bring:

- Your morning pain scores (first steps, 0 to 10) for the last few weeks, so the trend is clear.
- What you have done, how often, and how heavy: "heel raises" tells a clinician less than "one leg, 4 sets of 10, with a backpack".
- What makes it worse: a shift, a run, new shoes, barefoot floors.
- Anything that does not fit plantar fasciitis: night pain, tingling, both heels, other sore joints.

Ask whether the diagnosis still fits, whether an imaging test would change anything, and which of the guideline options above suit you.

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain is getting worse week after week, not just staying the same
- it started after a fall, a jump or a sudden snap, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- it hurts when you squeeze the sides of the heel, or it builds the longer you walk
- you feel burning, tingling or numbness in the heel, arch or toes
- it wakes you at night or hurts at rest
- both heels hurt with long morning stiffness, or other joints are sore or swollen
- the heel is red, warm or swollen, or you have a fever
- you have diabetes, reduced feeling in your feet or poor circulation

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app. It cannot tell you why your heel is stuck, and it does not replace a clinician’s check, but it covers the parts that often go missing: calf strength work that gets harder over time, and a lighter session on bad mornings instead of a week off.

#### Why is my plantar fasciitis not getting better?

The common reasons are a stretch-only plan with no calf strength work, a load that never gets harder, stopping when pain eases or after a flare, and daily load such as long shifts or runs. Sometimes it is not plantar fasciitis. The 2023 guideline grades stretching A and strength work B, so most plans need both.

#### Is plantar fasciitis permanent?

Usually not. About 90% of people get better with non-surgical care. In a hard-to-manage group of 174 people followed for a mean of 9.7 years, 54% were symptom-free and most of the rest had only minor symptoms. Some people do keep mild symptoms for years, so it is worth getting reassessed if you are stuck.

#### Can chronic plantar fasciitis still get better?

Yes. In a long-term study, people kept becoming symptom-free well after the first year, and 77.5% of those who still had pain had had a pain-free period at some point. The fascia also got thinner over time whether or not people still had pain. Slow is not the same as stuck for good.

#### Should I stop exercising if my heel pain flares up?

Usually not completely. Go back a step, for example from one-leg to two-leg heel raises, and keep going. Relapses are common: 31.9% of people who became symptom-free in a long-term study had at least one first. See a clinician if mornings keep getting worse week after week.

#### Is stretching enough for plantar fasciitis?

For some people it is, but adding calf strength work may help sooner. The 2023 guideline grades stretching A and strength work B. In a 48-person trial, heavy heel raises gave a better result than stretching at three months, though the groups were about even by one year.

#### Do steroid injections help plantar fasciitis that will not go away?

They can ease pain for a while, but the added benefit looks small. In a trial of 180 people, adding an injection to heel raises, advice and a heel cup made no difference patients would notice at any point up to a year. Whether one suits you is a decision for your doctor.

#### When is surgery considered for plantar fasciitis?

Only after a long trial of non-surgical care. A 2020 review says surgery is considered when pain and limits persist despite at least six months of non-surgical treatment, and that minimally invasive options such as injections or shockwave may be considered at that stage too. A foot and ankle specialist makes that call with you.

#### Could my heel pain be something other than plantar fasciitis?

Yes. The 2023 guideline tells clinicians to look for other causes when symptoms are not settling, such as inflammatory arthritis or heel fat pad thinning. Other causes include a trapped nerve and a heel stress fracture. Burning, tingling, night pain or pain that builds with walking are reasons to get checked.

#### Do insoles help if plantar fasciitis is not improving?

They may help as part of a wider plan. The 2023 guideline recommends against using insoles as the only treatment for short-term relief (grade B) and says they may be used combined with other care (grade C). Pair them with stretching and calf strength work rather than relying on them alone.

## Plantar fasciitis and menopause: why heel pain often starts in your 40s and 50s

Language: English · https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-menopause/ · published 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18

Plantar fasciitis is most common in women around the age of menopause: in Dutch family practice records, new cases in women peaked at 11.23 per 1000 patient-years at age 50, against a peak of 5.54 in men at age 55 (Rasenberg and colleagues, 2019). Whether falling hormone levels cause it is not known. The link is plausible, but no study has proven it (Douglas-Harris and colleagues, 2026). What does help is the same as at any age: plantar fascia and calf stretches, graded **A** in the 2023 heel pain guideline, and calf strength work, graded **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

- In records of about 1.9 million Dutch patients, new cases of heel pain in women peaked at 11.23 per 1000 patient-years at age 50. In men the peak was 5.54, at age 55. 62% of the 18,004 cases were women (Rasenberg and colleagues, 2019).
- The 2023 heel pain guideline says plantar fasciitis is most common between ages 40 and 60, and lists running and jobs with a lot of time on your feet as risk factors (Koc and colleagues, 2023).
- A link between menopause and heel pain is plausible but unproven: no study has measured the plantar fascia across menopause, and in a 2026 focus group study 76% of the 17 women had not connected the two (Douglas-Harris and colleagues, 2026).
- No trial has tested HRT for plantar fasciitis. Whether HRT suits you depends on your menopause symptoms and health history, and that is a decision to make with your doctor.
- Plantar fascia and calf stretches (grade **A**) and calf strength work (grade **B**) are the best-graded exercises, whatever your age (Koc and colleagues, 2023).

### Is plantar fasciitis more common around menopause?

**Yes, the timing lines up.** A Dutch study searched the family doctor records of about 1.9 million patients from 2013 to 2016 and found 18,004 new cases of plantar heel pain, the umbrella term that includes plantar fasciitis. 62% were women. Overall, women had 4.64 new cases per 1000 patient-years and men 2.98 (Rasenberg and colleagues, 2019).

The age pattern is the striking part. In women, new cases peaked at **11.23 per 1000 patient-years at age 50**. In men, the peak was lower and later: 5.54 at age 55 (Rasenberg and colleagues, 2019). The average age of menopause in the UK is 51, which is why researchers have started to ask whether the two are connected (Douglas-Harris and colleagues, 2026).

The 2023 heel pain guideline says plantar fasciitis is most common between ages 40 and 60 (Koc and colleagues, 2023). Women also tend to keep it longer: in a 5 to 15 year follow-up of 174 people, the risk of still having plantar fasciitis was higher in women and in people with pain in both heels (Hansen and colleagues, 2018).

Source: Rasenberg N, Bierma-Zeinstra SM, Bindels PJ, van der Lei J, van Middelkoop M. Incidence, prevalence, and management of plantar heel pain: a retrospective cohort study in Dutch primary care. British Journal of General Practice. 2019;69(688):e801–e808.
Source: Douglas-Harris M, Wilkins R, Ramaskandhan J, Mankelow J, Branthwaite H. Menopause and plantar heel pain: findings from a series of focus groups exploring lived experience. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2026;19(2):e70154.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.

### Does menopause cause plantar fasciitis?

**Nobody knows yet.** The authors of a 2026 study focused on menopause and heel pain write that whether a causal relationship exists is uncertain (Douglas-Harris and colleagues, 2026). That study was a set of focus groups with 17 women, not a measurement of hormones or heel tissue. Many websites state the link as fact. The evidence does not support that yet.

Source: Rasenberg N, Bierma-Zeinstra SM, Bindels PJ, van der Lei J, van Middelkoop M. Incidence, prevalence, and management of plantar heel pain: a retrospective cohort study in Dutch primary care. British Journal of General Practice. 2019;69(688):e801–e808.

### What else changes in your 40s and 50s that can strain the heel?

Plantar fasciitis usually starts when the load on the heel is more than it can handle and recover from. Several things that often change in midlife add to that load:

- **Weight.** In a review of 51 studies, a BMI over 27 came with 3.7 times the odds of plantar fasciitis, and the link was strongest in people who are not athletes (van Leeuwen and colleagues, 2016). Weight often changes in midlife; [weight and plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/weight-and-plantar-fasciitis/) covers what is known.
- **Stiffer calves and ankles.** In a study of 50 people with plantar fasciitis and 100 without, a stiff ankle was the strongest factor measured, with 23.3 times the odds (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). In 100 adults without foot problems, people around 80 had stiffer ankles, flatter feet and weaker toe muscles than people around 20 (Scott and colleagues, 2007).
- **A heel pad that gives less.** In an X-ray study of 70 people with heel pain and 200 without, the heel pad lost elasticity with age, and had lost more in people with heel pain (Prichasuk, 1994). A thinned fat pad causes its own kind of heel pain, covered in [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/).
- **A change in activity.** Starting a new walking or running plan, a new job on your feet, or a sudden jump in exercise can all add load quickly. A 2026 review lists rapid increases in physical activity among the things that raise the risk of overuse injuries such as plantar fasciitis in midlife women (Ansari and colleagues, 2026).

Long hours on your feet count too: spending most of the workday standing came with 3.6 times the odds in the same case-control study (Riddle and colleagues, 2003). Feet also tend to get a little flatter with age; see [do flat feet get worse with age](https://walkito.site/do-flat-feet-get-worse-with-age/).

Source: van Leeuwen KD, Rogers J, Winzenberg T, van Middelkoop M. Higher body mass index is associated with plantar fasciopathy/'plantar fasciitis': systematic review and meta-analysis of various clinical and imaging risk factors. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;50(16):972–981.
Source: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(5):872–877.
Source: Scott G, Menz HB, Newcombe L. Age-related differences in foot structure and function. Gait & Posture. 2007;26(1):68–75.
Source: Prichasuk S. The heel pad in plantar heel pain. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British). 1994;76(1):140–142.
Source: Ansari M, Hussain F, Shopon M, Ajmal H, Asif M, David S. Hormonal shifts and structural strain: a literature review of menopause and perimenopause in relation to overuse injuries and stress fractures. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2026;50(3):139–149.
Source: Chang AH, Rasmussen SZ, Jensen AE, Sørensen T, Rathleff MS. What do we actually know about a common cause of plantar heel pain? A scoping review of heel fat pad syndrome. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2022;15(1):60.

### Which exercises help plantar fasciitis around menopause?

No exercise study has looked at women in menopause on their own, so the best guide is the heel pain guideline for adults in general. Stretching the plantar fascia and calf gets the guideline’s top grade, **A**, and calf strength work gets a **B** (Koc and colleagues, 2023). These are the same starting doses as the main [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/) guide.

Do the first plantar fascia stretch sitting on the edge of the bed, before you stand: in a trial of 82 people, stretching before the first steps eased morning pain more than calf stretching alone (DiGiovanni and colleagues, 2003). In a trial of 48 people, slow heel raises with a towel under the toes eased pain faster than stretching alone at three months, and by twelve months both groups were even (Rathleff and colleagues, 2015). If any exercise takes your heel pain to 6 out of 10, stop for the day.

Strength work has a second reason in midlife. Muscle mass and balance tend to decline after menopause (Douglas-Harris and colleagues, 2026), and resistance training is one of the non-hormonal steps a 2026 review says is underused (Ansari and colleagues, 2026). Heel raises and balance work are a small, practical start. [Calf raises for plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/calf-raises-plantar-fasciitis/) goes deeper on the heel raise protocol.

- **Plantar fascia stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each foot): Sit down and cross the foot over the other knee. Pull the toes back until you feel the stretch in the arch, not the calf. Do the first one on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor. If crossing the leg is hard, loop a towel around the ball of the foot and pull gently instead.
- **Calf stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Put your hands on a wall. Keep the back leg straight, the back heel flat on the floor and the hips forward.
- **Soleus stretch** (2 holds of 30 seconds, each leg): Take the same position at the wall, keep the back heel flat on the floor, then bend the back knee until you feel the stretch lower down, near the heel. The soleus, the deeper calf muscle, only lets go with the knee bent.
- **Seated heel raises** (3 sets of 10, both feet): Sit with your feet flat and press up through the balls of your feet. Hands on the knees add resistance. With the knee bent, this mainly works the soleus, the deeper calf muscle. It is a gentle first step before the standing raises.
- **Heel raises with a towel** (4 sets of 10, each leg, with added weight): Stand on one foot on a step, with a rolled towel under your toes. Take three seconds to rise, hold for two at the top, and take three seconds to lower. At this level Walkito adds weight, such as a backpack. The towel is what makes this exercise work the plantar fascia and not just the calf. Hold a rail or wall for balance.
- **Single-leg hold** (3 holds of 20 seconds, each leg): Stand on one foot next to a counter and look at one fixed spot. Let the foot wobble. It is meant to, because that wobble is the foot doing the balancing. Lightly touch the counter with your fingertips if you need to.

Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
Source: DiGiovanni BF, Nawoczenski DA, Lintal ME, et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain: a prospective, randomized study. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American). 2003;85(7):1270–1277.
Source: Rathleff MS, Mølgaard CM, Fredberg U, et al. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2015;25(3):e292–e300.
Source: Douglas-Harris M, Wilkins R, Ramaskandhan J, Mankelow J, Branthwaite H. Menopause and plantar heel pain: findings from a series of focus groups exploring lived experience. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2026;19(2):e70154.
Source: Ansari M, Hussain F, Shopon M, Ajmal H, Asif M, David S. Hormonal shifts and structural strain: a literature review of menopause and perimenopause in relation to overuse injuries and stress fractures. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2026;50(3):139–149.

### Does HRT help plantar fasciitis?

**There is no trial of HRT for plantar fasciitis, so nobody can say whether it helps.** We searched for one and found none. HRT, also called menopausal hormone therapy, is used for menopause symptoms. It is not a recognized treatment for heel pain.

What exists is indirect. In the 2026 focus groups, some women said they noticed fewer foot pains on HRT (Douglas-Harris and colleagues, 2026). That is a report from a few people, not a measured result. Two small studies of the Achilles tendon found that active women on HRT had smaller tendons than active women not on it: one of 85 women (Cook and colleagues, 2007), and one of 14 pairs of identical twins, where the difference showed up only in the 5 physically active pairs (Finni and colleagues, 2009). Tendon size is not pain, and the Achilles is not the plantar fascia.

A 2026 review notes that HRT is not right for everyone, because of contraindications and each person’s balance of risks and benefits (Ansari and colleagues, 2026). Whether to take it depends on your menopause symptoms and health history. **That is a decision to make with your doctor.** Whatever you decide, the stretches and strength work on this page still apply.

Source: Douglas-Harris M, Wilkins R, Ramaskandhan J, Mankelow J, Branthwaite H. Menopause and plantar heel pain: findings from a series of focus groups exploring lived experience. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2026;19(2):e70154.
Source: Cook JL, Bass SL, Black JE. Hormone therapy is associated with smaller Achilles tendon diameter in active post-menopausal women. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2007;17(2):128–132.
Source: Finni T, Kovanen V, Ronkainen PH, et al. Combination of hormone replacement therapy and high physical activity is associated with differences in Achilles tendon size in monozygotic female twin pairs. Journal of Applied Physiology. 2009;106(4):1332–1337.
Source: Ansari M, Hussain F, Shopon M, Ajmal H, Asif M, David S. Hormonal shifts and structural strain: a literature review of menopause and perimenopause in relation to overuse injuries and stress fractures. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2026;50(3):139–149.

### How long does plantar fasciitis last in midlife?

About 90% of people with plantar fasciitis get better with non-surgical care such as stretching and insoles, though it often takes 3 to 6 months (Latt and colleagues, 2020). No study has looked at recovery in women going through menopause specifically.

For some people it lasts longer. In a follow-up of 174 people, 54% had no symptoms at follow-up, about 9 years after diagnosis on average, and the risk of still having it was higher in women and in people with pain in both heels (Hansen and colleagues, 2018). That is a reason to start the exercises early and keep them going, not a reason to expect the worst. [How long plantar fasciitis lasts](https://walkito.site/how-long-does-plantar-fasciitis-last/) has the full timeline.

If you are building up activity in midlife, for health or for weight, build up step by step rather than stopping: the guideline notes that plantar fasciitis usually starts after a change in weight-bearing activity (Koc and colleagues, 2023). [Walking with plantar fasciitis](https://walkito.site/walking-with-plantar-fasciitis/) explains how to build walking back up step by step.

Source: Latt LD, Jaffe DE, Tang Y, Taljanovic MS. Evaluation and treatment of chronic plantar fasciitis. Foot & Ankle Orthopaedics. 2020;5(1):2473011419896763.
Source: Hansen L, Krogh TP, Ellingsen T, Bolvig L, Fredberg U. Long-term prognosis of plantar fasciitis: a 5- to 15-year follow-up study of 174 patients with ultrasound examination. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(3):2325967118757983.
Source: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, et al. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.

### When is heel or foot pain in midlife something else?

Pain under the heel that is worst on your first steps in the morning and eases as you walk is the typical plantar fasciitis pattern. Other patterns point elsewhere:

- **Deep, bruise-like pain in the centre of the heel, worse barefoot on hard floors:** possibly the fat pad. See [heel fat pad syndrome](https://walkito.site/heel-fat-pad-syndrome/).
- **One arch slowly dropping, with pain or swelling on the inner ankle:** possibly the posterior tibial tendon. In a survey of 582 women over 40, 3.3% had early signs of this problem and none had been diagnosed (Kohls-Gatzoulis and colleagues, 2009). It is worth having checked early.
- **Pain that builds with activity and hurts when you squeeze the sides of the heel:** possibly a stress fracture. See [plantar fasciitis or stress fracture](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-vs-stress-fracture/).
- **Burning, tingling or numbness, or pain at night:** more likely a nerve problem. See [heel pain at night](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-at-night/).
- **Both heels hurting along with stiff, swollen joints elsewhere:** worth checking for an inflammatory joint condition.

If you take an aromatase inhibitor after breast cancer, new joint, muscle or foot pain is something to tell the team that prescribes it. A 2026 review lists aromatase inhibitor use among the factors that add to the risk of overuse injuries in midlife (Ansari and colleagues, 2026).

Source: Kohls-Gatzoulis J, Woods B, Angel JC, Singh D. The prevalence of symptomatic posterior tibialis tendon dysfunction in women over the age of 40 in England. Foot and Ankle Surgery. 2009;15(2):75–81.
Source: Ansari M, Hussain F, Shopon M, Ajmal H, Asif M, David S. Hormonal shifts and structural strain: a literature review of menopause and perimenopause in relation to overuse injuries and stress fractures. Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2026;50(3):139–149.

### See a clinician first if

- the pain started after a fall, a jump or a twist, or you cannot put weight on the foot
- it hurts when you squeeze the sides of the heel, or the pain keeps building with activity (possible stress fracture)
- one arch is dropping, or the inner ankle is painful or swollen
- the heel is swollen, red or warm, or you have a fever
- the pain is worse at night or at rest, or comes with burning, tingling or numbness
- both heels hurt along with stiff or swollen joints elsewhere
- you take an aromatase inhibitor and new joint or foot pain has started: tell the team that prescribes it
- one calf is painful and swollen (possible blood clot): get help the same day

### Doing it as a plan

Walkito is a heel and foot exercise app. It does not track hormones or menopause symptoms and gives no advice on HRT. It builds a plan from the stretches, calf strength work and balance exercises on this page, starting with seated versions on sore days.

#### Can menopause cause plantar fasciitis?

It might contribute, but no study has proven it. Plantar heel pain is most common in women around age 50, when menopause usually happens, and in one large study the peak in women was about twice the peak in men. Researchers describe a causal link as uncertain, and no study has measured the plantar fascia across menopause.

#### Why does plantar fasciitis peak in women around 50?

Nobody knows for sure. In Dutch records, new cases in women peaked at 11.23 per 1000 patient-years at age 50. Hormone changes may play a part, but so can things that often change at the same age: weight, stiffer calves and ankles, a less springy heel pad and new or heavier activity.

#### Can perimenopause cause heel pain?

Possibly, but it has not been shown for heel pain specifically. A review of 16 studies found that 71% of perimenopausal women report musculoskeletal pain, more than women who have not reached perimenopause. No study has looked at plantar fasciitis in perimenopause on its own, so if your heel hurts, the usual heel pain checks and exercises apply.

#### Does HRT help plantar fasciitis?

It is not known. No trial has tested HRT for plantar fasciitis. Some women in a 2026 focus group study said they noticed fewer foot pains on HRT, and small studies found differences in Achilles tendon size, but none measured heel pain. Whether HRT suits you is a decision to make with your doctor, based on your symptoms and health.

#### What is the best exercise for plantar fasciitis during menopause?

The same ones as at any age: plantar fascia and calf stretches, which the 2023 heel pain guideline grades A, and calf strength work, graded B. Slow heel raises with a towel under the toes eased pain faster than stretching alone in a 48-person trial. Strength work also supports muscle and balance, which tend to decline after menopause.

#### Is it plantar fasciitis or just aching feet from menopause?

Plantar fasciitis has a typical pattern: pain under the heel that is worst on your first steps in the morning or after sitting, and eases once you walk. General aches across both feet and other joints are a different pattern. If you are not sure, or several joints are stiff and swollen, see a clinician.

#### Does weight gain in menopause make plantar fasciitis worse?

A higher weight is linked to plantar fasciitis. In a review of 51 studies, a BMI over 27 came with 3.7 times the odds, mostly in people who are not athletes. Weight is one factor among several, though. In a long follow-up of 174 people, BMI did not predict who still had heel pain years later.

#### Will plantar fasciitis go away after menopause?

No study has followed heel pain through menopause, so there is no figure. For plantar fasciitis in general, about 90% of people get better with non-surgical care, often within 3 to 6 months. In a long follow-up, the risk of it lasting was higher in women and in people with pain in both heels.

## About Walkito

https://walkito.site/about/

Walkito is an exercise app for iPhone and Android for heel pain, plantar fasciitis and flat feet that adjusts to how your feet feel each morning. This page explains how the guides on this site are written and where their numbers come from. It also says what Walkito does not do, and how to tell us when something is wrong.

### Walkito at a glance

- **What it is:** an exercise app for heel pain, plantar fasciitis, flat feet and other foot and lower-leg pain.
- **Phones:** iPhone, on the [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6813076846), and Android, on [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.walkito.app).
- **Sessions:** 3, 5 or 10 minutes, at home. Walkito asks what you have, such as a towel or a step, and leaves out exercises that need anything else.
- **How often:** you pick 3, 5 or 7 training days a week. Each session adapts to how your morning went.
- **Progress:** a short test every 14 days.
- **Languages:** English, Russian, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and German.
- **Price:** free to download, with a yearly or weekly subscription inside the app. The App Store or Google Play shows the price in your currency before you subscribe.
- **Who makes it:** Rahim Hudaykulyyev and Rahman Bazarov, Walkito’s two co-founders.
- **What it is not:** a medical device. Walkito does not diagnose and does not replace a clinician.
- **Name:** Walkito is not related to walkito.com, a dog-walking service.

### What is Walkito?

Walkito is an iPhone and Android app that builds your exercise plan one week at a time around goals you can measure. It is not related to walkito.com, a dog-walking service.

There are five goals: pain-free mornings (morning pain at 1/10 or less for 14 days in a row), a 60-second arch hold, 25 single-leg calf raises, 30 seconds of balance on one leg, and a gap of less than 10% between your left and right sides. You start with up to three of them. If something hurts, pain comes first.

You pick 3, 5 or 7 training days a week and sessions of 3, 5 or 10 minutes. Each day's session adapts to how your morning went. Every 14 days, a short test shows whether your numbers are moving. Once you reach your first goal, the test comes every 28 days.

The plan has no fixed length. When you reach a goal, it moves to maintaining at a lower dose, and the next goal takes its place. That goes on for as long as you use Walkito. [How the plan works](https://walkito.site/program/).

Walkito is in English, Russian, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and German.

Walkito can also be used inside ChatGPT and Claude, where it answers with short exercise videos and a starter plan. [Walkito in ChatGPT and Claude](https://walkito.site/ai/).

### How we research

Walkito’s guides are built from more than 250 published studies and clinical guidelines. We read the full paper, not just the abstract, before a number goes on a page, and every grade and figure links to the study behind it, so you can open it and check. No licensed clinician has reviewed the guides yet.

Rahim Hudaykulyyev and Rahman Bazarov, Walkito’s two co-founders, write the guides on this site: [plantar fasciitis exercises](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/), [flat feet exercises](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-exercises/), [heel pain from running](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/) and [the evidence page](https://walkito.site/science/). We build them from clinical practice guidelines, randomized trials and systematic reviews. We don’t use blog posts, forums or other sites’ summaries as a source. When a summary cites a study, we go to the study.

Exercises and claims carry one of three evidence labels. **Strong** means a clinical guideline grades it highly, or several good trials agree. **Moderate** means at least one well-designed trial supports it. **Early** means the research is small or just starting: worth trying, and the label may change as more comes out. A popular rule that a trial tested and did not back is marked **Not supported**.

Walkito has no sponsors, no affiliate links and no paid placement. Nothing is on a page because someone paid for it. We recheck a page when new research on its topic comes out. Every guide follows five rules:

- **Every figure traces to a primary source.** That means a randomized trial, a meta-analysis or a clinical guideline. The source is printed and linked on the page that uses it. If we cannot trace a number to one, it does not go on the site. We have removed sentences for that reason.
- **The 2023 clinical practice guideline on heel pain is the reference point.** It comes from the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. It grades each intervention by how strong its evidence is, including the ones it advises against.
- **Qualifiers travel with the figures.** A three-month result is always printed with what happened at twelve months. Every claim about arch shape says which feet it was measured on.
- **Doses are Walkito’s own starting doses.** They show where Walkito’s exercises begin. They are not a prescription for you.
- **No promise of a cure.** The pages say what the research found and where its evidence stops.

### What does Walkito not do?

Walkito does not diagnose, does not treat, and does not replace a clinician. Walkito cannot tell you what is causing your pain. See a clinician first if:

- the pain followed an injury or a fall
- you cannot put weight on the foot, or you are limping
- it comes with numbness, tingling, burning, swelling or warmth
- the heel is red, or you have a fever or feel unwell
- it wakes you at night
- it is sharp, or getting worse despite easing the load
- squeezing the sides of the heel hurts, or the pain builds during runs after you increased your mileage; both can be signs of a stress fracture
- you have diabetes, reduced feeling in your feet or poor circulation
- both heels hurt and other joints are swollen or stiff
- it has not improved after several weeks of exercise and a lighter load
- one arch has flattened suddenly as an adult
- the arch stays flat even when the foot is off the ground

### Has a clinician reviewed Walkito’s guides?

No licensed clinician has reviewed Walkito’s guides yet. Rahim and Rahman write them from the published research cited on each page.

When a clinician does review them, this page will list their name, their credentials and what they checked. Until then, no page on this site claims a medical reviewer.

To report a mistake on this site, email hello@walkito.site. It might be a figure that does not match its source, a dose that reads wrong or a broken link. We correct the page itself.

Every page shows the date its content last changed. That date moves only when the content really changes.

Walkito’s [privacy policy](https://walkito.site/privacy/) explains what Walkito stores, what leaves your phone and how to delete it. In short, your plan and check-ins are saved to your account, and Apple Health data stays on your phone.

## Questions (https://walkito.site/faq/)

### What is Walkito?

Walkito is an exercise app for iPhone and Android for heel pain, plantar fasciitis and flat feet that adjusts to how your feet feel each morning. You pick three, five or seven training days a week and sessions of 3, 5 or 10 minutes. Walkito is not a medical device, and it is not related to walkito.com, a dog-walking service.

### Is Walkito available on Android?

Yes. Walkito is on Android, on Google Play, and on iPhone, on the App Store. On Android it reads Health Connect for steps, distance and sleep. The iPhone app reads Apple Health for steps, sleep and walking asymmetry. It also shows a Live Activity on the Lock Screen while a session runs. Walkito comes in English, Russian, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and German.

### Do I need an Apple Watch?

No, Walkito works without an Apple Watch. The step count, walking speed and walking asymmetry it uses come from the iPhone itself. A watch adds sleep and resting heart rate. Without one, the parts that need them stay quiet, such as a short night making the next session lighter. The rest of the plan works as normal.

### How many notifications will I get?

Walkito sends at most one notification a day, and nothing after 21:30. Most weeks, five is the limit. Only four kinds can go past it: a flare after a painful day, a big day on your feet, a change in your walking, and a test day. You can turn notifications off in your phone’s settings, on iPhone or Android, and the plan works the same.

### Will Walkito nag me if I stop using it?

No, Walkito backs off when you stop opening its messages. After three unopened notifications in a row, reminders drop to two a week. After seven, it goes quiet for a month and then sends one message. Then it stays quiet unless you come back on your own. Opening Walkito at any time resets the count.

### How does the streak work?

The Walkito streak counts showing up, not finishing workouts. A day counts if you logged your morning pain, finished a session, or the plan gave you a rest day. A rest day the plan set can never break your streak. So choosing three training days a week costs you nothing.

### What happens to my streak if I have a bad week?

A bad week does not have to end your streak, because Walkito gives you freezes. You earn one freeze for each week on the plan and can hold two at a time. A missed day uses one by itself. If the streak does end, Walkito never shows it as a failure. The number simply starts again.

### How long does the Walkito plan last?

The Walkito plan has no fixed length. It lasts as long as you use it. Walkito builds one week at a time around a focus goal, such as pain-free mornings or a 60-second arch hold. When you reach a goal, it moves to maintaining at a lower dose, and the next goal takes its place. [How the plan works](https://walkito.site/program/).

### How long is a session?

A Walkito session takes 5 minutes by default, and you can switch any session to 3 or 10. Each session has 2 to 4 exercises. The exercise for the week’s focus goal always stays in, even in the 3-minute version. A test day takes about four minutes and has no training in it.

### How many days a week do I train?

You choose to train three, five or seven days a week. Strength days never fall back to back. With five days, mobility and balance sessions fill the gaps, and seven days adds a recovery session. The other days are rest the plan sets, and a planned rest day never breaks your streak.

### Do I need any equipment?

No, you don’t need to buy anything to start Walkito. During setup, Walkito asks what you have at home: a step or stairs, a resistance band, a towel, a pillow or a massage ball. Exercises that need something you don’t have are left out of your plan. You can also answer “None of these”.

### What happens if I miss a few days?

Nothing is owed when you miss a few days, and nothing piles up. The week runs on dates, not attendance, so a missed session is not moved to tomorrow and there is no catch-up screen. What you did log still counts. Next week is built from how your sessions felt and from your morning pain.

### Do I need to log pain every day for the plan to work?

No, but the plan can only respond to what you log. A logged morning is what lets Walkito ease a bad day. The pain-free mornings goal also needs 14 mornings in a row at 1/10 or less, so a morning you skip breaks that run. With nothing logged, the day runs as the week planned it.

### What do the tests measure?

Walkito’s tests measure three things in about four minutes: calf raises to failure on each leg, how long you can hold your arch, and single-leg balance. The calf raises also show the gap between your left and right side. Tests come every 14 days, then every 28 once you reach your first goal. Goals are judged on these numbers and your morning pain.

### What happens when I reach a goal?

When you reach a goal, it moves to maintaining and the next goal takes its place. A maintained goal keeps a spot in your plan at a lower dose, so the work that got you there goes on. Tests move from every 14 days to every 28 once you reach your first goal.

### How long before I notice a difference?

No one can honestly promise a day, but one trial gives a guide. In a trial of 48 people with plantar fasciitis, all wearing shoe inserts, the group doing heavy heel raises was clearly ahead of the stretching group at three months. By twelve months the two groups were even. Your own tests show your numbers as they change.

### Is strength training better than stretching for plantar fasciitis?

Strength training works faster than stretching, but not better in the long run. In a trial of 48 people with plantar fasciitis confirmed by ultrasound, all wearing shoe inserts, heavy heel raises were clearly ahead at three months. By twelve months the groups were even. The 2023 guideline gives stretching an A, its top grade, and strength training a B. Walkito uses both.

### Can exercise change flat feet?

Exercise can measurably change flexible flat feet, where the arch comes back when the foot is off the ground. In a trial of 52 people with flexible flat feet, a six-week exercise program improved the arch more than in the control group. Rigid flat feet are structural, and exercise will not change their shape. The exercises are in [flat feet exercises](https://walkito.site/flat-feet-exercises/).

### How long do arch exercises take to work?

Arch exercises need six weeks or more, going by the trials. In a trial of flexible flat feet, six weeks of short-foot work (pulling the ball of the foot toward the heel so the arch lifts), hip work and stretching changed the arch more than control. A 2024 review of short-foot work alone found no significant difference overall. One arch measure improved only in programs longer than six weeks.

### Can Walkito tell me what is wrong with my foot?

No, Walkito cannot tell you what is causing your pain. It is an exercise plan. It does not diagnose, and it does not treat. See a clinician for pain that is sharp, getting worse, keeping you up at night, or that started after an injury. The warning signs are listed in [the heel pain guide](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/#see-a-clinician).

### Does the plan change if my pain gets worse?

Yes, Walkito changes the plan the same morning. A morning pain of 7/10 or more turns the day into about three minutes of seated work. A morning three points above your average for the past week steps each exercise back a level. Pain of 6/10 or more during a session ends it and steps the next two back. A good morning never speeds the plan up.

### Can I keep running while I do Walkito?

Yes, you can keep running while you do Walkito. The plan adjusts to your load instead of asking you to stop. When yesterday was a big day on your feet, today’s strength session becomes a lighter recovery one. Sharp pain, or pain that keeps getting worse, needs a clinician. More in [heel pain from running](https://walkito.site/heel-pain-runners/).

### Should I rest completely when my heel hurts?

Walkito’s answer is to change the load on your heel, not to stop everything. The 2023 guideline recommends learning to adjust the load on your feet in daily life, at work and in sport. It grades that advice E, which means it rests on theory, not trials. On a bad day, keep the stretches and drop the loaded work. In Walkito, a 7/10 morning or worse becomes three minutes of seated work.

### Do insoles and orthotics help heel pain?

The 2023 heel pain guideline advises against orthotics on their own for short-term pain relief, with a grade B. It says they may be used alongside other care, with a grade C, which means weaker evidence. Walkito does not recommend them as the only answer and does not sell any. The full table of grades is in [the heel pain guide](https://walkito.site/plantar-fasciitis-exercises/).

### Will the pain come back?

Heel pain can come back, and Walkito does not promise it won’t. What Walkito does is keep going after the pain stops. A reached goal moves to maintaining and keeps a place in the plan at a lower dose. Tests go on every 28 days once you reach your first goal, so you can see if your numbers start to slip.

### Does uneven walking mean I am injured?

Walkito never reads uneven walking as a sign of injury. Walking asymmetry is the percentage of time your steps with one foot are faster or slower than your steps with the other foot. Walkito compares it, as the iPhone estimates it, only with your own earlier readings, never with other people.

Walkito can tell you that your walking has changed. It will never tell you what that means or that you are injured. If something feels wrong, ask a clinician.

### Is my health data uploaded anywhere?

Walkito uploads what you log, but not your Apple Health data. Apple Health readings, from steps to sleep, stay on your iPhone. Your plan and what you log are copied to your Walkito account: pain scores, where it hurts, sessions, pain during sessions, test results and daily app time. That copy restores your plan and shows how the plan is used. See the [privacy policy](https://walkito.site/privacy/).

### Which Apple Health permissions does Walkito ask for?

On iPhone, Walkito asks Apple Health to read step count, walking speed, walking asymmetry, flights climbed, heart rate, resting heart rate, active energy, sleep and workouts, and to write workouts and mindful minutes. On Android, it reads steps, distance and sleep from Health Connect. Every permission is optional, and you can withdraw it in your phone’s settings. The plan keeps working without them. It just adapts less to your day.

### Does Walkito work offline?

Yes, Walkito works offline after setup. Setup needs a connection once, to sign you in with Apple, or with email if you already have an account. After that, everything saves on the phone first, and nothing in the daily flow waits for the network. What you log is copied to your Walkito account in the background when you are online.

### What happens to my plan if I get a new phone?

Your plan comes back when you sign in to the same Walkito account on the new phone, because your plan and what you log are saved to that account. To get a purchase back on iPhone, sign in with the same Apple ID and tap Restore Purchases in Walkito. On Android, use the same Google account in Google Play and the subscription comes back.

A subscription bought on iPhone does not carry over to Android, or the other way round, because Apple and Google bill separately. Apple Health readings are not part of that copy, because they stay on the phone.

### How do I delete my Walkito account and data?

Delete your account in Walkito under Profile, then Delete account. That removes your account from Walkito’s server with everything saved to it, and clears the phone. It cannot be undone. Deleting only the app leaves your account in place. Neither one cancels a subscription, which only Apple or Google can do. You can also write to hello@walkito.site.

### How much does Walkito cost?

Walkito is free to download, with a yearly or weekly subscription inside the app. The price is set by the store you buy from, the App Store on iPhone or Google Play on Android, which shows it in your currency before you subscribe. Both subscriptions renew on their own until you cancel, and the price the store shows is the one that applies.

### How do I cancel my Walkito subscription?

Cancel a Walkito subscription on your iPhone in Settings → your name → Subscriptions, at least 24 hours before the period ends. Canceling stops the next renewal, and you keep access until the end of the period you paid for.

On Android, open the Google Play app, tap your profile icon, then Payments & subscriptions → Subscriptions → Walkito → Cancel subscription; you also keep access until the end of the paid period.

Deleting the app or your account does not cancel it. Refunds are handled by the store: Apple on iPhone, Google Play on Android.
